lessons.title: Vessels: wall identification, microcirculation and development
lessons.summary: Read arteries, veins and exchange vessels from lumen to wall, then distinguish endothelial development from mural-cell recruitment.
lessons.section: Circulatory System — Histology of Blood Vessels

steps.title: Orient from the lumen, but do not let its shape make the diagnosis
steps.body:
First find a plausible lumen and trace a continuous endothelial boundary where visible. Move outward through the wall, identifying its cellular and extracellular components. Survey nearby vessels, surrounding organ and the plane of section. A round empty space without a convincing wall could be a tear or another structure.

A vein often collapses and an artery often retains a more regular profile, but neither is a rule that substitutes for wall analysis. Oblique sections exaggerate dimensions; contraction can make the luminal border corrugated; processing can wash away blood. Compare the wall with the lumen and with neighbouring structures rather than diagnosing from shape or red cells alone.

practice.prompt: An empty irregular channel contains no red cells. Is it necessarily a lymphatic?
practice.feedback: No. Blood can be lost during preparation, and a vein can collapse. Trace the wall, context and additional features before assigning identity.

steps.title: Intima, media and adventitia are compartments with different jobs
steps.body:
The intima includes endothelium on its basal lamina and variable subendothelial tissue. In many muscular arteries, an internal elastic lamina marks the boundary toward the media. The media contains circumferentially arranged smooth muscle and extracellular matrix; its proportions differ by vessel class. The adventitia blends with surrounding connective tissue and provides support, nerves and, in sufficiently large vessels, nourishing vessels.

Do not force three equally thick rings onto every vessel. Capillaries do not have a continuous muscular media; small vessels may have no sharply separable adventitia. An endothelial nucleus is evidence about the lining, not proof that the whole adjacent wall is endothelial.

practice.prompt: Which compartment is most directly responsible for active reduction of an arteriole’s radius?
practice.feedback: The smooth-muscle media. Endothelium regulates signals, but the circumferential contractile cells generate the wall movement.

steps.title: Elastic arteries distribute pulsatile energy through their media
steps.body:
In an elastic artery, multiple elastic lamellae alternate with smooth-muscle cells and other matrix within a thick media. Stretch during ventricular ejection and recoil between beats help buffer pulsatile pressure and maintain forward flow. Elastic tissue is therefore distributed through the media, not confined to a single border line.

An elastic stain makes lamellar organisation easier to follow than routine H&E. Examine several wall regions because tangential cutting, breaks and folds can distort the pattern. Large-vessel walls also require their own nutrient supply: vasa vasorum support outer regions beyond easy diffusion from luminal blood. Their presence does not mean that the large vessel’s lumen branches directly into every visible small vessel in that section.

practice.prompt: How does an elastic artery differ from a muscular artery with a prominent internal elastic lamina?
practice.feedback: Numerous medial elastic lamellae form a distributed elastic framework. One conspicuous boundary lamina alone does not establish an elastic artery.

steps.title: Muscular arteries: identify the media and its boundaries
steps.body:
A muscular artery has a media dominated by smooth-muscle layers. A conspicuous internal elastic lamina may form a wavy line, especially in a contracted vessel; an external elastic lamina may also be identifiable in larger examples. The adventitia contains collagen and elastic fibres but is not simply an extra smooth-muscle layer.

In transverse sections, circumferential smooth-muscle cells can show elongated nuclei following the wall. Do not equate every dark medial line with elastin: nuclei, folds and stain deposits can mimic boundaries. Where classification is uncertain, compare an elastic preparation and the broader wall pattern rather than counting arbitrary pink rings.

practice.prompt: A vessel has many smooth-muscle layers and one prominent wavy internal border. Which interpretation is favoured?
practice.feedback: A muscular artery, provided the whole wall supports it. Multiple elastic lamellae throughout the media would instead support an elastic artery.

steps.title: Veins: consider capacitance, wall composition and valves
steps.body:
Compared with a companion artery, a vein commonly has a larger irregular lumen and a less dominant media; its adventitia can be the conspicuous supporting layer. Some large veins contain substantial longitudinal smooth muscle in the adventitia. Thus, “veins have no muscle” and “veins always have a thin total wall” are poor rules.

Venous valves, where present, are folds of intima with connective-tissue cores covered by endothelium. They support directional flow when pressure gradients reverse, often working with external muscle compression. Not every vein contains valves and a random section can miss them. A free flap or tear should not be called a valve without its attachment and tissue continuity.

practice.prompt: Does an absent valve profile exclude a vein?
practice.feedback: No. Valves are not universal and may lie outside the section plane. Use the wall and anatomical context, not a single absent feature.

steps.title: Arterioles and venules: read the wall rather than a size label
steps.body:
An arteriole has a small lumen surrounded by a limited number of smooth-muscle layers; very small examples may have only one. This cuff changes radius and therefore strongly influences resistance. The smallest arterioles may lack an obvious internal elastic lamina. Size varies with plane and contraction, so it is safer to combine dimensions with wall organisation.

A postcapillary venule has endothelium with associated support cells but lacks the continuous muscular coat of an arteriole. Larger venules acquire more smooth muscle. Postcapillary venules are important sites of leukocyte trafficking; the detailed mechanisms depend on tissue and inflammatory context. A universal diagram of a precapillary sphincter at every capillary entrance would oversimplify real microvascular networks.

practice.prompt: Two small profiles are similar in diameter, but only one has a continuous smooth-muscle cuff. What discriminates them?
practice.feedback: The organised muscular wall favours an arteriole. Diameter alone is insufficient, especially if contraction or an oblique plane changes the profile.

steps.title: Capillaries: distinguish the lining from its mural support
steps.body:
A capillary is an endothelial tube supported by basal lamina, with associated pericytes in many tissues. It lacks a continuous smooth-muscle media. Endothelial nuclei may bulge toward a narrow lumen, and a red cell can occupy much of that lumen. A nearby nucleus is not automatically a pericyte: its relationship to the endothelial tube and shared basal-lamina environment needs evidence.

Endothelium is biologically active, controlling barrier properties, signalling and interactions with blood. Pericytes contribute to vessel organisation and stability in context-dependent ways. Distinguish cell identity, position and function; a single routine section rarely proves all three.

practice.prompt: Can you call every nucleus beside a capillary a pericyte?
practice.feedback: No. Nearby fibroblasts and other cells can resemble it. Position, appropriate markers and higher-resolution structural evidence are needed.

steps.title: Continuous, fenestrated and sinusoidal vessels answer different exchange needs
steps.body:
Continuous capillaries retain an uninterrupted endothelial lining and basal lamina, though their permeability varies greatly between organs. Fenestrated capillaries have transcellular openings adapted to exchange; many fenestrae have diaphragms, whereas glomerular fenestrae are a notable exception. Sinusoidal or discontinuous arrangements have wider, more irregular channels and tissue-specific discontinuities.

These are not interchangeable holes of increasing size. The endothelial junctions, glycocalyx, basal lamina and surrounding cells all contribute to the barrier. Liver sinusoids and renal glomerular capillaries therefore have different architecture and functions. Ordinary H&E can suggest an organ’s vascular pattern but cannot resolve individual fenestrae or their diaphragms; ultrastructure is required for that claim.

practice.prompt: A learner identifies individual endothelial fenestrae on a low-power H&E image. What is wrong with the claim?
practice.feedback: The resolution is insufficient. Organ context may suggest a capillary class, but the pores and diaphragms require appropriate ultrastructural evidence.

steps.title: Lymphatic versus blood vessel: build a differential
steps.body:
Small lymphatic channels often have thin, irregular walls and can appear empty. Larger collecting lymphatics can have valves and smooth muscle, so the phrase “lymphatics have no muscle” does not apply at every level. A thin wall or absent red cells is only a clue.

Follow the channel through the tissue and inspect its lining and contents. In uncertain cases, use appropriate endothelial-marker panels and anatomical context rather than a single stain result. A damaged blood vessel, collapsed venule or processing cleft can imitate part of the appearance. The honest conclusion from an inadequate section may be “thin-walled channel, identity unresolved.”

practice.prompt: What is a better practical answer than “empty, so lymphatic”?
practice.feedback: Describe the thin irregular lining, wall and tissue context, name a collapsed venule or cleft as an alternative, and state what additional evidence would distinguish them.

steps.title: Use stains and controls to answer one wall question at a time
steps.body:
H&E shows the overall relationship of nuclei, media and connective tissue. Elastic stains can clarify internal elastic laminae and medial lamellae; trichrome preparations help compare collagen-rich regions with muscle. PAS can highlight carbohydrate-rich structures, including some basement-membrane regions, but positive staining is not specific to one molecule.

Immunostains add molecular evidence but require controls and context. A smooth-muscle-associated marker is not a lineage tracer, and some markers are shared by activated stromal cells or immature populations. Keep adjacent sections aligned when comparing stains: a different plane may change the structure being compared. The correct preparation and control are part of the interpretation, not administrative details.

practice.prompt: A stain highlights an elastic network. Does it measure the living vessel’s compliance directly?
practice.feedback: No. It displays a structural component. Mechanical behaviour also depends on organisation, collagen, smooth-muscle tone, geometry and the conditions of measurement.

steps.title: Relate wall geometry to function without reading pressure from a slide
steps.body:
The media’s arrangement permits circumferential contraction, while elastin and collagen contribute differently to passive wall behaviour. Small changes in arteriolar radius can substantially alter resistance; veins can hold changing blood volumes with relatively small pressure changes over part of their operating range. These are functional principles, not measurements obtainable from a fixed specimen alone.

Fixation, contraction, loss of pressure and cutting angle change the apparent lumen and wall thickness. A section does not provide the original in-vivo pressure or compliance curve. State the structural feature that supports a function, then separate that inference from an actual physiological measurement.

practice.prompt: Can a narrow fixed lumen prove high resistance in the living patient?
practice.feedback: No. The specimen’s geometry may reflect processing or contraction. Structure supports a physiological explanation, but in-vivo resistance requires additional measurements.

steps.title: Build an endothelial network: vasculogenesis, sprouting and remodelling
steps.body:
Vasculogenesis describes formation of vessels from endothelial precursors; angiogenesis describes new vascular growth from existing vessels. Early endothelial assemblies establish a primitive network, which is then connected, remodelled and stabilised. Sprouting is one angiogenic mode, not a synonym for every vascular developmental process.

Network development requires more than producing endothelial cells. Cells must organise a patent lumen, connect to other segments, establish tissue-appropriate barriers and recruit support. Flow and local signals can alter which branches enlarge or regress. Distinguish an endothelial marker-positive cord from a perfused vessel: the second claim requires evidence of lumen continuity and flow.

practice.prompt: Does a cluster of endothelial-marker-positive cells prove that a functional vessel has formed?
practice.feedback: No. Identity, tubular organisation, connection, perfusion and stability are different developmental outcomes.

steps.title: VEGF and DLL4–Notch: separate a sprouting signal from branch organisation
steps.body:
A sprouting front is not made of equivalent cells all extending equally. In experimental systems, VEGF-responsive leading endothelial cells interact with neighbours through DLL4–Notch signalling, helping regulate the balance between leading and trailing behaviours. These are responsive cell states rather than permanent unrelated cell lineages.

Suchting and colleagues found increased tip-like features and branching after reducing Dll4 activity in their model, with the response dependent on VEGF signalling. This supports a role for DLL4 in restraining aspects of sprouting. It does not show that more branches always improve tissue perfusion, nor does it provide a clinical instruction to inhibit Notch.

practice.prompt: Why might “more branches” fail to mean “better blood supply”?
practice.feedback: Branch count does not establish connected lumens, productive flow, barrier integrity or stability. Measure the outcome being claimed.

steps.title: Recruit mural support: what the PDGF-B experiment can and cannot isolate
steps.body:
Endothelial–mural-cell communication helps organise the vessel wall. PDGF-B signalling contributes to pericyte recruitment and association with developing microvessels. Its local availability can matter as well as whether the protein is present.

Lindblom and colleagues altered the PDGF-B retention motif and observed defective pericyte investment, including partially detached cells. The mutant also had reduced expression, so the result is not a perfectly isolated test of spatial localisation at identical dose. A careful interpretation separates the proposed matrix-retention mechanism from the combined changes actually produced by the mutation. This is a useful example of why a mechanistic explanation needs both experimental design and limits.

practice.prompt: What extra control would strengthen a claim that localisation alone caused the phenotype?
practice.feedback: Compare conditions with matched biologically active ligand amounts while varying retention or distribution. Otherwise altered dose remains a competing contributor.

steps.title: Keep endothelial ancestry separate from smooth-muscle ancestry
steps.body:
A vessel is assembled from interacting compartments, not from one cell population that simply acquires three tunics. The endothelial tube and its surrounding mural and connective-tissue cells can have different developmental histories. Ask which compartment a lineage label occupies and which markers distinguish it.

In the proximal arterial wall, Harmon and Nakano demonstrated regional second-heart-field and neural-crest smooth-muscle contributions. The distribution depended on the vessel and region examined; it should not be turned into one rule for the entire circulation. A labelled arterial wall cell also does not establish the lineage of the adjacent endothelial cell.

practice.prompt: A lineage reporter marks aortic medial cells. Does that prove the endothelium has the same origin?
practice.feedback: No. Identify the labelled compartment and combine the reporter with cell-type evidence. Adjacent structures can have distinct origins.

steps.title: Coronary development illustrates multiple endothelial routes
steps.body:
Coronary vessels supply the heart, but their endothelial lining is not simply an extension of cardiac muscle. Chen and colleagues used mouse lineage approaches to identify regionally different endothelial contributions, including a sinus-venosus route and endocardial contributions. Perturbing VEGF-C affected the studied routes differently.

The useful lesson is to distinguish anatomical source, labelled progeny, territory and signalling requirement. A reporter’s specificity and induction timing shape the observed map. A mouse regional fate map is not a universal human timetable, and an endothelial-origin result should not be reused as proof of the smooth-muscle wall’s origin.

practice.prompt: What must be specified before saying “coronary cells come from the sinus venosus”?
practice.feedback: The cell type, species, labelled population, induction timing and coronary territory. The statement is too broad without those boundaries.

steps.title: Use a developmental experiment to distinguish identity from function
steps.body:
A useful study can combine lineage tracing, cell-type markers, three-dimensional structure and functional readouts. Each contributes a different piece: ancestry, current phenotype, organisation and performance. None is a complete substitute for the others. A permanent lineage reporter can remain after the initiating gene has stopped being expressed.

When reading a developmental paper, write down the perturbation, control, stage, anatomical site and measured endpoint. Ask whether the experiment changed cell number, position, maturation, survival or function. A missing mature vessel at one time point could follow several different earlier defects; follow-up stages or rescue experiments may distinguish them.

practice.prompt: What would help distinguish delayed vessel maturation from permanent failure?
practice.feedback: Compare appropriately staged observations and functional endpoints over time. A single early image cannot establish the final outcome.

steps.title: Give a lumen-to-wall identification with an explicit alternative
steps.body:
A strong practical answer names the preparation and plane, traces the lining, describes the media and adventitia, and uses those observations to classify the vessel. Add the structure–function link: distributed elastic lamellae for recoil, a muscular cuff for resistance control, or a thin endothelial barrier for exchange.

Then state what remains unresolved. A torn thin-walled region cannot be rescued by a filename that says “vein”; an uncalibrated image cannot supply an exact diameter; an ordinary section cannot show endothelial fenestrae. The developmental extension should name the endothelial and mural compartments separately and explain which experiment supports a proposed origin.

practice.prompt: An image title says “artery and vein,” but the adjacent thin wall is torn. What should you publish as the interpretation?
practice.feedback: Identify only the sufficiently preserved structures, explain the damaged region and withhold the clean artery–vein comparison claim. Source titles do not override visible evidence.

question.prompt: Which feature most clearly separates a capillary from an arteriole?

options.reason: Both vessel types can contain blood.

options.text: Absence of a continuous smooth-muscle media
options.reason: Correct: an arteriole has a muscular cuff; a capillary does not.

options.text: A connective-tissue adventitia thicker than the media
options.reason: This is more useful when comparing larger veins and arteries.

recall.prompt: How does wall structure support the function of an elastic artery?
recall.answer: Elastic lamellae stretch during ejection and recoil afterward, helping maintain flow between beats. The layered wall therefore contributes to pressure buffering.

objectives: Identify vessel classes by lining, media, adventitia and section context.
Distinguish structural clues from artefact and missing evidence.
Relate elastic, muscular and exchange architectures to function.
Choose stains and resolution appropriate to the claimed structure.
Separate vasculogenesis, sprouting, remodelling and mural-cell recruitment.
Interpret regional endothelial and smooth-muscle lineage experiments with their limits.
summaryChecklist: I trace the wall from the lumen instead of naming it from shape alone.
I distinguish elastic lamellae, smooth-muscle layers and collagenous support.
I can explain why absent red cells and missing valves are inconclusive.
I separate H&E observations from ultrastructural and functional claims.
I distinguish endothelial network formation from mural support and regional lineage.

oralExamination.prompt: Compare an elastic artery, muscular artery and vein in a practical.
oralExamination.answer: Start at the lumen, identify the intima, then compare media and adventitia. Distributed medial elastic lamellae support elastic-artery recoil; smooth-muscle-dominant media supports a muscular artery. A companion vein often has a larger irregular lumen and less dominant media, but contraction and section plane must be considered.

oralExamination.prompt: How is a vascular wall assembled during development?
oralExamination.answer: Endothelial differentiation and network formation are followed by context-dependent remodelling and support-cell interactions. Endothelial and mural cells can have different regional origins. A marker-positive cord is not yet proof of a stable perfused vessel.

workedExample.title: Two similar lumens, different wall evidence
workedExample.prompt: Two small circular vascular profiles have similar diameters. One has a continuous muscle cuff; the other has only a thin lining and scattered nearby nuclei. Explain the distinction and its limits.
solution: The continuous circumferential muscle cuff supports an arteriole; diameter alone does not decide.
The thin-walled profile could be an exchange vessel or venule depending on size, context and further views.
Do not assign every nearby nucleus to a pericyte without positional or molecular evidence.
A fixed section cannot establish live flow, pressure or developmental origin.

lessons.subject: histology
lessons.title: Lymphoid organs: practical identification, routes and developmental origins
lessons.summary: Identify lymphoid organs from architecture, interpret cells and germinal centres, and connect lymph-node stromal development with experimental evidence. Practise on a credited specimen and explain each identification from visible relationships.
lessons.section: Original preparation, identification and developmental teaching with section-level reference mapping

steps.title: Start with a map of the whole section
steps.body:
An isolated round, blue-purple cell collection is not an organ diagnosis. First inspect the outer boundary, any mucosal surface, the arrangement of pale and dark regions, and their relation to vessels. Ask whether the repeated unit is a follicle, a cortex–medulla lobule, or lymphoid tissue next to a surface. Then seek a second independent landmark. A germinal centre occurs in several secondary lymphoid tissues; its presence does not uniquely identify a lymph node. A pale thymic medulla is not a germinal centre. State the tissue-level conclusion before trying to infer a disease.

Try it: Compare a follicle with a thymic lobule: which surrounding boundary would you inspect?

steps.title: Lymph node: orient capsule, follicles, paracortex and medulla
steps.body:
Trace the connective-tissue capsule and look immediately beneath it for the subcapsular sinus. Follicles lie in the outer cortex. The deeper paracortex is a predominantly T-cell region, with high endothelial venules; it is not simply another B-cell follicle. In the medulla distinguish cellular cords from the intervening lymph sinuses. Cords may contain plasma cells, B lymphocytes and macrophages. The distinction is tissue versus passage, not merely dark versus light. A limited core may omit the capsule or hilum; report that sampling limit rather than asserting that the whole organ lacks them.

Try it: Mark a cellular cord and its adjacent sinus as different structures.

steps.title: A follicle is a structure within an organ
steps.body:
Use follicle for a rounded lymphoid compartment, not for an entire lymph node. In a primary follicle, small lymphocytes form a relatively uniform dense population. A secondary follicle contains a germinal centre surrounded by a mantle of smaller lymphocytes. The change in nuclear size, cytoplasm and cellular density helps explain the paler centre; it is not an empty lumen. A section through the edge of a three-dimensional follicle may miss its centre. Before classifying every dark profile as primary, inspect adjacent fields and, when available, levels.

Tonsils and spleen can also contain follicles. First establish the larger tissue relationship: capsule and sinuses, mucosal surface and crypts, or an arteriole-associated white-pulp island. Only then classify the follicle. This prevents a correct recognition of a germinal centre from becoming an incorrect organ identification.

practice.prompt: A round dark profile has no pale centre in one section. What is the strongest defensible statement?
practice.feedback: The sampled profile lacks an obvious germinal centre. A primary follicle is possible, but an off-centre cut and limited sampling must be considered before excluding a secondary follicle.

steps.title: Use nucleus, cytoplasm and neighbourhood to recognise cells
steps.body:
At higher magnification, a small lymphocyte has a dense rounded nucleus and little visible cytoplasm. A plasma cell instead combines an eccentric nucleus, coarse chromatin, basophilic cytoplasm and a pale perinuclear Golgi region. Its abundant secretory machinery fits antibody production. A plasmablast is typically larger, with more conspicuous nucleolar activity; one feature alone is insufficient. Look for plasma cells in the cellular medullary cords rather than assuming every cell in a pale sinus is one.

A macrophage containing ingested nuclear debris can interrupt the densely cellular germinal-centre field. Describe the visible debris and surrounding architecture before applying a name. These are high-power tasks: the overview photograph below does not resolve all these features. Nuclear darkness alone cannot distinguish B from T lymphocytes.

practice.prompt: Why is an eccentric nucleus alone insufficient to identify a plasma cell?
practice.feedback: Combine nuclear position and chromatin with basophilic cytoplasm, the perinuclear Golgi region and the tissue setting; other cells and section planes can mimic a single feature.

steps.title: Connect germinal-centre zones to a process, not a colour code
steps.body:
Germinal-centre B cells proliferate and diversify their antigen receptors, then compete for selection. In the light-zone environment, a B cell captures antigen retained on follicular dendritic cells, internalises it and presents peptide–MHC II to follicular helper T cells. Help can support renewed proliferation in the dark zone. The original antigen recognised by the B-cell receptor and the processed peptide recognised by the T cell are different presentations of the same response.

Victora and colleagues spatially marked cells using a photoactivatable reporter and followed them by multiphoton microscopy in mice. Movement and antigen-presentation perturbations supported selective return from light to dark zone. Thus, the zones are connected stages of a cycling population, not sealed boxes or a compulsory one-way conveyor. A fixed section cannot reveal a particular cell’s trajectory or receptor affinity.

practice.prompt: Which evidence would distinguish cell movement between zones from two populations merely occupying different zones?
practice.feedback: Follow marked cells over time, with appropriate controls for the marking and imaging method. A single immunostained section provides localisation rather than a trajectory.

steps.title: How selection changes the next proliferative round
steps.body:
Selection does more than allow a B cell to remain alive. In Gitlin and colleagues’ mouse experiments, selectively increasing antigen presentation to helper T cells changed subsequent cell-cycle behaviour. The selected germinal-centre B cells progressed faster through the cycle, including DNA synthesis, while preserving the relative order of replication-origin activation. More help could therefore change both time spent in a proliferative compartment and the pace of proliferation.

The experiment compared targeted antigen with an irrelevant-antigen control and used cell-cycle readouts; it did not infer division speed from how dark a germinal centre looked. Connect this result to affinity maturation as selective expansion of variants, rather than antigen intentionally designing a better receptor. Continue to the antibody-mutation lesson for the distinction between variable-region diversification and constant-region switching.

practice.prompt: Would more cells in a dark zone alone prove a faster cell cycle?
practice.feedback: No. Recruitment, residence time, survival and cycling can all affect abundance. A time-resolved cell-cycle measurement is needed to distinguish them.

steps.title: Separate the scaffold, stromal cells and antigen-presenting cells
steps.body:
Reticular fibres are extracellular matrix; reticular cells are living cells. A silver stain can highlight the supporting fibre network without proving the identity of every adjacent cell. Follicular dendritic cells are specialised stromal cells of the B-cell compartment. Their name describes a branched appearance and does not make them interchangeable with conventional dendritic cells that activate T cells through processed peptide presentation.

In a follicle, distinguish antigen retained for B-cell recognition from peptide–MHC presentation to T cells. B cells themselves process captured antigen and present peptide to follicular helper T cells. These relationships explain why several interacting populations occupy a germinal centre. They cannot all be labelled reliably from the size and darkness of nuclei in a low-power photograph.

practice.prompt: Does a black reticular network on a silver preparation identify every follicular dendritic cell?
practice.feedback: No. It demonstrates a matrix pattern. Cell-type localisation requires an appropriate validated cell-identification method interpreted with tissue context.

steps.title: Follow a boundary before naming a pale space
steps.body:
A lymph-node sinus, a blood-vessel lumen, an adipocyte profile and a processing separation can all look pale at low power. Ask where the space lies, whether its boundary is continuous, what it contains, and how it connects to nearby structures. The subcapsular position is useful for a sinus; a recognisable vascular wall and luminal blood support a vessel. An empty-looking circle is not enough to call either.

Medullary cords are cellular tissue between sinuses. Do not turn every central pale region into a medullary sinus or every dark island into a follicle. Trace several neighbouring fields. When the available image cannot resolve the boundary, an explicit unresolved label is more accurate than a confident wrong one.

practice.prompt: What should you do when a low-power field cannot resolve whether a pale profile is a vessel or a sinus?
practice.feedback: Retain the differential and obtain a more informative view or preparation. Do not assign a vessel type from an empty appearance alone.

steps.title: Keep lymph drainage separate from lymphocyte entry from blood
steps.body:
Use two differently labelled routes. Lymph arriving from drained tissue enters through afferent lymphatics, then the subcapsular and deeper sinus system, before leaving through an efferent lymphatic at the hilum. Circulating lymphocytes can instead leave blood through specialised postcapillary high endothelial venules in the paracortex. An HEV is a blood vessel, not an afferent lymphatic. The paracortex is a cellular region containing vessels; it is not an extra sinus to insert into a flow mnemonic. Both routes can bring material or cells into the same organ while retaining distinct boundaries.

Try it: Trace one afferent-lymph path and one blood-to-tissue path without merging their entry vessels.

steps.title: Why the endothelium is called high—and what H&E cannot prove
steps.body:
HEV endothelial cells have a relatively plump appearance compared with the flattened endothelial profile familiar from many other vessels. This morphology can be useful when combined with location and the surrounding lymphoid organisation. It does not turn a single cuboidal profile into proof of a measured trafficking rate. The 2021 HEV review integrates anatomical, molecular and functional studies; an H&E identification exercise shows only a subset of that evidence. Similarly, a stain for one associated antigen is an assay result, not a complete functional demonstration.

Try it: Separate a directly visible endothelial profile from an inferred lymphocyte-migration function.

steps.title: Research bridge: a node is not a uniformly stirred bag
steps.body:
Roozendaal and colleagues used mouse lymph nodes and imaging approaches, including multiphoton intravital microscopy, to compare antigen transport. Their findings supported delivery of small soluble antigens through follicular conduits, whereas larger antigens followed different interactions involving subcapsular sinus macrophages and B cells. This gives a mechanistic reason to preserve spatial compartments when interpreting immune encounters. It does not establish a universal molecular-size cutoff for every antigen or a patient-specific transit time. Ordinary H&E cannot show the labelled-antigen trajectories measured in that experiment.

Try it: Name the experimental observation needed to support transport, beyond a still photograph of a follicle.

steps.title: Spleen: use the arteriole–white-pulp relationship
steps.body:
In spleen, look for white-pulp islands within red pulp rather than a peripheral cortical band surrounding a medulla. White pulp is lymphoid tissue associated with central arterioles. A periarteriolar lymphatic sheath (PALS) is a T-cell-rich arrangement; adjacent B-cell nodules may contain germinal centres. The word central names the vascular relationship and does not guarantee that the arteriole occupies the geometric centre of every two-dimensional nodule. Seek the vessel in another field or section when it is not intersected. A trabecular vessel and a white-pulp arteriole have different surrounding tissue relationships.

Try it: Identify the vessel-associated lymphoid pattern before calling a dark island white pulp.

steps.title: Red pulp: distinguish cords from vascular sinusoids
steps.body:
Red pulp contains blood-filled sinusoidal spaces and intervening splenic cords. The cords contain cells and a supporting framework rather than constituting an empty vascular lumen. Its blood-processing role differs from white-pulp immune organisation. H&E colour is helpful in context, but uneven blood content, section quality or processing can change the visual impression. Do not reverse the names: white pulp is the lymphoid compartment; red pulp is the blood-rich cord–sinusoid compartment. A section supports structural identification, not direct observation of how quickly an erythrocyte passes through.

Try it: Compare a cord with a sinusoid using the boundary and contents, not pink colour alone.

steps.title: Thymus: repeated cortex–medulla units and epithelial support
steps.body:
Look for incomplete connective-tissue septa and repeated darker cortical regions around paler medullary tissue. Hassall corpuscles are concentrically arranged epithelial structures in the medulla and strongly support thymus when the wider pattern fits. They are not germinal centres. The thymic supporting microenvironment includes epithelial reticular cells; a dense population of small lymphocytes can obscure their processes in routine sections. Involution can leave adipose tissue among residual thymic regions. Fat alone neither establishes thymus nor disproves it. Compare residual organisation with age and preparation context.

Try it: Reject a lymph-node follicle interpretation by identifying a medullary epithelial corpuscle and lobular context.

steps.title: Palatine tonsil: find the mucosal boundary and crypt
steps.body:
A surface lined by stratified squamous epithelium, with epithelial invaginations and underlying lymphoid follicles, supports palatine tonsillar tissue. Lymphocytes may infiltrate the epithelium, making its boundary harder to trace. Follow continuity with the surface before calling a pale gap a crypt. This is a surface-associated arrangement, unlike a lymph-node subcapsular sinus beneath a connective-tissue capsule. This particular epithelial description must not be applied indiscriminately to every tonsil of Waldeyer’s ring. A missing surface in a cropped field leaves the differential open.

Try it: Decide whether a space is epithelial-lined or lies beneath a capsule; state when the field is insufficient.

steps.title: Development explains why thymic stroma and thymocytes differ
steps.body:
Treat an organ as a composite of populations. Human thymic epithelial development is associated with the third pharyngeal pouch, while incoming haematopoietic progenitors supply the lymphoid population. Farley and colleagues reported spatial and temporal molecular evidence supporting a third-pouch origin for human thymic epithelium. Their human developmental study matters because older accounts and some other species differ. It does not make every thymic cell endodermal. For spleen, review the mesenchymal origin in the dorsal mesogastrium separately; “lymphoid organ” is a functional grouping, not one common epithelial germ-layer origin.

Try it: Explain why shared adult lymphoid function does not imply a shared origin for thymic epithelium and splenic stroma.

steps.title: Research bridge: interpret human developmental evidence
steps.body:
In Farley and colleagues’ study, in situ hybridisation mapped developmental gene expression and immunostaining distinguished cell populations. FOXN1 expression supported the third-pouch thymic domain; the authors did not detect it in the fourth pouch. The study labels ages after fertilisation, which must not be silently relabelled as obstetric gestational age. A marker pattern supports a developmental interpretation within the sampled stages; it is not a direct lineage-tracing experiment in a living human. Keep human observations separate from the mouse experiments used for mechanistic comparison.

Try it: State the species, age convention and measured signal before interpreting a developmental figure.

steps.title: Build lymph-node development from interacting populations
steps.body:
A lymph-node primordium, or anlage, forms through interactions between several populations. Haematopoietic lymphoid tissue inducer cells (LTi) meet local mesenchymal lymphoid tissue organiser cells (LTo), beside a developing endothelial compartment. LTi and LTo therefore name different partners, not successive names for one cell. This differs from the third-pouch epithelial contribution to thymus.

In the mouse developmental framework, CXCL13 is a recruiting chemokine and CXCR5 is its receptor on responding inducer cells. Cell-surface lymphotoxin α1β2 on LTi cells engages LTβR on stromal cells. The stromal response increases adhesion molecules and chemokines, helping retain and recruit further cells: a reinforcing interaction, rather than a capsule simply forming around a random lymphocyte aggregate. Distinguish a chemokine receptor from a lymphotoxin receptor; they transmit different parts of the programme.

practice.prompt: Why is the statement “all cells in a lymphoid organ share the same origin” inadequate?
practice.feedback: It collapses haematopoietic, stromal and endothelial populations into one label. Their origins and interactions must be considered separately.

steps.title: Distinguish initiation from later stromal organisation
steps.body:
Early recruitment and later maturation must be tested separately. In van de Pavert and colleagues’ mouse study, retinoic acid induced stromal CXCL13 before lymphotoxin-dependent organisation. This did not establish that retinoic acid alone supplies the entire organiser programme. Nearby neurons were a proposed retinoic-acid source, not cells shown to turn into lymph nodes.

Compare ages and anatomical sites when interpreting a mutant. An early failure of clustering was followed by later rudimentary mesenteric structures in one receptor-deficient model. A delayed primordium, a persistent but immature structure, and an absent adult node are different endpoints.

practice.prompt: A mutant lacks an early cluster at one stage. Can you conclude that every adult node will be absent?
practice.feedback: No. Examine later stages and different node sites. The endpoint and sampling time are part of the claim.

steps.title: Test the developmental sequence with a receptor perturbation
steps.body:
Bénézech and colleagues compared embryonic mouse nodes using microscopy, flow cytometry and organ culture. Mesenchymal cells progressed from low or absent ICAM-1/VCAM-1 expression to an intermediate phenotype, then to a mature organiser phenotype with high adhesion-molecule expression and MAdCAM-1. The intermediate population still appeared without LTi cells or LTβR, whereas full maturation was impaired.

Stimulating LTβR in organ culture increased the mature phenotype without an accompanying rise in cell number. Together, these results supported a maturation step rather than simply expansion of an already mature population. The proposed sequence is evidence from the studied mouse preparations, not a directly observed human lineage tree. Developmental mechanisms become clearer when the prediction is explicit: removing a late signal may leave an early population present but unable to complete its programme.

practice.prompt: If intermediate stromal cells persist after receptor loss, what does that say about the receptor?
practice.feedback: In this setting it is required for a later maturation step, not for every event that produces the initial intermediate population.

steps.title: Read human developmental observations beside mouse fate mapping
steps.body:
Hoorweg and colleagues identified organiser-like stromal populations in human fetal material using marker combinations, localisation and transcript measurements. These observations supported a human stromal niche, but did not directly follow a human fetal cell into adulthood. The precursor–descendant experiment instead used a mouse Il7-Cre reporter and supported a relationship between a labelled organiser subset and adult marginal reticular cells.

The word subset matters. Reporter coverage and regulatory behaviour limit what an unlabelled population can tell you. A negative label is not automatically proof that a lineage relationship is impossible. Always state the organism, the population actually labelled and the type of measurement before converting a research figure into an embryology claim.

practice.prompt: Which finding most directly tests a precursor–descendant relationship: human marker colocalisation or a controlled genetic fate map?
practice.feedback: The fate map addresses ancestry in its experimental organism. Colocalisation addresses spatial association; neither result alone establishes an identical human lineage history.

steps.title: Choose a stain to answer a structural question
steps.body:
H&E supports an initial architectural survey. A connective-tissue stain can make capsule and trabeculae easier to distinguish from densely cellular parenchyma; the cited lymph-node comparison uses Azan. A silver preparation can reveal a reticular-fibre network that is poorly resolved in H&E. The stain is not an organ label: combine the highlighted component with its anatomical position. Antibody-based cell mapping is another method, with validation and control requirements. Do not infer B/T identity for every small dark nucleus from H&E alone, or interpret one marker as a complete activation or lineage history.

Try it: State the extra structural question you would ask before selecting a special stain.

steps.title: Give a practical answer that can be checked
steps.body:
Use a short evidence chain: organ candidate, two independent landmarks, a rejected alternative and a sampling limit. For a lymph-node candidate, combine a peripheral cortical arrangement with a capsular or sinus relationship. Explain why a mucosal crypt, repeated thymic lobule or arteriole-centred splenic pattern would change the interpretation. Do not invent a missing landmark to finish the answer.

Separate what the image shows from what the source tells you. In the licensed image selected for this exercise, the creator identifies a normal lymph node. The photograph supports an architectural task, but lacks a stated stain, exact magnification and scale bar. It cannot support numerical cell measurements, a complete cell inventory or a patient diagnosis.

practice.prompt: Can enlarging a photograph supply its missing physical scale or prove its stain?
practice.feedback: No. Display enlargement changes apparent size. A calibrated scale and documented preparation are separate information.

question.prompt: An organ has lobules, pale medullae and Hassall corpuscles. Which is most likely?

options.reason: Lymph nodes instead show follicles, paracortex and lymph sinuses.
Spleen is organized into red and white pulp.
Correct: the architecture and Hassall corpuscles strongly support thymus.

recall.prompt: Compare the principal jobs of a lymph node, spleen and thymus.
recall.answer: A lymph node samples tissue lymph, spleen samples blood, and thymus supports T-cell development and selection.

Use a real section to construct an identification with two landmarks and a defensible limit.

workedExample.title: Two pale spaces, different meanings
workedExample.prompt: One section shows a space beneath a connective-tissue capsule and nearby follicles. Another shows an epithelial invagination continuous with a stratified squamous surface. How would you distinguish them?
solution: Follow each boundary before naming the space: subcapsular position supports a node sinus; epithelial continuity supports a palatine tonsillar crypt.
Use another independent feature: cortex/paracortex/medulla organisation versus surface-associated lymphoid tissue.
A cropped field lacking the surface or capsule may not resolve the comparison. Request a wider field instead of guessing.

oralExamination.prompt: Mark a cellular cord and its adjacent sinus as different structures.
oralExamination.answer: Trace the connective-tissue capsule and look immediately beneath it for the subcapsular sinus. Follicles lie in the outer cortex. The deeper paracortex is a predominantly T-cell region, with high endothelial venules; it is not simply another B-cell follicle. In the medulla distinguish cellular cords from the intervening lymph sinuses. Cords may contain plasma cells, B lymphocytes and macrophages. The distinction is tissue versus passage, not merely dark versus light. A limited core may omit the capsule or hilum; report that sampling limit rather than asserting that the whole organ lacks them.

oralExamination.prompt: Trace one afferent-lymph path and one blood-to-tissue path without merging their entry vessels.
oralExamination.answer: Use two differently labelled routes. Lymph arriving from drained tissue enters through afferent lymphatics, then the subcapsular and deeper sinus system, before leaving through an efferent lymphatic at the hilum. Circulating lymphocytes can instead leave blood through specialised postcapillary high endothelial venules in the paracortex. An HEV is a blood vessel, not an afferent lymphatic. The paracortex is a cellular region containing vessels; it is not an extra sinus to insert into a flow mnemonic. Both routes can bring material or cells into the same organ while retaining distinct boundaries.

oralExamination.prompt: Explain why shared adult lymphoid function does not imply a shared origin for thymic epithelium and splenic stroma.
oralExamination.answer: Treat an organ as a composite of populations. Human thymic epithelial development is associated with the third pharyngeal pouch, while incoming haematopoietic progenitors supply the lymphoid population. Farley and colleagues reported spatial and temporal molecular evidence supporting a third-pouch origin for human thymic epithelium. Their human developmental study matters because older accounts and some other species differ. It does not make every thymic cell endodermal. For spleen, review the mesenchymal origin in the dorsal mesogastrium separately; “lymphoid organ” is a functional grouping, not one common epithelial germ-layer origin.

lessons.subject: histology
lessons.title: Respiratory system: wall identification, exchange surfaces and lung development
lessons.summary: Trace airway levels and the alveolar interface, then explain how specification, branching and maturation build the lung.
lessons.section: Original system-specific explanations and applications with section-level source mapping

steps.title: Read the airway wall from the lumen outward
steps.body:
Begin with the epithelial lining, then trace the connective tissue, smooth muscle, glands and cartilage in the same wall. A tracheal section typically has pseudostratified ciliated epithelium, seromucous glands and a C-shaped hyaline-cartilage framework with posterior trachealis muscle. An intrapulmonary bronchus instead has cartilage plates, a circumferential smooth-muscle component and surrounding alveolated lung. Cartilage establishes a supported conducting airway but its arrangement and surrounding tissue determine the level. An incomplete section can omit a cartilage plate or gland, so a small cartilage-free fragment is not sufficient evidence for a bronchiole. Use the architecture of the sampled wall rather than memorising one colour or diameter.

Try it: Trace the entire visible wall and name the additional landmark needed to distinguish trachea from intrapulmonary bronchus.

steps.title: Airway epithelial cells divide the work of clearance, secretion and renewal
steps.body:
Pseudostratified respiratory epithelium contains cells of different heights, with all epithelial cells contacting the basal lamina. Nuclei at several levels therefore do not imply a truly stratified lining. Ciliated cells move surface material toward the pharynx; goblet cells and submucosal glands contribute mucus; basal cells occupy the basal compartment. In smaller conducting airways the lining becomes simpler, with club cells contributing protective secretions and epithelial maintenance. These are patterns along the respiratory tree, not a requirement that every cell type be visible in one field. Separate a ciliated surface, a mucus-producing cell and a gland duct: they are related to clearance but are not the same structure.

Try it: Explain how mucus production and ciliary transport cooperate while remaining different cellular functions.

steps.title: Recognise specialised upper-airway mucosa and a true vocal fold
steps.body:
The olfactory region has specialised receptor neurons, supporting cells and basal cells, with serous glands and nerve bundles in the underlying tissue. That combination distinguishes it from ordinary respiratory mucosa more securely than epithelial thickness alone. The epiglottis has an elastic-cartilage core and different epithelial environments on its surfaces. A true vocal fold has a protective stratified squamous lining over a vocal ligament and vocalis skeletal muscle; its free vibrating edge lacks the gland-rich appearance of a false fold. Do not use “respiratory tract” as a synonym for one epithelial type. The mechanical demands of a vibrating or exposed surface help explain why local lining and support differ.

Try it: Name two independent clues for a true vocal fold and the alternative they help exclude.

steps.title: Terminal or respiratory bronchiole: demonstrate an opening, not an adjacent alveolus
steps.body:
A bronchiole lacks cartilage and submucosal glands and has a relatively simple epithelium with smooth muscle. A terminal bronchiole is the final purely conducting segment. A respiratory bronchiole retains bronchiolar wall segments interrupted by alveolar openings. Both may be surrounded by alveoli, so adjacency does not establish that an alveolus opens into the airway. Trace continuity from lumen through the wall in a well-oriented region. If only a short segment is available, failure to see an opening is a sampling limitation rather than proof of a complete terminal-bronchiolar wall. State the strongest identification supported by the section and which relationship would increase confidence.

Try it: Distinguish “alveolus near the airway” from “alveolus opening through its wall.”

steps.title: Alveolar ducts, sacs, acini and lobules describe different levels of organisation
steps.body:
An alveolar duct is a passage whose boundary is formed largely by alveolar openings; small smooth-muscle elements occur at their rims. A sac describes alveoli sharing a terminal common space. An acinus comprises the gas-exchanging territory distal to one terminal bronchiole. A secondary pulmonary lobule contains several acini and is bounded by connective-tissue septa to a variable degree. Pulmonary arterial branches usually accompany the airway centrally, whereas pulmonary veins and lymphatic routes are associated with interlobular septa. A two-dimensional section may not show a complete acinar or lobular boundary. Use these as spatial definitions, not interchangeable names for any cluster of air spaces.

Try it: Place an alveolus, acinus and secondary lobule in a hierarchy, then mark which is defined by a terminal bronchiole.

steps.title: Build the blood–air barrier and distinguish its neighbouring cells
steps.body:
The thin exchange route crosses surface lining material, attenuated type I alveolar epithelium, closely apposed or fused epithelial and endothelial basal laminae, and capillary endothelium. Thicker septal regions contain connective tissue and supporting cells; the whole septum is not uniformly minimal. Type II cells are more cuboidal and contribute surfactant production and epithelial repair. An alveolar macrophage is a phagocyte, not an epithelial member of the barrier. A flattened nucleus in a septum could belong to endothelium or alveolar epithelium; relationship to a capillary lumen and the air-facing surface matters. Fine barrier layers and lamellar-body structure require appropriate ultrastructural evidence, rather than an ordinary low-power H&E field.

Try it: Trace from alveolar air to capillary blood and explain why a macrophage is not an obligatory layer on that route.

steps.title: Stain and preparation determine which lung question a slide can answer
steps.body:
H&E provides a useful architectural overview of airways, septa and vessels. Elastic-fibre and connective-tissue stains can address supporting networks; immunostains address selected targets and require validated controls. A coloured signal does not automatically identify a lineage or prove cell function. Lung inflation during fixation, collapse, tears and oblique sections can alter apparent air-space size and septal thickness. Compare intact regions and record specimen preparation before interpreting a broad empty space as an enlarged alveolus. Likewise, absence of macrophages in a field may reflect sampling or processing. A virtual slide’s on-screen enlargement is not a calibrated magnification; use a supplied scale bar for measurement.

Try it: Name one preparation variable and one additional method before claiming that a single thick-looking septum proves disease.

steps.title: Embryology begins with interacting epithelial and mesenchymal compartments
steps.body:
The lower respiratory epithelial primordium develops from ventral foregut endoderm. Surrounding mesoderm contributes much of the supporting mesenchyme, including connective-tissue and muscular components. Branching epithelium grows within that environment; the lung is not formed by endoderm alone. This separation helps explain why development must coordinate an airway lining, its support and an approaching vascular network. Germ-layer origin is a starting map, not a complete catalogue of every later cell population. Keep alveolar epithelium, vascular endothelium and immune cells conceptually distinct. The adult thin exchange interface requires contributions from multiple compartments to be brought into close spatial relation.

Try it: Draw epithelial and supporting compartments separately before joining them into the developing organ.

steps.title: Specification and branching are related but different developmental questions
steps.body:
Specification asks how foregut cells acquire respiratory identity; branching asks how an established epithelial bud generates a tree. In mouse experiments, Goss and colleagues tested Wnt2/2b and beta-catenin signalling using genetic perturbations and respiratory-marker readouts. This supports a causal role in specification in that experimental model. Bellusci and colleagues investigated mesenchymal Fgf10 expression and embryonic mouse lung responses in culture, linking an extracellular growth factor to epithelial budding behaviour. Neither study makes every human branching event a single-signal mechanism. Distinguish a ligand outside a cell, a signalling pathway inside it and a transcription-factor marker of its state; an expression pattern and a perturbation experiment provide different strengths of evidence.

Try it: Explain why loss of a respiratory marker and a change in branch shape are different measured outcomes.

steps.title: Pseudoglandular and canalicular patterns: follow changing architecture
steps.body:
The pseudoglandular pattern resembles a branching gland: many epithelial tubes are embedded in relatively abundant mesenchyme, without the mature exchange architecture of an adult lung. In the canalicular transition, distal spaces enlarge, epithelial differentiation progresses and the vascular network becomes more closely related to the epithelium. These are tissue-organisational changes, not simply an increase in overall lung size. Regions can mature at different rates, so one field should not be treated as a precise clock. Published age ranges overlap and may use gestational age or postconception age. Record the convention explicitly rather than combining numbers from different timelines or deriving a viability threshold from morphology alone.

Try it: Compare two fields using lumen size, epithelial form, mesenchymal abundance and capillary proximity before assigning a developmental pattern.

steps.title: Saccular maturation and alveolarisation require more than surfactant
steps.body:
During saccular maturation, expanded distal spaces and thinner intervening tissue bring epithelial and vascular surfaces into closer relation. Type I and type II epithelial differentiation and surfactant-related maturation contribute to preparation for gas exchange. Subsequent alveolarisation subdivides distal spaces through secondary septation and continued remodelling of the septal support and capillary network. The number of spaces, diffusion distance, vascular arrangement and mechanical stability therefore develop together. Surfactant reduces surface tension, but its presence alone is not a complete measure of respiratory readiness. Alveolarisation continues after birth; an adult-like outline should not be imposed on every fetal or neonatal section.

Try it: Give three structural reasons why a branching fetal lung is not equivalent to a mature gas-exchange organ.

steps.title: Human organoids connect a developmental marker with an experimental test
steps.body:
Sun and colleagues compared SOX2/SOX9-labelled human fetal lung tips with tip-derived organoids, then reduced SOX9 activity and measured organoid behaviour. Their experimental results support a role for SOX9 in maintaining the progenitor state under those conditions. The figure separates tissue localisation, confirmation of the perturbation and later growth-related outcomes. Co-expression in an image alone would not establish that function; the perturbation supplies a different part of the argument. An organoid is a model with a selected environment, not an intact fetal lung with its complete vasculature and mechanics. When comparing panels, retain the distinction between donor-derived organoid lines, different guide RNAs and repeated measurements.

Try it: Identify which panel type asks “where is the protein?” and which tests “what happens when its activity is reduced?”

steps.title: Integrate a slide answer with a developmental explanation
steps.body:
A strong practical answer has four linked parts: describe the observed architecture, identify the most likely structure, explain the structure–function relationship, and name a relevant developmental process. For example, a bronchiolar wall interrupted by clear alveolar openings supports a respiratory bronchiole. The interruptions connect a conducting route with exchange surfaces. Development must therefore produce both a branching airway and differentiated distal epithelium associated with capillaries. Finish by naming a limitation: a section cannot by itself establish three-dimensional continuity, molecular expression or developmental age. This approach adds embryology to the interpretation instead of attaching a memorised germ-layer label to an otherwise disconnected slide description.

Try it: Write a four-sentence answer for an unfamiliar distal-airway field using architecture, alternative, function and development.

question.prompt: Which feature favors a bronchiole over a bronchus?

options.reason: Correct: use this alongside the epithelial and smooth-muscle pattern.
Cartilage plates support a bronchus.
That is not the typical bronchiolar lining.

recall.prompt: Explain why the alveolar wall is thin but a conducting airway needs a more substantial wall.
recall.answer: Alveoli minimize diffusion distance. Conducting airways must maintain patency, regulate flow and clear inhaled material before it reaches the exchange surface.

objectives: Distinguish airway levels by wall organisation and alveolar openings.
Explain the alveolar interface and the evidence needed to identify its cells.
Connect epithelial and mesenchymal origins with specification, branching and maturation.
Interpret developmental stages and organoid experiments within their stated scope.

workedExample.title: Resolve an identification using relationships
workedExample.prompt: An alveolus sits beside a small airway. What must you see before calling the airway respiratory?
solution: Trace the airway wall rather than using surrounding alveoli as the deciding feature.
Look for an alveolar opening that interrupts a bronchiolar epithelial segment.
If continuity is not shown, retain the sampling limitation and inspect another region or plane.
