oralExamination.answer: The steady-barrier rate and the free-diffusion characteristic time are different quantities under different stated conditions. Their inverse-distance and squared-distance dependences are not interchangeable.

oralExamination.prompt: Why is a DLCO result more than a membrane-thickness measurement?
oralExamination.answer: Carbon-monoxide transfer involves gas delivery/distribution, the membrane and capillary blood with haemoglobin binding. A defined test and its conditions must be distinguished from an invented geometric model.

oralExamination.prompt: What does the selected retrospective haemoglobin study add, and what does it not establish?
oralExamination.answer: It supports a contribution of haemoglobin to DLCO variation in its selected population. It does not create a universal reference equation, prove a single cause of an individual result or demonstrate a membrane lesion.

summaryChecklist: I can distinguish ventilation, perfusion and diffusion.
I can name the total-transfer quantity before dividing by area.
I can calculate all factor ratios and state which factors are held constant.
I can give two different constructions producing a halved total rate.
I can separate a steady-barrier rate from a characteristic free-diffusion time.
I can explain the limits of a model and of the selected measurement evidence.

lessons.subject: cell-biology
lessons.title: Cell signaling through G proteins
lessons.summary: Trace the receptor, molecular switch, effector and second messenger without skipping the cell compartment.
lessons.section: Section 1.3: G-Protein-Coupled Receptors and signal termination

steps.title: Activate a membrane switch
steps.body: A ligand binds a seven-transmembrane receptor at the cell surface. Receptor activation promotes GDP–GTP exchange on the alpha subunit of a heterotrimeric G protein. The alpha subunit and beta-gamma complex can then regulate downstream effectors.

steps.title: Choose the effector pathway
steps.body: Gs stimulates adenylyl cyclase, increasing cAMP and protein kinase A signaling. Gi reduces adenylyl cyclase activity in its canonical pathway. Gq activates phospholipase C, producing IP3 and DAG; IP3 releases calcium from internal stores, while DAG helps activate protein kinase C.

steps.title: Terminate and interpret the signal
steps.body: GTP hydrolysis resets the G-protein switch. Second messengers are removed, calcium is transported back into stores or out of the cytosol, and protein phosphorylation can be reversed. The same messenger can have different effects because different cells express different targets.

question.prompt: Which pathway directly produces IP3 and DAG?

options.reason: That pathway raises cAMP rather than directly producing IP3 and DAG.
Correct: phospholipase C cleaves PIP2 to produce these two second messengers.
DNA ligase is unrelated to this membrane-signaling reaction.

recall.prompt: Why is naming a receptor insufficient to predict a whole-organ response?
recall.answer: The response also depends on the coupled G protein, available effectors, intracellular targets, cell type and interacting signals. Receptor location and pathway context matter.

lessons.subject: physiology
lessons.title: Cell transport: follow the energy
lessons.summary: Connect membrane permeability, the sodium–potassium pump and secondary active transport before predicting where a solute moves.
lessons.section: Sections 1.1–1.2: fluid compartments, tonicity and membrane transport

steps.title: Separate a gradient from a pathway
steps.body: A concentration gradient can favour movement without providing a route across a membrane. The lipid bilayer limits the movement of most ions and polar solutes. Channels provide selective pores; carriers bind and change conformation. For an ion, both concentration and voltage contribute to its electrochemical gradient.

steps.title: Locate the ATP-consuming step
steps.body: The sodium–potassium ATPase moves three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in per ATP hydrolysed. It maintains the gradients used by excitable cells and transport epithelia. A sodium–glucose cotransporter does not hydrolyse ATP directly: it couples inward sodium movement down its electrochemical gradient to glucose transport.

steps.title: Distinguish osmolarity from tonicity
steps.body: Osmolarity counts dissolved particles per litre of solution. Tonicity predicts the sustained effect on cell volume and depends on solutes that do not readily cross the relevant membrane. A solution can be isosmotic without being isotonic when its solute enters the cell. Always state which membrane and time scale you are considering.

question.prompt: Which process directly hydrolyses ATP?

options.reason: This uses the sodium gradient; the sodium–potassium pump supplies the energy indirectly.
The ATPase directly couples ATP hydrolysis to ion transport against the maintained gradients.

options.text: Potassium flow through an open channel
options.reason: Channel-mediated flow is passive down the electrochemical gradient.

recall.prompt: Explain how ATP can support glucose uptake without binding to its cotransporter.
recall.answer: ATP powers the sodium–potassium pump, which maintains a low intracellular sodium concentration. Sodium then enters through a cotransporter down its electrochemical gradient, providing energy for coupled glucose uptake.

lessons.subject: physiology
lessons.title: Three muscle types, three calcium stories
lessons.summary: Compare how skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle convert a calcium signal into force, and explain why their responses differ.
lessons.section: Sections on skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle excitation–contraction coupling

steps.title: Skeletal muscle: activate the thin filament
steps.body: At the neuromuscular junction, acetylcholine produces an end-plate depolarisation that can initiate a muscle action potential. In skeletal muscle, the T-tubule voltage sensor couples to sarcoplasmic-reticulum calcium release. Calcium binds troponin C, moving the tropomyosin constraint on actin–myosin interaction. ATP supports cross-bridge cycling and calcium reuptake.

steps.title: Cardiac muscle: trigger calcium-induced release
steps.body: In cardiac working myocytes, calcium entering through L-type channels triggers further calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Troponin C again regulates the thin filament. The prolonged action potential and refractory period strongly limit summation into tetanus, allowing filling between contractions. This working-myocyte model differs from nodal pacemaker activity.

steps.title: Smooth muscle: regulate myosin
steps.body: Smooth muscle uses calcium–calmodulin to activate myosin light-chain kinase. Phosphorylation of myosin supports interaction with actin; myosin light-chain phosphatase favours relaxation. Smooth muscle lacks the troponin switch used in striated muscle. Stretch, local signals and autonomic input can regulate force, sometimes without a full action potential.

question.prompt: What is the main calcium-dependent regulatory switch in smooth muscle?

options.reason: Troponin regulates skeletal and cardiac thin filaments, not the principal smooth-muscle switch.
These initiate neuromuscular transmission; they do not describe smooth-muscle contractile regulation.

options.text: Calcium–calmodulin activation of myosin light-chain kinase
options.reason: This promotes myosin phosphorylation and permits effective actin–myosin interaction.

recall.prompt: Compare the role of calcium in skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle.
recall.answer: Skeletal and cardiac muscle use troponin C to regulate actin access. Skeletal coupling primarily releases stored calcium through voltage-sensor coupling; cardiac muscle needs trigger calcium entry. Smooth muscle uses calcium–calmodulin and myosin light-chain kinase to regulate myosin.

lessons.subject: physiology
lessons.title: Autonomic signals: receptor before response
lessons.summary: Use receptor location and intracellular signalling to predict an autonomic response without memorising one effect for every organ.
lessons.section: Signal transduction and autonomic receptor comparison sections

steps.title: Start with the wiring
steps.body: Both sympathetic and parasympathetic preganglionic neurons release acetylcholine onto neuronal nicotinic receptors. Most sympathetic postganglionic neurons release noradrenaline, whereas most parasympathetic postganglionic neurons release acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors. Sympathetic innervation of eccrine sweat glands is an important cholinergic exception.

steps.title: Follow the receptor pathway
steps.body: Many beta-adrenoceptor responses use Gs, adenylyl cyclase and cyclic AMP. Alpha-1 responses commonly use Gq, phospholipase C, IP3 and intracellular calcium. M2 receptors in the heart couple to Gi/o; reduced cyclic AMP and G-protein beta–gamma regulation of potassium channels help slow nodal activity. These are useful dominant pathways, not an exhaustive catalogue.

steps.title: Predict the tissue response
steps.body: The same second messenger can produce different effects in different tissues because the target proteins differ. Beta-1 stimulation supports cardiac rate and force, while beta-2 stimulation can relax bronchial smooth muscle. Name the receptor, cell and effector before predicting a change; avoid treating sympathetic activity as a universal contraction signal.

question.prompt: Why can beta stimulation increase cardiac force but relax bronchial smooth muscle?

options.text: The target cells contain different downstream effector machinery
options.reason: A shared signalling pathway can act on different proteins and produce tissue-specific responses.

options.text: Cyclic AMP has no role in either tissue
options.reason: Gs and cyclic AMP participate in these receptor pathways.

options.text: All sympathetic postganglionic neurons release acetylcholine
options.reason: Most release noradrenaline; the statement also fails to explain receptor-specific effects.

recall.prompt: Give a receptor-to-response explanation of slowing at the sinoatrial node.
recall.answer: Acetylcholine activates cardiac M2 receptors. Gi/o signalling reduces cyclic AMP, while beta–gamma subunits can activate GIRK potassium channels. These changes reduce pacemaker activity and slow the heart.

lessons.subject: physiology
lessons.title: The cardiac cycle: pressure opens the valves
lessons.summary: Read valve events and ventricular volume together, then predict the isolated effects of preload, afterload and contractility.
lessons.section: Sections 2.3–2.4: cardiac cycle and pressure–volume loops

steps.title: Use pressure differences to order the cycle
steps.body: During filling, atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure and the atrioventricular valve is open. As ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure, that valve closes. Before ventricular pressure exceeds arterial pressure, both valves are closed: pressure rises at almost constant volume. The arterial valve opens when the ventricular-to-arterial pressure difference favours ejection.

steps.title: Read the loop rather than its shape alone
steps.body: The width of a ventricular pressure–volume loop is stroke volume: end-diastolic minus end-systolic volume. Its area represents external stroke work. Isovolumetric contraction and relaxation are nearly vertical because volume changes little while pressure changes. Real measurements depend on loading conditions and valve function; a teaching loop simplifies these details.

steps.title: Change one variable at a time
steps.body: With other conditions held fixed, increased filling can raise stroke volume through the Frank–Starling mechanism. An isolated increase in afterload tends to increase end-systolic volume and reduce stroke volume on that beat. Increased contractility tends to reduce end-systolic volume. In an intact circulation, reflexes and subsequent filling can change the later response.

question.prompt: Both ventricular valves are closed while pressure rises. Which phase is this?

options.reason: Ejection requires an open arterial valve and a falling ventricular volume.
Pressure rises before the arterial valve opens, with little change in chamber volume.
Filling requires an open atrioventricular valve and an increasing volume.

recall.prompt: Predict the immediate effect of an isolated afterload increase on a pressure–volume loop.
recall.answer: At unchanged preload and contractility, the ventricle must develop more pressure before ejection. It generally ejects less on that beat, leaving a larger end-systolic volume and a narrower loop. Later reflex and filling responses may modify this.

lessons.subject: physiology
lessons.title: Ventilation: make each breath count
lessons.summary: Connect pressure-driven breathing with dead space and calculate why equal minute ventilation can give different alveolar ventilation.
lessons.section: Section 3.1: respiratory mechanics, dead space and alveolar ventilation

steps.title: Create a pressure gradient
steps.body: During quiet inspiration, diaphragm contraction expands the thorax. Alveolar pressure transiently falls below atmospheric pressure, so air flows inward. Airflow stops when the pressures equalise. Quiet expiration is mainly driven by elastic recoil. The diaphragm receives motor supply through the phrenic nerves, principally from C3–C5.

steps.title: Distinguish pressure from resistance
steps.body: For a simplified airway, airflow equals the pressure difference divided by airway resistance. At the same pressure difference, doubling resistance halves airflow. Use this relationship to interpret the pressure diagram and resistance question below.

steps.title: Subtract the non-exchanging volume
steps.body: Minute ventilation equals tidal volume multiplied by respiratory rate. Alveolar ventilation is approximated by (tidal volume minus dead-space volume) multiplied by rate, using consistent units. Anatomic dead space is conducting-airway volume; alveolar dead space is ventilation that receives little or no effective perfusion.

steps.title: Compare two fictional breathing patterns
steps.body: With a fixed dead space of 150 mL, 500 mL breaths at 12/min give 4.2 L/min alveolar ventilation. Breaths of 300 mL at 20/min give only 3.0 L/min, despite the same 6.0 L/min minute ventilation. This is a simplified teaching calculation. Actual dead space and carbon-dioxide production vary; these examples are not ventilation prescriptions.

question.prompt: At 500 mL per breath, 150 mL dead space and 12 breaths/min, what is alveolar ventilation?

options.reason: This is total minute ventilation and includes dead-space ventilation.
This is the dead-space component: 150 mL multiplied by 12.
Subtract 150 from 500 mL, multiply by 12, then convert 4200 mL/min to litres/min.

recall.prompt: Explain why rapid shallow breaths can be less efficient than slower deeper breaths at the same minute ventilation.
recall.answer: A fixed conducting-airway volume takes up more of each small breath. After subtracting dead space, less fresh air reaches gas-exchanging alveoli each minute, even when total minute ventilation is unchanged.

lessons.subject: physiology
lessons.title: Water balance: distinguish ADH from aldosterone
lessons.summary: Follow the separate signals for osmolality and effective circulating volume, and connect them to collecting-duct transport.
lessons.section: Section 4.4 and integrated body-fluid regulation addendum

steps.title: Identify the regulated variable
steps.body: Osmolality describes the concentration of osmotically active particles, whereas extracellular volume reflects the amount of fluid in that compartment. Sodium balance is a major determinant of extracellular volume; water balance strongly influences osmolality. The two variables interact, but an explanation should identify which change is driving the response.

steps.title: Use ADH to alter water permeability
steps.body: ADH binds basolateral V2 receptors on collecting-duct principal cells and promotes insertion of aquaporin-2 into the apical membrane. Water can then move into the hyperosmotic medullary interstitium. ADH uses the gradient; it does not create the entire countercurrent system by itself. Both osmotic signals and sufficiently strong volume signals can regulate its release.

steps.title: Use aldosterone to adjust sodium and potassium handling
steps.body: Aldosterone promotes sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion in responsive distal nephron cells by altering transport proteins, including epithelial sodium channels and the sodium–potassium ATPase. Angiotensin II and plasma potassium are important regulators. Predicting water retention additionally requires attention to water permeability, intake and the other control systems.

question.prompt: What directly increases collecting-duct apical water permeability?

options.reason: ADH promotes aquaporin-2 trafficking, allowing water to follow the medullary osmotic gradient.
Aldosterone chiefly regulates sodium and potassium transport; this is not its direct water-channel mechanism.

options.text: Blocking all sodium transport in the loop of Henle
options.reason: This can weaken the medullary gradient rather than directly increasing apical water permeability.

recall.prompt: Distinguish what ADH changes from what aldosterone changes.
recall.answer: ADH increases collecting-duct water permeability through aquaporin-2 trafficking. Aldosterone enhances distal sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion. Their effects interact with medullary gradients, intake and circulating-volume signals.

lessons.subject: physiology
lessons.title: Haemostasis: build and stabilise the plug
lessons.summary: Distinguish platelet adhesion, platelet aggregation and fibrin formation, then locate intrinsic tenase in the sequence.
lessons.section: Sections 5.2–5.3: primary haemostasis, intrinsic tenase and coagulation

steps.title: Anchor platelets at an injured surface
steps.body: Vascular injury exposes adhesive structures and immobilised von Willebrand factor. Platelet GPIb-IX-V binds von Willebrand factor, while collagen receptors help stabilise adhesion. Platelets then change shape, release mediators and recruit further platelets. Adhesion attaches a platelet to the injured surface; it is not the same event as platelet-to-platelet aggregation.

steps.title: Connect platelets to one another
steps.body: Activation changes the affinity of integrin alpha-IIb-beta-3, also called GPIIb/IIIa. Fibrinogen can bridge these receptors on neighbouring platelets. ADP, thromboxane and thrombin help amplify activation. Platelets also expose a phospholipid surface that supports coagulation-complex assembly, linking primary and secondary haemostasis.

steps.title: Amplify thrombin and stabilise fibrin
steps.body: Intrinsic tenase contains factor IXa with its cofactor VIIIa on a calcium-dependent phospholipid surface; it activates factor X. Factor Xa with Va forms prothrombinase, producing thrombin from prothrombin. Thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin, and factor XIIIa crosslinks fibrin. These overlapping processes stabilise the plug; they are not two completely separate timelines.

question.prompt: Which enzyme–cofactor pair forms intrinsic tenase?

options.reason: This forms prothrombinase, which converts prothrombin to thrombin.
On an appropriate phospholipid surface with calcium, this complex efficiently activates factor X.
Thrombin cleaves fibrinogen to form fibrin; this is not the intrinsic-tenase complex.

recall.prompt: Explain the difference between adhesion, aggregation and fibrin stabilisation.
recall.answer: Adhesion anchors platelets to an injured surface. Aggregation joins activated platelets through fibrinogen bridges between alpha-IIb-beta-3 receptors. Coagulation generates thrombin and fibrin, and factor XIIIa crosslinks fibrin to stabilise the plug.

lessons.subject: physiology
lessons.title: Digestion: coordinate movement and secretion
lessons.summary: Connect enteric circuits, local signals and gastrointestinal hormones to explain how a meal is processed.
lessons.section: Sections 6.1–6.5: enteric control, motility, secretion and absorption

steps.title: Give the gut a local control loop
steps.body: The enteric nervous system contains interconnected networks in the myenteric and submucosal plexuses. Myenteric circuits are strongly involved in motility, while submucosal circuits help regulate secretion and local blood flow. Autonomic input modifies these circuits. Local sensory input can therefore coordinate a response without requiring every step to be commanded by the brain.

steps.title: Match the hormone to the incoming material
steps.body: Acid arriving in the duodenum stimulates secretin release, supporting pancreatic ductal bicarbonate secretion. Fat and protein digestion products stimulate cholecystokinin, supporting pancreatic enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction. These signals help match the composition of secretions to what the meal requires.

steps.title: Separate mixing, propulsion and absorption
steps.body: Segmentation mainly mixes intestinal contents and increases contact with the mucosa, whereas coordinated peristalsis produces forward propulsion. Digestion breaks macromolecules into absorbable components; absorption moves those components across the epithelium. Pancreatic enzymes, bile-mediated lipid handling and membrane transport each contribute different steps.

question.prompt: Which response is most directly associated with acid entering the duodenum?

options.text: Secretin chiefly causing gastric acid secretion
options.reason: Secretin helps neutralise the duodenal acid load rather than acting chiefly to increase it.

options.text: CCK acting as the only controller of bicarbonate secretion
options.reason: CCK and secretin have overlapping interactions, but acid-driven ductal bicarbonate secretion is classically linked to secretin.

options.text: Secretin supporting pancreatic ductal bicarbonate secretion
options.reason: Bicarbonate helps neutralise acidic chyme and provides a suitable environment for intestinal digestion.

recall.prompt: Explain how a meal containing fat and acid can recruit different pancreatic responses.
recall.answer: Duodenal acid stimulates secretin and bicarbonate-rich ductal secretion. Fat and protein products stimulate cholecystokinin and enzyme-rich secretion, with neural signals coordinating the response. The pathways interact rather than operating as isolated switches.

lessons.subject: physiology
lessons.title: Energy balance: connect intake, storage and use
lessons.summary: Follow energy through the fed and fasting states and distinguish long-term balance from a single meal.
lessons.section: Section 6.6: energy balance, food intake and body weight

steps.title: Use a conservation statement
steps.body: Over a defined interval, the change in stored body energy reflects absorbed energy intake minus energy expenditure. Expenditure includes basal cellular work, physical activity and the thermic effect of food. Body mass also changes with water and gastrointestinal contents, so a short-term weight change is not a direct measurement of a change in fat energy.

steps.title: Connect the fed state to storage
steps.body: After a mixed meal, insulin supports storage and use of absorbed nutrients. Glucose can enter insulin-responsive tissues, glycogen stores can be replenished, and lipid storage is favoured. The exact response depends on tissue transporters and metabolic pathways; not every tissue requires insulin for glucose uptake.

steps.title: Connect fasting to mobilisation
steps.body: As the interval since eating increases, a lower insulin-to-glucagon signal supports hepatic glucose production and mobilisation of stored fuels. Glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis contribute on different time scales, while fatty acids supply many tissues. Hormonal control redistributes available fuels; it does not create energy from nothing.

question.prompt: Why is one day's body-mass change an unreliable measure of fat-energy change?

options.text: Water and gut contents also contribute to measured mass
options.reason: Short-term mass changes can occur without an equivalent change in stored fat energy.

options.text: Conservation of energy does not apply to humans
options.reason: Energy balance still applies; interpreting mass requires knowing what changed.

options.text: All tissues stop consuming energy during fasting
options.reason: Basal cellular work continues and fasting recruits stored fuels.

recall.prompt: Compare nutrient handling after a meal and during fasting.
recall.answer: The fed state favours use and storage of absorbed nutrients under a higher insulin signal. Fasting promotes mobilisation of stored fuels and hepatic glucose production under a lower insulin-to-glucagon signal. Energy is transferred and transformed, not created.

lessons.subject: physiology
lessons.title: Endocrine axes: read the feedback loop
lessons.summary: Track a hypothalamic–pituitary–target-gland axis and use the pattern of hormones to explain negative feedback.
lessons.section: Sections 7.1 and 7.3: hypothalamic–pituitary control and thyroid physiology

steps.title: Name the three levels
steps.body: In the hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid axis, hypothalamic TRH supports pituitary TSH release, and TSH stimulates the thyroid. Thyroid hormones then act on many target tissues. Drawing the levels separately helps distinguish a gland's response to stimulation from the actions of its hormone elsewhere in the body.

steps.title: Close the feedback loop
steps.body: Thyroid hormone feeds back on the hypothalamus and pituitary, reducing stimulation when hormone availability rises. Feedback is a regulatory relationship, not simply a label attached to every endocrine pathway. Some hormones use different controlling variables, and secretion can be pulsatile or follow daily rhythms.

steps.title: Explain a simplified pattern
steps.body: In a simplified primary thyroid-gland failure model, reduced thyroid hormone removes inhibitory feedback and TSH rises if the pituitary can respond. If the defect instead lies centrally, TSH may be low or inappropriately normal despite low thyroid hormone. Real interpretation requires clinical context, assay limitations and other influences; this example teaches the feedback logic.

question.prompt: In a simplified primary thyroid-gland failure model, what happens to TSH?

options.text: It must be suppressed because the thyroid is underactive
options.reason: Reduced thyroid hormone removes feedback inhibition, rather than directly suppressing pituitary TSH.

options.text: It rises if the pituitary response is intact
options.reason: Lower thyroid hormone permits increased hypothalamic–pituitary stimulation.
TSH is a pituitary signal to the thyroid, not a precursor converted into thyroid hormone.

recall.prompt: Explain why a target-gland hormone and its pituitary signal can move in opposite directions.
recall.answer: A target-gland hormone can inhibit its upstream control signals. When target-gland secretion falls, reduced negative feedback permits the pituitary signal to rise, provided the central components of the axis remain functional.

lessons.subject: physiology
lessons.title: Reproductive physiology: connect the two cycles
lessons.summary: Relate ovarian events to endometrial changes and explain the transition from negative to positive feedback around ovulation.
lessons.section: Sections 7.7–7.9: reproductive function, ovarian cycle and pregnancy

steps.title: Begin with a coordinated axis
steps.body: Pulsatile hypothalamic GnRH supports pituitary LH and FSH secretion. In the ovary, gonadotrophins support follicular development and steroid production. In the testis, LH supports Leydig-cell testosterone production, while FSH acts on Sertoli cells in support of spermatogenesis. The same pituitary signals act within different tissue arrangements.

steps.title: Connect follicular growth to ovulation
steps.body: Developing ovarian follicles produce estradiol. During most of the cycle, ovarian hormones contribute inhibitory feedback. Sustained sufficiently high estradiol near ovulation can instead generate positive feedback and an LH surge. The surge promotes final oocyte maturation, ovulation and luteinisation. A 28-day diagram is an illustration, not a schedule every person must follow.

steps.title: Match the endometrium to ovarian hormones
steps.body: Estradiol supports proliferative endometrial growth. After ovulation, the corpus luteum produces progesterone, promoting secretory differentiation. If pregnancy does not maintain luteal function, falling progesterone and estradiol contribute to menstruation. Fertilisation usually occurs in the uterine-tube ampulla; implantation is a later, distinct event in the uterus.

question.prompt: Which change normally links the late follicular phase to ovulation?

options.text: A permanent absence of GnRH pulses
options.reason: Normal gonadotrophin secretion depends on appropriate pulsatile stimulation.

options.text: Progesterone replacing all ovarian follicular activity before growth begins
options.reason: Progesterone is especially associated with the post-ovulatory corpus luteum.

options.text: Sustained high estradiol contributing to an LH surge
options.reason: The feedback switch near ovulation supports the surge that triggers ovulatory events.

recall.prompt: Relate the ovarian and endometrial phases without assuming a fixed calendar.
recall.answer: Follicular estradiol supports endometrial proliferation. A sustained estradiol rise can trigger an LH surge and ovulation. Luteal progesterone supports secretory endometrium; falling luteal hormones contribute to menstruation when pregnancy does not maintain the corpus luteum.

lessons.subject: physiology
lessons.title: Neural integration: from release to a response
lessons.summary: Follow chemical transmission across a synapse, then explain how a neuron combines excitatory and inhibitory inputs.
lessons.section: Section 8.1: chemical synapses, postsynaptic potentials and summation

steps.title: Release a chemical signal
steps.body: An action potential reaching a presynaptic terminal opens voltage-gated calcium channels. Local calcium entry activates the vesicle-fusion machinery, allowing neurotransmitter release into the synaptic cleft. The transmitter then acts on postsynaptic receptors. Calcium links the arriving electrical event to release; it is not the transmitter crossing the cleft.

steps.title: Interpret the postsynaptic conductance change
steps.body: Ionotropic receptors directly regulate channel opening, whereas metabotropic receptors recruit intracellular signalling. Whether an input is excitatory or inhibitory depends on the conductance change, its reversal potential and the receiving cell's state. Inhibitory input can reduce excitability by shunting current even when the membrane does not become much more negative.

steps.title: Combine inputs in time and space
steps.body: Temporal summation combines inputs arriving close together in time. Spatial summation combines inputs from different locations. Dendritic filtering, synapse position and inhibitory conductance shape the result. An action potential is generated when the combined effect reaches the relevant threshold; a single postsynaptic potential need not cause a spike.

question.prompt: Which event most directly triggers rapid neurotransmitter release at a typical chemical synapse?

options.reason: A local calcium rise activates the release sensor and vesicle-fusion machinery.

options.text: Calcium carrying the transmitter across the cleft
options.reason: Transmitter diffuses after release; calcium is a presynaptic release signal.

options.text: A postsynaptic action potential returning through every vesicle
options.reason: This is not the normal causal sequence of chemical transmission.

recall.prompt: Distinguish chemical transmission from temporal and spatial summation.
recall.answer: Chemical transmission releases a transmitter that changes postsynaptic signalling or conductance. Temporal summation combines closely timed inputs; spatial summation combines inputs at different sites. Their combined effect helps determine whether the receiving neuron fires.

lessons.subject: physiology
lessons.title: Special senses: convert a stimulus into a signal
lessons.summary: Compare how photoreceptors and inner-ear hair cells convert physical stimuli into changes in neurotransmitter release.
lessons.section: Special-sense sections: vision, phototransduction, hearing and vestibular function

steps.title: Light reduces photoreceptor depolarisation
steps.body: In darkness, cyclic-GMP-dependent channels support the photoreceptor dark current. Light activates the phototransduction cascade, reducing cyclic GMP and closing these channels. The photoreceptor hyperpolarises and releases less glutamate. This is a graded receptor response; it is not a conventional all-or-none action potential in the rod or cone.

steps.title: Hair bundles gate a mechanically sensitive current
steps.body: Deflection of a sensory hair bundle in its excitatory direction opens mechanotransduction channels. Potassium-rich endolymph and the electrochemical arrangement favour an inward current that depolarises the hair cell. This changes calcium entry and transmitter release to sensory afferents. Deflection in the opposite direction reduces the response.

steps.title: Keep the sensory code and route separate
steps.body: Cochlear position helps encode sound frequency because different parts of the basilar membrane respond best to different frequencies. Vestibular organs instead contribute information about head movement and orientation. A complete explanation names the stimulus, receptor response, transmitter change and afferent pathway, rather than saying that every sensory receptor fires in the same way.

question.prompt: What does light normally do to a vertebrate rod photoreceptor?

options.text: Opens more cyclic-GMP-gated channels and increases the dark current
options.reason: The light-activated cascade lowers cyclic GMP and closes these channels.

options.text: Hyperpolarises it and reduces glutamate release
options.reason: Channel closure reduces the inward dark current and changes graded transmitter release.

options.text: Causes the rod to fire a conventional motor-neuron action potential
options.reason: Rod signalling is graded; retinal ganglion cells provide the spiking output.

recall.prompt: Compare the direction of the initial receptor response to light and to excitatory hair-bundle deflection.
recall.answer: Light closes cyclic-GMP-gated channels and hyperpolarises a photoreceptor. Excitatory hair-bundle deflection opens mechanically gated channels and depolarises a hair cell. Both graded responses regulate transmitter release.

lessons.subject: physiology
lessons.title: Microcirculation: return the filtered fluid
lessons.summary: Connect capillary filtration, the endothelial barrier and lymphatic return without assuming that every capillary reabsorbs fluid at its venous end.
lessons.section: Sections 2.7–2.8: microcirculation, Starling forces and venous return; original web supplement: mechanism comparison and worked reasoning, 2 November 2026

steps.title: Separate pressure from permeability
steps.body: Capillary hydrostatic pressure favours outward fluid movement. Plasma proteins contribute an opposing colloid osmotic effect, but the endothelial barrier and its glycocalyx determine how those forces act. A pressure change alone does not fully describe exchange when permeability or protein distribution also changes.

steps.title: Include the lymphatic route
steps.body: Lymphatic vessels return filtered interstitial fluid and proteins to the circulation. Sustained venous-end reabsorption is not a universal feature of all systemic capillaries. In many tissues, lymphatic return handles much of the net filtration. Different organs have specialised exchange arrangements, so one diagram should not be treated as a universal map.

steps.title: Distinguish entry junctions from the transport route
steps.body: Initial lymphatic endothelial cells can have discontinuous button-like junctions anchoring overlapping cell borders. Openings between these junctions provide an entry route; collecting lymphatics instead have continuous zipper-like junctions. Buttons and zippers describe cell junctions, not valves projecting into the vessel lumen. This distinction comes from experimental vessel microscopy, including mouse tissues; it is a simplified structural model, not a rule that every lymphatic segment is identical.

steps.title: Build an oedema mechanism
steps.body: Oedema can result when filtration exceeds the capacity for return. Increased venous pressure, increased permeability, reduced plasma protein concentration or impaired lymphatic drainage can contribute through different mechanisms. In a teaching explanation, specify which part changed and then trace its effect; appearance alone does not establish a cause.

question.prompt: Which statement best represents the role of lymphatics in tissue-fluid balance?

options.text: They carry only cells and never return proteins
options.reason: Lymphatic vessels return interstitial fluid and proteins as well as transporting immune cells.

options.text: They are unnecessary because all filtered fluid is reabsorbed at venous capillary ends
options.reason: This is an oversimplification; sustained venous-end reabsorption is not universal.

options.text: They return net filtered fluid and proteins to the circulation
options.reason: Lymphatic return is a major component of tissue-fluid balance.

recall.prompt: Explain how venous pressure and lymphatic obstruction can both produce fluid accumulation.
recall.answer: Higher venous pressure can increase capillary hydrostatic pressure and filtration. Lymphatic obstruction reduces the route that returns filtered fluid and proteins. Both can increase interstitial fluid, but through different parts of the balance.

objectives: Separate capillary filtration from lymphatic fluid return.
Distinguish lymphatic entry junctions from collecting-vessel junctions.
Explain fluid accumulation without assuming universal venous-end reabsorption.

workedExample.title: Follow a return-route obstruction
workedExample.prompt: In a hypothetical tissue, lymphatic outflow falls while capillary filtration continues. Explain why fluid can accumulate even without an increase in capillary pressure.
solution: Start with two distinct flows: entry into the interstitium and removal from it.
Reduced lymphatic outflow lowers removal; filtration need not increase for the balance to become positive.
Accumulation depends on the imbalance and compensatory changes over time. This model alone cannot diagnose the cause of swelling.

oralExamination.prompt: Does the word button identify an intraluminal valve?
oralExamination.answer: No. It describes a discontinuous endothelial junction. Distinguish the cell-border entry arrangement from a valve within the vessel lumen.

oralExamination.prompt: Why is a diagram with complete venous-end reabsorption an incomplete general model?
oralExamination.answer: It omits sustained net filtration and lymphatic return in many tissues. State the tissue and steady-state assumptions rather than applying that diagram universally.

summaryChecklist: Trace fluid from capillary to interstitium and into the lymphatic return route.
Identify the difference between button-like and zipper-like junctions.
Explain why reduced removal can cause accumulation without increased filtration.

lessons.subject: physiology
lessons.title: Measure body-fluid compartments by indicator dilution
lessons.summary: Choose a tracer, correct for losses and calculate measured and derived fluid volumes with consistent units.
tags: Measure body-fluid compartments by indicator dilution
lessons.section: 1.1 Body-Fluid Compartments and Their Determination

steps.title: Begin with conservation of the indicator
steps.body: A known amount of indicator is placed into an unknown fluid volume. After mixing, concentration equals the amount remaining divided by that volume. Rearranging gives volume = amount remaining / equilibrated concentration. The indicator should mix throughout the compartment of interest, remain measurable and avoid appreciable entry into other compartments during the measurement. The calculation measures the distribution space of the tracer; naming that space requires understanding its behaviour.

steps.title: Match the tracer to the compartment
steps.body: Labelled water can distribute across cell membranes and therefore estimates total body water. An extracellular marker that is largely excluded from cells estimates extracellular fluid. An indicator retained with plasma proteins estimates plasma volume. Intracellular fluid is usually derived as total body water minus extracellular fluid. Interstitial fluid is approximately extracellular fluid minus plasma volume; whether small transcellular spaces are included depends on the tracer and measurement convention.

steps.title: Correct the numerator before dividing
steps.body: If an indicator is excreted or otherwise lost before the equilibrium sample, subtract that loss from the administered amount. Dividing the full administered amount by a concentration already reduced by loss overestimates volume. Concentration must use units compatible with the dose: milligrams divided by milligrams per litre gives litres. A concentration in milligrams per millilitre instead gives millilitres. Do the unit cancellation explicitly before deciding whether an answer is plausible.

steps.title: Interpret the estimate rather than memorising a person
steps.body: The familiar total-body-water fraction is an illustrative average, not a constant for every person. Body composition and age alter the fractions. A result may also be distorted by sampling before complete mixing, indicator leakage or uncorrected disappearance. Subtraction combines the uncertainty of two measurements. Blood volume and plasma volume are different: in a simplified model, blood volume = plasma volume / (1 − haematocrit), with haematocrit expressed as a fraction.

objectives: Choose a tracer from the barrier it can cross.
Calculate compartment volume after correcting indicator loss.
Distinguish measured volume from a volume found by subtraction.

workedExample.title: A loss-corrected measurement
workedExample.prompt: A fictional extracellular tracer dose is 150 mg. By sampling, 10 mg has been lost and the equilibrated concentration is 10 mg/L. Total body water was measured separately as 42 L. Find extracellular and intracellular volumes.
solution: Remaining tracer = 150 − 10 = 140 mg.
Extracellular volume = 140 mg / 10 mg/L = 14 L.
Intracellular volume = 42 − 14 = 28 L.
Using 150 mg would give 15 L and overestimate extracellular volume by 1 L.

question.prompt: What happens if indicator loss is ignored but the final concentration is correctly measured?

options.reason: The numerator is too large when loss is ignored, so the calculated volume rises.
The administered amount exceeds the amount remaining; dividing that larger numerator by the same concentration overestimates volume.
The numerator and denominator must refer to the same amount of indicator at the measurement time.

recall.prompt: Explain why intracellular volume is usually calculated indirectly.
recall.answer: A total-body-water tracer enters both intracellular and extracellular water, while an extracellular tracer is largely excluded from cells. Subtracting the extracellular estimate from total body water gives intracellular volume. The result depends on the assumptions and measurement error of both tracer studies.

lessons.subject: physiology
lessons.title: ECG: connect time, conduction and lead direction
lessons.summary: Read a basic ECG as a timed electrical signal, calculate rate and distinguish a lead projection from the spread of activation.
tags: ECG: connect time, conduction and lead direction
lessons.section: 2.2 Cardiac vector and electrocardiography

steps.title: Keep the electrical and mechanical stories separate
steps.body: The ECG records changing voltage differences at the body surface. The P wave reflects atrial depolarisation, the QRS complex ventricular depolarisation and the T wave ventricular repolarisation. Atrial repolarisation is usually obscured by the much larger QRS. These are electrical events that precede or overlap mechanical events. A QRS complex is not itself a measurement of ejection or stroke volume, and an electrical tracing alone does not establish effective blood flow.

steps.title: Read the calibration first
steps.body: At a paper speed of 25 mm/s, one 1-mm small square represents 0.04 s and one 5-mm large square represents 0.20 s. At 50 mm/s the same distances represent half those times. Standard voltage calibration is often 10 mm/mV, but it must be checked rather than assumed. For a regular rhythm, heart rate in beats/min = 60 / R–R interval in seconds. Counting large squares with the 300 rule only applies at 25 mm/s.

steps.title: Define the interval endpoints
steps.body: The PR interval starts at P-wave onset and ends at QRS onset. It includes atrial depolarisation and conduction toward the ventricles; it is not simply the duration of the AV node alone. The PR segment begins after the P wave ends. QRS duration measures ventricular depolarisation. The QT interval extends from QRS onset to T-wave end and includes ventricular depolarisation and repolarisation. QT varies with rate, so a raw interval is not interpreted independently of heart rate.

steps.title: Project the vector onto a lead
steps.body: A lead has a positive and a negative direction. A net depolarisation vector toward its positive electrode produces an upward deflection; a vector pointing away produces a downward deflection. A nearly perpendicular vector can produce a small or biphasic signal. The same activation can therefore look different in different leads. Limb leads sample the frontal plane and chest leads the horizontal plane. Begin with calibration, rate, regularity, P-to-QRS relationship and intervals before making an interpretation.

objectives: Relate P, QRS and T to electrical events.
Convert ECG grid distances into time and rate.
Predict how a lead records a depolarisation vector.

workedExample.title: Read a calibrated strip
workedExample.prompt: A fictional regular tracing at 25 mm/s has four large squares between successive R peaks and four small squares from P onset to QRS onset. Calculate rate and PR interval.
solution: Rate = 60 / 0.80 = 75 beats/min.
If the speed were 50 mm/s, the same distances would instead represent 150 beats/min and 0.08 s. Calibration is essential.

question.prompt: At 25 mm/s, a regular R–R interval of five large squares corresponds to which rate?

options.reason: Five large squares last 1 second at this speed, not half a second.
That rate corresponds to four large squares at 25 mm/s.
Five times 0.20 s is 1 s per beat, so there are 60 beats per minute.

recall.prompt: Why can one depolarisation produce different deflections in two leads?
recall.answer: Each lead records the component of the changing electrical vector along its own axis. A vector toward one positive electrode may be nearly perpendicular to another lead. The leads are different views of the same activation, not different cardiac contractions.

lessons.subject: physiology
lessons.title: Alveolar ventilation: why breathing pattern matters
lessons.summary: Compare equal minute ventilations, account for dead space and predict carbon dioxide changes under stated assumptions.
tags: Alveolar ventilation: why breathing pattern matters
lessons.section: Dead space, alveolar ventilation and gas transport

steps.title: Separate total movement from useful ventilation
steps.body: Minute ventilation is tidal volume multiplied by breathing frequency. It measures the air moved at the airway opening per minute. Some air fills conducting passages and does not exchange gas with blood. In a simple model, alveolar ventilation = (tidal volume − dead-space volume) × frequency. Use the same units for both volumes. The expression describes effective ventilation only as well as the dead-space estimate represents the non-exchanging volume.

steps.title: Distinguish the two sources of dead space
steps.body: Anatomical dead space is the conducting-airway volume. Alveolar dead space represents ventilation reaching alveoli with absent or inadequate perfusion. Physiological dead space combines the two. The fixed anatomical value used in a classroom exercise is an assumption, not a universal patient measurement. A ventilation–perfusion disturbance may change physiological dead space even when conducting-airway anatomy has not changed.

steps.title: Compare patterns at the same minute ventilation
steps.body: For each breath, dead-space filling is paid before the remainder contributes to alveolar ventilation. When tidal volume is small, that cost takes a larger fraction of each breath. Increasing frequency can preserve minute ventilation while alveolar ventilation falls. This explains why the total litres breathed per minute cannot by itself tell you how effectively carbon dioxide is being removed.

steps.title: State the assumptions of the carbon dioxide prediction
steps.body: At steady state, arterial carbon dioxide tension varies approximately with carbon dioxide production divided by alveolar ventilation. If production is unchanged and alveolar ventilation halves, carbon dioxide tension tends to double. The relationship is a physiological model, not an instruction for setting a ventilator. Changing metabolism, non-steady-state conditions and altered gas exchange can make a simple numerical prediction inappropriate. Oxygenation also depends on inspired oxygen and gas-exchange matching, not ventilation alone.

objectives: Calculate minute and alveolar ventilation.
Explain why rapid shallow breaths waste more ventilation.
Use the inverse relationship between alveolar ventilation and carbon dioxide cautiously.

workedExample.title: Same total ventilation, different result
workedExample.prompt: Compare pattern A: 500 mL × 12/min and pattern B: 250 mL × 24/min. Assume a fixed 150 mL dead space.
solution: Both patterns give minute ventilation of 6,000 mL/min, or 6 L/min.
A: (500 − 150) × 12 = 4,200 mL/min alveolar ventilation.
B: (250 − 150) × 24 = 2,400 mL/min alveolar ventilation.
B has less alveolar ventilation despite the same total ventilation. At unchanged carbon dioxide production, steady-state carbon dioxide tension would tend to rise.

question.prompt: With 150 mL dead space, what is alveolar ventilation for 400 mL breaths at 15/min?

options.reason: Subtract 150 from 400 first, then multiply 250 mL by 15 and convert to litres.
This is minute ventilation and includes air that fills dead space.
This is the alveolar portion of one breath in litres, before multiplying by frequency.

recall.prompt: Explain why a normal-looking minute ventilation can hide ineffective ventilation.
recall.answer: Minute ventilation includes dead-space ventilation. Smaller, more frequent breaths can move the same total volume but devote a larger share to dead space. Increased alveolar dead space also reduces effective gas exchange. Calculate or assess the useful component before drawing conclusions about carbon dioxide removal.

lessons.subject: histology
lessons.title: Myelin and glia: identify the cell before the function
lessons.summary: Compare glial roles, nerve coverings and sensory versus autonomic ganglia. Read three separately documented peripheral-nerve preparations, then connect visible arrangement with developmental lineage and bounded experimental evidence.
tags: Myelin and glia: identify the cell before the function
lessons.section: Supporting Cells; Myelination; Peripheral Nerve Structure; current selected nerve and ganglion text; original branch-versus-relay reasoning; original peripheral-nerve preparation, compartment and developmental-evidence practical

steps.title: Begin with location and relationships
steps.body: A supporting cell should be interpreted in its tissue context. Astrocytes regulate the neuronal environment, including extracellular potassium and transmitter handling. Oligodendrocytes form CNS myelin, while microglia are resident immune cells. Ependymal cells line most ventricular surfaces. In peripheral ganglia, satellite cells surround neuronal cell bodies. Schwann cells associate with peripheral axons. The word glia groups several distinct cell types rather than describing one universal support function.

steps.title: Count internodes rather than whole axons
steps.body: One myelinating Schwann cell forms one internode of one peripheral axon. A long axon therefore needs many successive Schwann cells. A single oligodendrocyte can extend processes to form internodes on several CNS axons. Nodes of Ranvier interrupt the myelin sheath and contain membrane specialised for regenerating the action potential. Myelin increases membrane resistance and reduces effective capacitance, helping local current spread toward the next node.

steps.title: Do not equate unmyelinated with unsupported
steps.body: Small peripheral axons can lie in grooves within a non-myelinating Schwann cell as a Remak bundle. They have Schwann-cell support without a compact multilamellar myelin sheath. Electrical conduction along axonal membrane is also different from axonal transport. Microtubule-based transport moves vesicles, proteins and organelles inside the axon; the propagation of a voltage change does not carry those materials down the nerve.

steps.title: Read the connective compartments at the right scale
steps.body: Start with one fibre, then one fascicle, then the entire nerve. Delicate endoneurial matrix surrounds individual axon–Schwann-cell units within a fascicle and contains capillaries. A layered perineurial cellular sleeve encloses the fascicle; its junctions help regulate diffusion across that boundary. Epineurial connective tissue supports the whole nerve and extends between fascicles, carrying larger vessels and sometimes adipose tissue. The vascular blood–nerve barrier is associated with endoneurial capillary endothelium, a different boundary from the perineurial sleeve. In the transverse teaching image, the pale separation cleft is not itself a cellular sheath. Look for a continuous tissue boundary before assigning a perineurial label. The broad peripheral fibrous region can be described without claiming that every part of it is one specialised cell layer. Routine processing can dissolve myelin lipid, leaving pale rings or spaces. Preparation and image context remain essential when interpreting a dark nucleus.
steps.highlight: Follow the scale: individual fibre → fascicle → whole nerve. A space is not a cellular sheath.

steps.title: Read the field at two scales
steps.body: Begin with the arrangement of the whole field. The longitudinal specimen contains parallel, undulating profiles; the transverse specimen contains many small profiles within a broad fascicular region. Then inspect nuclei, boundaries and surrounding matrix. These independent images illustrate different views of elongated structures. They do not show one bundle rotated in real time or adjacent sections of one specimen. Compare organisation before inferring a named cell.
steps.highlight: Orientation changes the profile. A profile is not a complete cell.

steps.title: Choose preparation for the biological question
steps.body: Routine architecture, lipid-rich sheath contrast and protein localisation are different questions. The third specimen is explicitly described by its provider as osmium-tetroxide prepared; its dark longitudinal profiles give useful myelin-related contrast. The other two providers do not document their stains. Pink and purple colours alone are insufficient to supply that missing history. When planning an actual supervised laboratory study, record the tissue, orientation, fixation, processing, stain, controls and imaging settings. Use the laboratory's validated procedure rather than inventing a universal preparation recipe from a photograph.
steps.highlight: Documented preparation has priority over a colour-based guess.

steps.title: Do not turn a display magnification into a ruler
steps.body: The historical 100× and 200× descriptions concern acquisition. Browser resizing, cropping and display density change how large the same pixels appear. None of these three files supplies a calibrated scale bar. They support qualitative comparisons of organisation, but not a defensible measurement of axon diameter or myelin thickness. Similarly, a two-dimensional profile count is not automatically the count of complete cells in a three-dimensional organ. A quantitative study needs a defined sampling method and calibration appropriate to its question.
steps.highlight: A larger display is not a new measurement.

steps.title: Locate cell bodies before naming a ganglion
steps.body: A peripheral ganglion is a region containing neuronal cell bodies as well as their processes, supporting cells and connective tissue. A nerve fascicle is organised mainly around travelling axons and their supporting sheaths. Finding a fibre bundle next to a ganglion does not turn the bundle into a second ganglion. First describe whether the field contains neuronal somata, fascicles or both; then connect it with the known anatomical location.

steps.title: Follow one spinal sensory neuron through a branch point
steps.body: A typical mature dorsal-root-ganglion sensory neuron is pseudounipolar. A short process from its soma joins peripheral and central axonal processes. These processes belong to one neuron; their junction is not an obligatory relay onto a second neuron in the ganglion. A drawing that shows the soma beside the main route is a circuit explanation, not a promise that the junction will appear in one routine section. This comparison concerns typical spinal sensory neurons, not every sensory neuron or cranial ganglion.

steps.title: Place both cell bodies in an autonomic chain
steps.body: In a typical autonomic efferent chain, the preganglionic neuron has its soma in the CNS and sends an axon to a peripheral autonomic ganglion. There it synapses on a postganglionic neuron, whose soma lies in the ganglion and whose axon continues toward the effector. The chain contains two neurons, but that does not put both cell bodies inside the ganglion. Axons merely passing through a region must not automatically be assigned a synapse there.

steps.title: Separate a supporting-cell relationship from a cell count
steps.body: Satellite glia are associated with neuronal somata in peripheral ganglia; Schwann cells support peripheral axons, including compact-myelin and non-myelinating arrangements. This location-based distinction complements the earlier internode comparison. It does not identify every small dark nucleus in a field. Fibroblasts, vascular cells and other cells can also contribute nuclei. Section plane and preparation affect the visible profiles. A pale space around a neuronal soma is not sufficient evidence of compact myelin, and a ring-like appearance does not establish a universal glia-to-neuron ratio.

steps.title: Work two fully specified models without adding an unseen relay
steps.body: Model A is an invented complete drawing of one neuron S. Its peripheral process P and central process C meet at junction J; a short stem connects J with S’s soma. All three drawn segments are explicitly parts of S, and no synapse is drawn at J. The model therefore has one neuron, two named functional branches and no specified neuron-to-neuron synapse at J. Model B is a different invented path: neuron N1 has its soma in the CNS and makes one specified synapse on neuron N2 in a peripheral ganglion; N2 sends an axon to an effector. That path has two neurons, one specified neuronal synapse and one of its two somata in the ganglion. Counts refer only to the defined paths, not to every cell in an actual ganglion. Neither model supplies myelin status or conduction speed.

steps.title: Keep structural, physiological and research evidence distinct
steps.body: An ordinary section can support an anatomical interpretation without displaying the complete branching geometry or proving a functional synapse. Morphology, a molecular marker, an anatomical contact and an activity measurement answer different questions. For example, Kumari and colleagues studied neuron-satellite-glia relationships in mouse sympathetic ganglia using structural and functional measurements. Their findings are bounded by that study’s model and outcomes; they do not make a routine human section a measurement of neuronal activity. The ordinary sensory-versus-autonomic wiring comparison is also not a claim that no other local cell interactions can occur.

steps.title: Connect an adult nerve with embryology
steps.body: A spinal motor axon can lie in a peripheral nerve while its neuron's soma and developmental origin belong to the neural tube. Its Schwann-cell support follows a neural-crest-associated lineage. Adult proximity therefore does not establish shared ancestry. Trace the cell body, axon and supporting cell as separate components. A lineage experiment marks a defined progenitor population and follows descendants; an adult location or one marker-positive image is not that experiment. Developmental models also need their organism and stage stated.
steps.highlight: An axon in the PNS does not make its entire neuron neural-crest derived.

steps.title: Separate necessity, rescue and sufficiency
steps.body: Taveggia and colleagues compared sensory neurons from normal and NRG1 type III-deficient mice while supplying postnatal rat Schwann cells. Supplying the glia helps separate the neuronal-signal question from an earlier failure to generate enough Schwann cells. They assessed myelin proteins and ultrastructural ensheathment; restoring neuronal NRG1 type III rescued the defects. But Schwann cells grown with NRG1-expressing non-neuronal CHO cells did not express the measured myelin marker, despite increased Schwann-cell accumulation. Thus this signal was necessary and instructive in the tested setting, while other axonal signals were also needed. Loss, rescue and an alternative cellular context answer different questions. These experiments do not quantify NRG1 in the teaching photographs or establish a human treatment.
steps.highlight: Restoration strengthens a causal interpretation; a different cellular context tests whether the signal alone is enough.

steps.title: Separate developmental origin from an injury response
steps.body: Arthur-Farraj and colleagues studied a c-Jun-dependent Schwann-cell response to nerve injury in mice. Their work supports a specialised repair programme rather than treating an injured adult Schwann cell as simply identical to its embryonic precursor. A perturbation that impairs recovery after injury does not, by itself, show that the same factor was required for every earlier developmental step. Compare injured and uninjured controls and keep structural, molecular and functional outcomes distinct.
steps.highlight: Repair state, embryonic lineage and normal adult appearance are different questions.

steps.title: Follow descendants rather than assuming one route
steps.body: Erickson and colleagues combined lineage tracing and selective nerve ablation in mouse embryos. They found contributions from nerve-associated Schwann-cell precursors to sympathetic neurons and satellite glia after the initial neural-crest seeding of the ganglia. This adds developmental detail to a simple origin table; it does not make all ganglion cells descendants of mature myelinating Schwann cells. The authors reported no randomisation or blinding in the experimental analyses, which should remain visible when discussing evidential strength.
steps.highlight: A precursor contribution is not a claim about every mature cell.

objectives: Compare Schwann cells with oligodendrocytes.
Distinguish myelination from axonal transport.
Use tissue organisation to recognise a peripheral nerve.
Distinguish a typical spinal sensory neuron’s branches from a two-neuron autonomic efferent chain.
Locate the preganglionic and postganglionic somata without placing both inside a peripheral ganglion.
Separate observed cell relationships from complete-cell counts, functional contacts and research outcomes.
Compare nerve orientation and preparation without inventing undocumented stains or scale.
Separate visible nerve profiles from cellular identity, molecular expression and developmental ancestry.
Distinguish loss, rescue, cellular context and injury-response evidence in selected experiments.

workedExample.title: Reconstruct a nerve from a description
workedExample.prompt: A section shows several rounded fascicles, each with a concentric cellular boundary. Fine connective tissue surrounds individual fibres; thicker connective tissue lies between bundles.
solution: The boundary of each fascicle is perineurium.
The delicate tissue within the fascicle is endoneurium.
The tissue joining and surrounding fascicles is epineurium.
These relations support peripheral-nerve identification. They do not by themselves prove the physiological class of each fibre.

question.prompt: Which statement correctly compares myelinating cells?

options.text: One Schwann cell myelinates the entire length of a peripheral axon
options.reason: Each cell forms one internode, so long axons require many Schwann cells.

options.text: An oligodendrocyte can form internodes on multiple CNS axons
options.reason: Its processes can contact several axons, unlike the one-internode arrangement of a myelinating Schwann cell.

options.text: An unmyelinated peripheral axon cannot contact a Schwann cell
options.reason: Remak bundles contain small axons supported by non-myelinating Schwann cells.

recall.prompt: Give a structured oral comparison of CNS and PNS myelin.
recall.answer: Name oligodendrocytes in the CNS and Schwann cells in the PNS. Compare one cell serving several CNS internodes with one Schwann cell per peripheral internode. Explain the nodes and saltatory conduction, then distinguish compact myelin from non-myelinating Schwann-cell support.

oralExamination.prompt: Why do peripheral and central processes not require two sensory neurons in the defined Model A?
oralExamination.answer: The model explicitly makes both processes and the somal stem parts of neuron S. A branch divides a process within that cell; a neuron-to-neuron synapse would be an additional relationship that the model does not specify at J.

oralExamination.prompt: Where are the two somata in the defined Model B?
oralExamination.answer: N1’s soma is in the CNS. N2’s soma is in the peripheral ganglion. The two-neuron chain does not imply two somata inside that ganglion, and says nothing about all the other cells an actual ganglion contains.

oralExamination.prompt: How does the satellite-glia/Schwann-cell distinction connect with the original myelin lesson?
oralExamination.answer: Satellite glia are associated with peripheral neuronal somata; Schwann cells support axons. A myelinating Schwann cell forms an internode, while non-myelinating Schwann cells support axons without compact myelin. None of these statements identifies a cell solely from one dark nucleus.

oralExamination.prompt: Does failure to see a T-shaped profile refute a pseudounipolar organisation?
oralExamination.answer: No. A section may miss part of a three-dimensional cell and its junction. The usual organisation comes from anatomical evidence; it must not be presented as a feature directly resolved in every field.

oralExamination.prompt: What can a pale halo or a cluster of small nuclei establish by itself?
oralExamination.answer: Neither establishes compact myelin, an exact glial subtype or a universal cell ratio. Describe the profiles, location and preparation; further evidence may be needed for cell identity or complete counts.

oralExamination.prompt: Why must a mouse sympathetic-ganglion study remain distinct from routine human histology?
oralExamination.answer: Organism, tissue, experimental conditions and measured outcomes define its scope. An observation of structure or contact is not itself an activity measurement or a demonstrated human clinical effect.

summaryChecklist: Locate neuronal somata, axonal regions and connective-tissue boundaries before naming the structure.
Count cells and branches as different units in a fully specified model.
Place the autonomic preganglionic soma in the CNS and postganglionic soma in the peripheral ganglion.
Distinguish soma-associated satellite glia from axon-associated Schwann cells without over-reading a nucleus.
State what the section does not resolve: complete geometry, exact cell identity or functional contact.
Keep research organism, tissue and outcome separate from an unmeasured human response.

lessons.subject: histology
lessons.title: Brain and CSF barriers: tissue structure, development and transport
lessons.summary: Identify choroid-plexus architecture, trace the endothelial and epithelial interfaces, and connect developmental evidence to selective transport experiments.
lessons.section: CNS interfaces: histology and embryology

steps.title: Start with compartments and a direction of travel
steps.body: Blood, brain interstitial fluid and ventricular cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) are different compartments. Draw them separately before naming a barrier. Blood inside a vessel has not entered the surrounding brain, and material reaching ventricular fluid has not necessarily reached a neuron at the same concentration. The route from a typical brain capillary to interstitial fluid crosses endothelium. The route from a choroid-plexus capillary to ventricular CSF also encounters a specialised epithelial covering. A useful explanation names the starting compartment, the destination and every intervening cell layer. The word barrier describes selective exchange; it does not mean that all substances are permanently excluded.

practice.prompt: Why can a measurement in ventricular CSF be insufficient to establish the concentration inside a brain cell?
practice.feedback: The sample and the cell occupy different compartments. Additional interfaces, transport and distribution separate them; a concentration in one compartment is not a direct measurement in another.

steps.title: Recognise the epithelial covering and vascular core
steps.body: In the supplied H&E image, follow the outside of several projecting profiles. Closely arranged epithelial cells form the covering; their nuclei make a peripheral row. Inside lie pale stromal material and vascular lumina containing strongly eosinophilic erythrocytes. The epithelium, stroma and blood vessels are components of one frond, not three separate organs. The source identifies human lateral-ventricle choroid plexus. That context matters because an isolated epithelial-covered vascular projection is not unique to this organ. Describe the repeated epithelial–stromal pattern first, then use its location to support the identification.

steps.title: Put the apical and basal surfaces in the right places
steps.body: The epithelial apical surface faces ventricular CSF outside the frond. Its basal surface faces the underlying stromal compartment, while lateral surfaces contact neighbouring epithelial cells. This is the reverse of an interpretation that treats the vascular centre as a glandular lumen. The mature covering is generally simple cuboidal to low columnar, with an apical microvillous surface and a specialised transport apparatus. Individual microvilli, membrane infoldings and transporter molecules cannot be reliably resolved in this H&E field. Distinguish the polarity inferred from tissue organisation from ultrastructural features established by other methods.

steps.title: A ring in a section need not be a secretory acinus
steps.body: A branching three-dimensional frond can be cut longitudinally, obliquely or across its tip. These cuts create elongated profiles, rounded islands and apparently disconnected pieces within one section. Look inside a ring: erythrocytes within an internal vessel and an intervening stromal core favour a vascular projection rather than an epithelial acinus surrounding a secretory lumen. A crowded nuclear edge may reflect an oblique cut or fold rather than true stratification. Compare several intact profiles and obtain lower-power orientation or serial sections when the relationship remains uncertain.

practice.prompt: A rounded profile has peripheral epithelial nuclei and a central erythrocyte-filled lumen. What two levels of structure must you separate?
practice.feedback: The epithelial-covered frond is the larger structure. The blood-vessel lumen lies inside its stromal core; it is not a secretory lumen directly bounded by the outer epithelium.

steps.title: Use H&E contrast to locate structures, not to measure function
steps.body: Hematoxylin-based nuclear staining depends on oxidised dye and a mordant; after bluing, nuclear material appears blue to purple. Eosin provides contrasting pink-to-red staining of many protein-rich structures, including cytoplasm and erythrocytes. In this specimen, use nuclear position, epithelial continuity and the boundaries of erythrocyte-containing spaces together. Strong pink staining does not identify a transporter, and dark nuclei do not directly quantify metabolic activity. Stain balance, processing and section thickness influence appearance. H&E helps you recognise the architecture in which a barrier operates; it is not a direct assay of permeability or secretion.

steps.title: Explain what preparation contributes to the slide
steps.body: A routine paraffin workflow stabilises tissue by fixation, supports it by embedding, produces thin sections, and adds contrast by staining. Solvent exchange and cutting change the specimen: shrinkage, extraction, compression and tearing can alter apparent spaces. During H&E staining, paraffin is removed and sections are brought into conditions compatible with aqueous nuclear staining; differentiation is used in some protocols, followed by bluing, counterstaining and preparation for mounting. Exact reagents and timings belong to the laboratory's validated procedure. The image provider gives H&E and a 50 µm scale bar but not fixation, embedding or section thickness, so those details remain unknown for this field.

steps.title: Choose a method that can answer the structural question
steps.body: Light microscopy shows the epithelial covering, connective-tissue core and vascular lumina. Transmission electron microscopy can resolve membrane profiles, junctional contacts, microvilli and organelles at a different scale. In the Xu study, electron-microscopy specimens underwent aldehyde fixation, heavy-metal contrast, resin embedding and ultrathin sectioning; the resulting contrast is not H&E colour. Immunolabelling addresses molecular localisation, while a tracer experiment addresses passage under specified conditions. Increasing digital magnification cannot recover unresolved structures from the H&E photograph. Decide whether the question concerns architecture, ultrastructure, a molecular target or a functional measurement before choosing the method.

steps.title: A protein label establishes a location before it establishes a mechanism
steps.body: Praetorius and Nielsen used immunoperoxidase histochemistry in human choroid plexus to map membrane proteins. Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase α1 and NKCC1 immunoreactivity was apical, whereas several acid–base transporters were basolateral. This supports a polarised epithelial organisation. It does not directly measure the rate or direction of transport in a living cell. A staining experiment also needs appropriate positive and negative controls and comparable tissue processing. Do not equate absence of detectable staining with proof that a protein can never be expressed, or treat a brown reaction product as a measurement of CSF secretion.

steps.title: Trace blood to CSF through the choroid plexus
steps.body: Follow the route in order: vascular lumen, fenestrated capillary wall, stromal extracellular space, epithelial basal surface, epithelial layer and ventricular CSF. The capillary endothelium here permits exchange with the stroma more readily than typical brain-capillary endothelium. The principal blood–CSF junctional boundary lies between adjacent choroid epithelial cells near their apical region. Material in the stroma still faces that epithelial interface. Transport through epithelial cells and restricted passage between them are distinct routes. A fenestrated capillary therefore does not provide a direct, unregulated opening from blood into the ventricle.

steps.title: Trace blood to brain through the endothelial interface
steps.body: At typical CNS capillaries, continuous endothelial cells form the luminal lining. Junctions between them restrict paracellular passage, and low nonspecific transcytosis limits vesicular transport through the cells. These are complementary properties, not two names for the same mechanism. Needed substances still cross through appropriate pathways; a selective interface is not an absolutely impermeable wall. In a drawing, place the endothelial cell between blood and the surrounding basement-membrane and support-cell environment. In H&E, identifying a capillary or its nucleus does not demonstrate that its junctional proteins and transport pathways are functioning normally.

steps.title: Distinguish pericytes and astrocytic support from the sealing cell
steps.body: Pericytes closely associate with the abluminal endothelial surface and its basement-membrane environment. Astrocytic endfeet approach from the nervous tissue. Both participate in the neurovascular unit, but neither should replace endothelium as the principal blood–brain sealing layer. Their proximity also makes identification from isolated small nuclei unreliable. Molecular labelling, ultrastructure or a clearly oriented diagram may establish relationships that routine H&E cannot. When discussing an experiment, distinguish the cell that was altered from the cell whose permeability changed: a supporting population can influence an endothelial property without becoming the endothelial junction itself.

steps.title: Ordinary ependyma and choroid epithelium are different interfaces
steps.body: Ordinary ependyma lines the ventricles and central canal over nervous tissue; its apical cilia can contribute to local fluid movement. Choroid epithelium covers a vascular stromal core and has the specialised junctional and transport organisation of the blood–CSF interface. Sharing a ventricular-facing surface does not make these tissues functionally identical. Likewise, describing choroid epithelium as specialised ventricular epithelium should not imply that mature ordinary ependymal cells simply acquire capillaries to form it. Its developmental specification and regional progenitors need to be considered separately. In a practical, identify what lies beneath the lining before assigning the tissue.

steps.title: Place the glia limitans at its own boundary
steps.body: The superficial glia limitans includes astrocytic endfeet and associated basement membrane beneath the pia. Perivascular astrocytic organisation surrounds penetrating vessels and their associated boundaries.
