lessons.summary: Convert transmission into absorbance and design a defensible concentration measurement.
lessons.section: Combined notes, practical questions 22–32

steps.title: Establish the reference
steps.body: Measure a blank containing the appropriate solvent and container contribution. Then compare sample intensity I with blank intensity I₀. Use A = −log₁₀(I/I₀), taking transmission as a fraction rather than a percentage. A monochromator selects a wavelength range; it does not remove every instrumental error.

steps.title: Compare two samples
steps.body: Absorbance 1 means 10% transmission and absorbance 3 means 0.1%. The second transmits 100 times less light, although its absorbance is only three times as large. Under Beer–Lambert assumptions, concentration is proportional to absorbance at fixed wavelength and path length.

steps.title: Work a dilution
steps.body: A fivefold diluted sample has A = 0.40, and the calibration gives concentration 2 units per absorbance unit. Diluted concentration is 0.80 units; original concentration is 4.0 units. Apply the dilution factor after using the calibration, and keep concentration units consistent.

steps.title: Recognise failed assumptions
steps.body: Stray light, turbidity, chemical changes and detector limits can bend a calibration. A reading beyond the validated range should prompt suitable dilution or method review. A blank cannot make a scattering suspension behave like an ideal clear solution.

question.prompt: Absorbance changes from 1 to 3. Transmission changes by…

options.reason: Absorbance is logarithmic, so transmission does not follow its simple ratio.
Higher absorbance means lower transmission.
10⁻³/10⁻¹ = 10⁻², or one hundredth.

recall.prompt: Explain blanks, dilution and absorbance: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: 10⁻³/10⁻¹ = 10⁻², or one hundredth. 0.6 × 10 = 6 concentration units. Stray light, turbidity, chemical changes and detector limits can bend a calibration. A reading beyond the validated range should prompt suitable dilution or method review. A blank cannot make a scattering suspension behave like an ideal clear solution.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Practical: optical rotation and chirality
lessons.summary: Distinguish optical rotation from absorption and use a polarimetric calibration.
lessons.section: Combined notes, practical questions 33–42

steps.title: Prepare a polarised reference
steps.body: A polariser produces a defined polarisation state; an analyser compares the emerging orientation. Optical activity rotates the plane of linearly polarised light in suitable chiral media. Linear, circular and elliptical polarisation describe field evolution, not different photon charges.

steps.title: State Biot's relation
steps.body: For suitable conditions, rotation α = [α]lc, with specific rotation [α], path length l and concentration c in the convention used by the calibration. Temperature and wavelength must be specified. Opposite enantiomers can rotate equally in opposite directions; a racemic mixture may cancel net rotation.

steps.title: Work a path change
steps.body: A sample rotates light by +8° in a 1 dm cell. Under the same conditions, a 2 dm cell gives +16°. If concentration also halves, the rotation returns to +8°. Keep the sign because clockwise and counterclockwise rotations should not be reduced to unsigned brightness values.

steps.title: Interpret a null result
steps.body: Zero net rotation does not prove that no chiral molecules are present. Opposite contributions may cancel, concentration may be too low, or the measurement may be unsuitable. A polarimeter alone also does not determine a molecule's complete three-dimensional structure.

question.prompt: Path length doubles while concentration halves. Ideal optical rotation…

options.reason: In α = [α]lc, multiplying l by 2 and c by 1/2 cancels.
Both path length and concentration must be included.
The product lc remains unchanged rather than vanishing.

recall.prompt: Explain optical rotation and chirality: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: In α = [α]lc, multiplying l by 2 and c by 1/2 cancels. A null net signal can reflect cancellation rather than absence of chiral species. Zero net rotation does not prove that no chiral molecules are present. Opposite contributions may cancel, concentration may be too low, or the measurement may be unsuitable. A polarimeter alone also does not determine a molecule's complete three-dimensional structure.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Practical: eye optics and visual acuity
lessons.summary: Relate refractive error and angular resolution to the eye's optical system.
lessons.section: Combined notes, practical questions 43–58

steps.title: Use a simplified eye
steps.body: The eye's combined optical power is often approximated near 60 D, with a major contribution from the cornea. Accommodation changes lens shape and power. This reduced-eye model is useful for reasoning but does not capture every refracting surface or individual variation.

steps.title: Locate the focus
steps.body: In myopia, parallel rays focus in front of the retina in the uncorrected relaxed eye; a diverging correction reduces effective convergence. In hyperopia, the relaxed focus would lie behind the retina; a converging correction can help. Presbyopia concerns reduced accommodation rather than being identical to either axial refractive error.

steps.title: Interpret acuity
steps.body: Acuity tests assess the smallest resolvable angular detail under defined conditions. If minimum resolvable angle is 2 arcminutes, decimal acuity under the conventional reciprocal relation is 0.5. Viewing distance, contrast and correct use of the chart matter; an acuity value alone does not measure all aspects of vision.

steps.title: Explain the blind spot
steps.body: The optic disc lacks photoreceptors where the nerve exits. A target can disappear at the corresponding visual-field position despite intact surrounding vision. This is anatomically different from optical blur caused by defocus, and it is not the same structure as the fovea.

question.prompt: What optical correction is used conceptually for myopia?

options.text: A lens that moves the retina physically
options.reason: A spectacle lens alters ray convergence, not retinal position.
Reducing convergence helps move the focus back toward the retina.

options.text: A converging lens that adds more positive power
options.reason: More convergence would move the relaxed focus farther in front of the retina.

recall.prompt: Explain eye optics and visual acuity: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: Reducing convergence helps move the focus back toward the retina. Decimal acuity is 1/2 = 0.5 for this convention. The optic disc lacks photoreceptors where the nerve exits. A target can disappear at the corresponding visual-field position despite intact surrounding vision. This is anatomically different from optical blur caused by defocus, and it is not the same structure as the fovea.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Practical: scintillation spectra and background
lessons.summary: Distinguish pulse height, energy calibration and count rate.
lessons.section: Combined notes, practical questions 59–66, 127–132

steps.title: Trace the chain
steps.body: Scintillator light produces photoelectrons, dynodes amplify them and electronics shape a pulse. A spectrum bins pulses by height; calibration relates channel to deposited energy. Increasing photomultiplier gain can shift a peak along the channel axis without changing the radionuclide's emission energy.

steps.title: Account for background
steps.body: Subtract expected background counts with an appropriate time scaling. For independent counts, variances add when subtracting. A discriminator can reject low pulses, but raising the threshold may remove true low-energy events as well as noise. Signal-to-noise improvement must be assessed, not assumed.

steps.title: Work a rate
steps.body: A sample-plus-background count of 1200 over 60 s gives 20 counts/s. Background 300 over 60 s gives 5 counts/s, so net rate is 15 counts/s. The uncertainty of the difference is based on both counts, approximately √1500/60 ≈ 0.65 counts/s in the simple Poisson model.

steps.title: Separate efficiency from activity
steps.body: A source with 1000 decays/s may produce far fewer detected counts because of geometry, branching and detector efficiency. Changing source distance alters count rate without changing physical activity. Dead time and pile-up complicate high-rate measurements and can distort both counts and spectral shapes.

question.prompt: Detector gain increases and a peak moves to a higher channel. The emitted photon energy…

options.text: Must have increased in the source
options.reason: Electronic amplification does not change nuclear transition energies.
A channel shift does not imply missing energy.
Gain changes the channel–energy mapping and requires suitable calibration.

recall.prompt: Explain scintillation spectra and background: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: Gain changes the channel–energy mapping and requires suitable calibration. Net rate is 30 − 8 = 22 counts/s. A source with 1000 decays/s may produce far fewer detected counts because of geometry, branching and detector efficiency. Changing source distance alters count rate without changing physical activity. Dead time and pile-up complicate high-rate measurements and can distort both counts and spectral shapes.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Practical: half-value layers and shielding curves
lessons.summary: Translate exponential attenuation into thickness while recognising beam assumptions.
lessons.section: Combined notes, practical questions 67–75

steps.title: Define attenuation quantities
steps.body: For a narrow monoenergetic beam in a uniform material, I/I₀ = exp(−μx). Linear attenuation coefficient μ has inverse-length units. Mass attenuation coefficient μ/ρ separates density, and areal density ρx has mass-per-area units. Absorption and removal from the direct beam are not identical.

steps.title: Use layer definitions
steps.body: Half-value layer is ln 2/μ; tenth-value layer is ln 10/μ. Two half-value layers leave one quarter and three leave one eighth. For a broad polyenergetic beam, scatter and beam hardening can prevent a single constant half-value layer from describing every depth.

steps.title: Work thickness
steps.body: If the half-value layer is 2 cm in the stated model, reducing direct intensity to 1/16 requires four layers, or 8 cm. This is a mathematical teaching example, not a shielding design specification. Actual shielding depends on the spectrum, geometry and regulatory context.

steps.title: Compare materials fairly
steps.body: Lead attenuation varies with photon energy; it has no universal percentage reduction per millimetre. Water and steam at the same thickness have different areal densities. At equal composition and appropriate energy, using mass thickness clarifies why density changes the linear attenuation.

question.prompt: Three half-value layers leave what direct-beam fraction?

options.reason: Each half-value layer halves the remaining direct beam, so three layers give (1/2)³ = 1/8.
Each layer halves the remaining beam.
Attenuation cannot increase the direct beam under this model.

recall.prompt: Explain half-value layers and shielding curves: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: (1/2)³ = 1/8. cm⁻¹ multiplied by cm gives a dimensionless exponent. Lead attenuation varies with photon energy; it has no universal percentage reduction per millimetre. Water and steam at the same thickness have different areal densities. At equal composition and appropriate energy, using mass thickness clarifies why density changes the linear attenuation.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Practical: oscillations, damping and resonance
lessons.summary: Predict frequency changes and interpret a driven oscillator's response.
lessons.section: Combined notes, practical questions 76–83

steps.title: Start with an ideal oscillator
steps.body: For a mass on an ideal spring, f = (1/2π)√(k/m). Displacement, velocity and acceleration have related but different phases. The model requires small motion in a linear spring regime; a biological structure may be nonlinear or have several modes.

steps.title: Add damping and driving
steps.body: Damping dissipates mechanical energy and reduces free-oscillation amplitude. Periodic forcing produces a frequency-dependent response, with resonance shaped by damping. Greater damping usually broadens and lowers the resonance peak. Resonance does not mean a device produces energy without external input.

steps.title: Work a change
steps.body: Doubling mass at fixed k multiplies frequency by 1/√2 ≈ 0.707. Doubling k at fixed mass multiplies frequency by √2. A cantilever can act as a mechanical sensor because changes in effective stiffness or mass affect its oscillation response.

steps.title: Read a decay curve
steps.body: An exponentially decaying amplitude should not be confused with the energy envelope: in a simple harmonic mode, energy scales with amplitude squared. A halved amplitude therefore corresponds to one quarter of the oscillation energy under the same stiffness.

question.prompt: Mass quadruples at unchanged spring stiffness. Frequency…

options.reason: The square root makes the factor one half.
f scales as 1/√m, so a fourfold mass halves frequency.
Mass appears in the denominator inside the square root.

recall.prompt: Explain oscillations, damping and resonance: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: f scales as 1/√m, so a fourfold mass halves frequency. The energy ratio is (1/2)² = 1/4. An exponentially decaying amplitude should not be confused with the energy envelope: in a simple harmonic mode, energy scales with amplitude squared. A halved amplitude therefore corresponds to one quarter of the oscillation energy under the same stiffness.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Practical: resistance, capacitance and biological impedance
lessons.summary: Explain why tissue response depends on signal frequency and electrode arrangement.
lessons.section: Combined notes, practical questions 84–93

steps.title: Separate electrical quantities
steps.body: Resistance relates voltage and current for an ideal resistor, V = IR. Resistivity also accounts for geometry through R = ρL/A. A capacitor stores separated charge, Q = CV, and has capacitive reactance magnitude Xc = 1/(2πfC). Reactance introduces a phase relationship as well as a magnitude.

steps.title: Model a membrane or skin interface
steps.body: An RC equivalent circuit can represent some frequency-dependent behaviour, but real tissue and electrode interfaces are more complex. Higher frequency reduces capacitive reactance. Electrode placement, contact quality and geometry influence a measured impedance; it is not an intrinsic tissue number independent of the method.

steps.title: Work a frequency change
steps.body: For C = 1 μF at f = 1000 Hz, Xc ≈ 159 Ω. At 2000 Hz it is about 79.6 Ω. An ideal capacitor blocks steady DC after charging but can carry changing current; this does not mean charge crosses its insulating layer as in a resistor.

steps.title: Distinguish peak and RMS
steps.body: For a sinusoidal voltage, Vrms = Vpeak/√2. Resistive power uses Vrms²/R for that waveform. Combining peak voltage with an RMS power formula produces a factor-of-two error. Classroom circuit equations do not establish safe currents or electrode procedures for use on people.

question.prompt: Frequency doubles for an ideal capacitor. Reactance magnitude…

options.reason: Frequency is in the denominator of 1/(2πfC).
Capacitive reactance is frequency dependent.
Doubling f halves Xc at fixed capacitance.

recall.prompt: Explain resistance, capacitance and biological impedance: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: Doubling f halves Xc at fixed capacitance. 10/√2 ≈ 7.07 V. For a sinusoidal voltage, Vrms = Vpeak/√2. Resistive power uses Vrms²/R for that waveform. Combining peak voltage with an RMS power formula produces a factor-of-two error. Classroom circuit equations do not establish safe currents or electrode procedures for use on people.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Practical: gain, decibels and bandwidth
lessons.summary: Use gain ratios correctly and recognise when amplification loses information.
lessons.section: Combined notes, practical questions 94–103

steps.title: Define the ratio
steps.body: Voltage gain is output voltage divided by input voltage. For a voltage ratio, gain in decibels is 20 log₁₀|Vout/Vin|; interpreting that as power gain requires appropriate impedance conditions. Power ratios use 10 log₁₀(Pout/Pin). A decibel value needs its reference and quantity.

steps.title: Read a frequency response
steps.body: Amplifier gain can vary with frequency. Bandwidth identifies a useful range under a stated criterion, commonly relative to a midband level. Negative feedback can improve stability and linearity while changing gain and bandwidth. It cannot recover information already clipped at an earlier stage.

steps.title: Work a gain
steps.body: A 2 mV input becomes 200 mV, giving voltage gain 100 and 40 dB. A further stage with gain 10 gives total gain 1000, or 60 dB. Linear gains multiply, while their decibel values add when defined consistently.

steps.title: Check clipping and loading
steps.body: A signal that exceeds available output range clips, distorting the waveform and adding spectral components. A voltage divider's output also changes when a load draws current. Write down input range, output limit and loading assumptions before treating an amplifier as a perfect multiplier.

question.prompt: A voltage gain of 10 corresponds to…

options.reason: 20 log₁₀10 = 20 dB.
Voltage gain uses 20 log₁₀ of the ratio.
Decibel gain is logarithmic, not the square of the ratio.

recall.prompt: Explain gain, decibels and bandwidth: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: 20 log₁₀10 = 20 dB. The first multiplies by 5 and the second by 4, giving 20. A signal that exceeds available output range clips, distorting the waveform and adding spectral components. A voltage divider's output also changes when a load draws current. Write down input range, output limit and loading assumptions before treating an amplifier as a perfect multiplier.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Practical: electrical cell counting
lessons.summary: Connect an impedance pulse to particle volume and identify coincidence errors.
lessons.section: Combined notes, practical questions 104–111

steps.title: Explain the aperture
steps.body: In a Coulter-type measurement, particles suspended in conducting electrolyte pass through a small aperture. A particle displaces conducting liquid and changes electrical resistance, producing a pulse. Under calibrated conditions, pulse size relates to displaced volume, while pulse count relates to the number of detected passages.

steps.title: Control the suspension
steps.body: An appropriate electrolyte and suspension preserve meaningful particle behaviour. Dilution reduces the chance that two particles occupy the sensing region together. Debris, aggregation and particles outside the calibrated range can distort a distribution; the instrument does not identify every cell type from volume alone.

steps.title: Work a dilution correction
steps.body: A diluted sample yields 200 counted particles per μL after the instrument's volume calculation. With a 100-fold dilution, the original estimate is 20,000 per μL. This assumes representative mixing, correct sampled volume and negligible unresolved coincidence.

steps.title: Interpret coincidence
steps.body: Two cells passing together may generate one larger event, biasing both count and apparent size. Lowering concentration can test whether coincidence contributes. A histogram peak is a population pattern, not proof that every event represents one normal cell.

question.prompt: What most directly influences pulse height in a calibrated Coulter measurement?

options.reason: The method senses an electrical displacement effect, not sequence.
Pulse amplitude is related to the volume displacing conducting electrolyte.

options.text: Only the number of cells in the entire tube
options.reason: Total sample count and individual pulse height are different measurements.

recall.prompt: Explain electrical cell counting: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: Pulse amplitude is related to the volume displacing conducting electrolyte. Reduced concentration lowers coincidence probability under suitable counting conditions. Two cells passing together may generate one larger event, biasing both count and apparent size. Lowering concentration can test whether coincidence contributes. A histogram peak is a population pattern, not proof that every event represents one normal cell.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Practical: diffusion slopes and uncertainty
lessons.summary: Calculate a diffusion scale and explain why a straight-line plot needs a model.
lessons.section: Combined notes, practical questions 112–116

steps.title: Choose the observed quantity
steps.body: For one-dimensional free diffusion, ⟨x²⟩ = 2Dt, so a mean-squared-displacement versus time slope estimates 2D. A concentration profile requires a different fit and suitable boundary conditions. Individual trajectories fluctuate; one displacement is not the ensemble average.

steps.title: Work a scale
steps.body: With D = 2 × 10⁻¹⁰ m²/s and t = 1 s, root-mean-square displacement is √(2Dt) = 2 × 10⁻⁵ m, or 20 μm. At 4 s it is 40 μm. The distance grows with the square root of time, not linearly.

steps.title: Test the interpretation
steps.body: Drift adds directed motion and can make a simple diffusion estimate misleading. Temperature, viscosity, particle size, confinement and binding also matter. In an optical concentration experiment, converting signal into concentration introduces calibration uncertainty before the transport model is fitted.

steps.title: Compare transport routes
steps.body: Convection carries material with bulk flow; diffusion reflects random motion and concentration redistribution. A membrane may add a permeability barrier rather than merely extending a free-fluid distance. State which region and transport mechanism the measured coefficient describes.

question.prompt: For 1D diffusion, the slope of mean squared displacement versus time is…

options.reason: The standard relation is ⟨x²⟩ = 2Dt.
Faster diffusion produces a larger, not inverse, slope.
Differentiating ⟨x²⟩ = 2Dt gives slope 2D.

recall.prompt: Explain diffusion slopes and uncertainty: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: Differentiating ⟨x²⟩ = 2Dt gives slope 2D. √9 = 3 gives a threefold distance scale. Convection carries material with bulk flow; diffusion reflects random motion and concentration redistribution. A membrane may add a permeability barrier rather than merely extending a free-fluid distance. State which region and transport mechanism the measured coefficient describes.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Practical: sound levels and audiograms
lessons.summary: Distinguish physical sound level from a frequency-dependent hearing threshold.
lessons.section: Combined notes, practical questions 133–142

steps.title: Use a reference
steps.body: Intensity level is 10 log₁₀(I/Iref). Sound-pressure level uses 20 log₁₀(prms/pref) under the corresponding acoustic conditions. A 10 dB intensity-level increase means ten times the intensity, not necessarily ten times perceived loudness. A level without its reference is incomplete.

steps.title: Read the axes
steps.body: An audiogram plots hearing threshold against frequency using a specified hearing-level reference. It does not directly plot a sound wave or the cochlear displacement. Test conditions and masking can matter when distinguishing responses of the two ears; a curve alone should not be treated as a full diagnosis.

steps.title: Compare perception
steps.body: Equal-loudness contours show frequency dependence of perception. Phon compares loudness with a 1 kHz tone; sone expresses relative loudness. In the conventional relation above the reference region, a 10-phon increase corresponds approximately to doubled sones, distinct from the physical intensity ratio.

steps.title: Work a level difference
steps.body: An intensity rises from I to 100I, giving a 20 dB increase. If RMS pressure doubles in the same medium, sound-pressure level rises by about 6 dB. These two examples use different underlying ratios, which is why their logarithmic multipliers differ.

question.prompt: Intensity increases by a factor of 100. Level rises by…

options.reason: 10 log₁₀100 = 20 dB.
Intensity level uses the logarithm of the ratio.
The 20 multiplier applies to a pressure ratio, not this intensity ratio.

recall.prompt: Explain sound levels and audiograms: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: 10 log₁₀100 = 20 dB. 20 log₁₀2 ≈ 6.02 dB. An intensity rises from I to 100I, giving a 20 dB increase. If RMS pressure doubles in the same medium, sound-pressure level rises by about 6 dB. These two examples use different underlying ratios, which is why their logarithmic multipliers differ.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Practical: ECG calibration and pulse timing
lessons.summary: Convert a recorded trace into voltage and time, and distinguish pulse-generator behaviours.
lessons.section: Combined notes, practical questions 143–157

steps.title: Read calibration first
steps.body: An ECG trace needs both voltage and paper-speed calibration. At 10 mm/mV, a 12 mm deflection represents 1.2 mV. At 25 mm/s, a 2 mm interval is 0.08 s. These are measurement exercises; voltage or timing alone is insufficient for a clinical interpretation.

steps.title: Compare leads and rejection
steps.body: Standard limb leads obey II = I + III in the ideal consistent-sign description. Differential amplifiers measure a voltage difference and aim to reject common-mode interference. Poor contact and motion can still introduce artifacts; a large recorded deflection need not reflect a larger cardiac source.

steps.title: Classify pulse behaviour
steps.body: An astable circuit oscillates without a stable resting state, a monostable returns to its stable state after a triggered pulse, and a bistable has two stable states. These concepts help explain timing electronics. A conceptual pulse exercise is not an instruction to construct or program a pacemaker.

steps.title: Work a pulse train
steps.body: A period of 1 s gives frequency 1 Hz. A pulse lasting 2 ms every second has duty cycle 0.2%. For an ideal rectangular voltage pulse across a resistor, energy is V²t/R. Shape, load and safety controls matter in real devices, so this ideal expression is used only for the classroom model.

question.prompt: At 25 mm/s, a 5 mm interval corresponds to…

options.reason: Millimetres are not seconds without applying the calibration.
5 mm divided by 25 mm/s equals 0.20 s.
Divide length by speed: 5/25 seconds.

recall.prompt: Explain ecg calibration and pulse timing: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: 5 mm divided by 25 mm/s equals 0.20 s. A monostable temporarily leaves its single stable state after a trigger. A period of 1 s gives frequency 1 Hz. A pulse lasting 2 ms every second has duty cycle 0.2%. For an ideal rectangular voltage pulse across a resistor, energy is V²t/R. Shape, load and safety controls matter in real devices, so this ideal expression is used only for the classroom model.

lessons.subject: genetics
lessons.title: Gene therapy: target, delivery and evidence
lessons.summary: Separate gene addition, editing and gene silencing, then decide whether an in-vivo or ex-vivo strategy can reach the relevant cells.
lessons.section: Topic 14: Genetic Therapy — therapeutic goals, delivery systems, viral vectors, and in-vivo versus ex-vivo approaches

steps.title: Start with the therapeutic job
steps.body: A genetic intervention must be matched to a defined molecular problem. Gene addition supplies a functional sequence when additional expression is the goal. Gene editing changes an existing sequence. Expression-modifying approaches can reduce, increase or otherwise alter gene output without being the same thing as adding a replacement gene. These categories overlap in clinical language, but they should not be treated as interchangeable mechanisms.

steps.title: Follow the cargo and the route
steps.body: The therapeutic payload may be nucleic acid, a gene-editing system, or cells that have been modified outside the body. Delivery is a separate problem: the payload must reach the intended cells at a useful dose while limiting unwanted exposure. Viral vectors, non-viral nucleic-acid delivery systems and patient-derived modified-cell products solve this problem in different ways. A vector is a delivery vehicle, not the therapy's biological effect by itself.

steps.title: Distinguish in vivo from ex vivo
steps.body: In vivo therapy delivers the intervention to cells within the body. Ex vivo therapy removes cells, modifies them under controlled conditions, then returns them to the person. Ex vivo approaches can allow testing or selection of modified cells before infusion; in-vivo approaches depend on targeting and delivery inside the body. Neither label alone establishes safety, durability or suitability for a particular disease.

steps.title: Keep evidence and mechanism separate
steps.body: A plausible molecular strategy is not automatically an established treatment. For each proposed therapy, ask what is modified, which cells receive it, how it is delivered, how the intended effect is measured, and what evidence supports benefit and risk. Regulatory approval, trial status and availability vary by product, disease and country. This lesson explains the framework; it is not treatment advice.

question.prompt: Which statement best distinguishes an ex-vivo gene therapy approach from an in-vivo approach?

options.text: Cells are removed, modified outside the body, then returned to the person.
options.reason: Correct: ex-vivo approaches modify collected cells before administration back to the person. The delivery and biological effect still need to be evaluated separately.

options.text: A viral vector is always injected directly into the target tissue.
options.reason: Viral vectors can be used in different delivery designs, including to modify cells outside the body; the vector alone does not define the route.

options.text: Any intervention that changes gene expression permanently repairs DNA.
options.reason: Changing expression can occur without permanently repairing DNA. Gene addition, editing and expression modulation are distinct mechanisms.

recall.prompt: Give a structured explanation of a gene-therapy proposal before deciding whether it is clinically established.
recall.answer: Name the molecular problem and therapeutic goal, then state whether the intervention adds genetic material, edits an existing sequence or modifies expression. Identify the target cells, payload and delivery route, and distinguish in-vivo from ex-vivo handling. Finally, separate the biological rationale from the evidence for safety and benefit; approval or trial status must be checked for the specific product and setting.

objectives: Distinguish gene addition, genome editing and expression-modifying strategies without treating them as synonyms.
Compare in-vivo and ex-vivo delivery by identifying where cells are modified and how the therapeutic cargo reaches them.
Evaluate a proposed genetic therapy by separating target, delivery route, biological rationale, and evidence of clinical benefit and risk.

workedExample.title: Choose the route before naming the vector
workedExample.prompt: A proposal says: “Collect a patient's cells, introduce a therapeutic sequence in a controlled laboratory setting, check the resulting cell population, and infuse the cells back.” Is this in vivo or ex vivo? What information is still missing before you can judge the proposal?
solution: It is an ex-vivo approach because the cells are collected and modified outside the body before being returned.
The proposal still needs a defined target-cell population, payload and modification method, as well as evidence that the returned cells reach or persist in the intended setting.
A complete assessment also requires disease-specific evidence of benefit and harms; the route alone does not prove efficacy, safety or regulatory approval.

lessons.subject: physiology
lessons.title: Physiology Foundations: Membrane Transport and Resting Potential
lessons.summary: Distinguish transport mechanisms, follow the energy that maintains ion gradients, and predict how selective permeability produces a resting membrane potential.
lessons.section: Membrane transport; resting voltage, selective permeability and potassium equilibrium potential

steps.title: A selective boundary
steps.body:
The phospholipid bilayer separates intracellular from extracellular fluid. Small non-polar molecules such as oxygen cross the lipid phase; ions require membrane proteins. A channel provides a selective pore, whereas a carrier binds its cargo and changes conformation.

Passive movement follows the electrochemical gradient: the combined effects of concentration and voltage. For an uncharged solute, the concentration gradient is sufficient; for an ion, concentration alone cannot always predict direction.

steps.title: Follow the energy
steps.body:
Facilitated diffusion uses a channel or carrier but does not directly consume ATP. Primary active transport couples uphill movement to an energy source: the sodium–potassium ATPase uses one ATP to export three Na⁺ and import two K⁺.

Secondary active transport couples one substance moving downhill to another moving uphill. In an intestinal epithelial cell, sodium–glucose cotransport uses the Na⁺ gradient maintained by the basolateral pump. The cotransporter does not itself hydrolyse ATP.

steps.title: Explain a negative resting potential
steps.body:
Membrane potential is the voltage inside relative to outside. A value of −70 mV means that the inside is 70 mV more negative; it is an illustrative neuronal value, not a universal value for every cell.

Many resting neurons are more permeable to K⁺ than to Na⁺. K⁺ tends to leave down its concentration gradient; the resulting electrical force opposes further outward movement. The resting voltage depends on several ions and their permeabilities, so it is usually near, but not identical to, the K⁺ equilibrium potential.

steps.title: Separate a steady state from equilibrium
steps.body:
At an ion’s equilibrium potential, electrical and chemical forces balance for that ion and its net passive flux is zero. A resting cell is a maintained steady state: ongoing passive leaks are balanced by transport processes.

The sodium–potassium pump is electrogenic and maintains the concentration gradients over time. It does not generate the entire resting potential by itself. Changes in extracellular K⁺ or selective conductance can alter voltage without first equalising all ion concentrations.

question.prompt: A carrier moves glucose down its concentration gradient without coupling it to another solute or ATP. Which mechanism is this?

options.reason: Primary active transport uses an energy source such as ATP to drive uphill movement; neither is specified here.
Carrier-mediated movement down the glucose concentration gradient without energy coupling is facilitated diffusion.
Secondary active transport requires coupling to a downhill gradient of another substance; none is present here.

recall.prompt: Connect the main concepts in a one-minute explanation, including the assumptions behind your prediction.
recall.answer: Permeability determines which substances can cross; electrochemical gradients determine passive direction. ATP-dependent pumps maintain gradients that can also power cotransport. Selective ion permeability and unequal ion distributions produce a resting voltage. Rest is a steady state with continuing transport, not equal concentrations on both sides.

objectives: Classify simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion and active transport by pathway and energy coupling.
Explain how the sodium–potassium pump supports secondary active transport.
Interpret membrane voltage as inside relative to outside.
Distinguish an ion equilibrium potential from a maintained resting state.

workedExample.title: Worked Example
workedExample.prompt: In a hypothetical neuron, resting voltage is −70 mV and the K⁺ equilibrium potential is −90 mV. Only K⁺ conductance increases. With ion concentrations fixed initially, predict the direction of voltage change.
solution: Compare the starting voltage with the K⁺ equilibrium potential: the membrane is initially 20 mV more positive.
Increasing K⁺ conductance increases the influence of K⁺ on the voltage and drives it towards −90 mV.
The initial change is hyperpolarisation. The final voltage need not equal −90 mV because other conductances remain; the prediction assumes their properties and the initial gradients are unchanged.

oralExamination.prompt: Why does the presence of a transport protein not prove active transport?
oralExamination.answer: Channels and facilitated-diffusion carriers support passive transport. Establish the direction relative to the electrochemical gradient and identify an energy-coupling mechanism before classifying transport as active.

oralExamination.prompt: Why is a resting neuron not at complete electrochemical equilibrium?
oralExamination.answer: Ions continue to leak through channels while energy-dependent transport sustains unequal concentrations. Zero net change in voltage or concentration over time does not require zero flux through every pathway.

summaryChecklist: Classify simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion and active transport by pathway and energy coupling.
Explain how the sodium–potassium pump supports secondary active transport.
Interpret membrane voltage as inside relative to outside.
Distinguish an ion equilibrium potential from a maintained resting state.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Biochemistry Foundations: Enzymes, Kinetics and Regulation
lessons.summary: Use a simple enzyme model to interpret reaction rate, distinguish concentration from velocity, and explain how cells regulate a metabolic pathway.
lessons.section: Catalysis, Michaelis–Menten initial-rate kinetics, competitive inhibition and feedback regulation

steps.title: Catalysis changes the route, not the destination
steps.body:
An enzyme accelerates a reaction by lowering its activation barrier. It does not change the overall free-energy difference or the equilibrium constant, and it is regenerated during catalysis. Faster catalysis therefore does not mean a larger final equilibrium yield.

Substrate recognition depends on the active site and the enzyme’s conformation. Changes in temperature, pH or molecular interactions can alter activity; they do not all act by the same mechanism.

steps.title: Read a saturation experiment
steps.body:
For a simple Michaelis–Menten enzyme, initial velocity v = Vmax × [S] / (Km + [S]). Here [S] and Km are concentrations; v and Vmax are reaction rates. Use initial rates with substrate in excess of enzyme, before substantial substrate depletion or product accumulation.

Km is the substrate concentration at half Vmax. Vmax is the limiting rate for the amount of active enzyme present. Km is not a rate and is not, in general, a direct binding dissociation constant. Cooperative enzymes may require a different model.

steps.title: Distinguish inhibition from loss of enzyme
steps.body:
In the ideal reversible competitive model, substrate and inhibitor compete for the enzyme: apparent Km increases while Vmax is unchanged. More substrate is required to reach half the same limiting rate. This statement assumes the same amount of active enzyme and unchanged assay conditions.

Reducing the amount of active enzyme instead lowers Vmax. A change in a single measured rate does not identify the inhibition mechanism; compare rates across substrate concentrations.

steps.title: Connect kinetics with pathway regulation
steps.body:
Regulation can change enzyme activity, enzyme abundance or substrate availability. An allosteric regulator binds away from the active site and alters function. Allosteric regulation is not synonymous with the special kinetic category of pure non-competitive inhibition.

In feedback inhibition, a downstream product reduces activity at an earlier step in its pathway. This links supply to demand. Always specify which reaction is regulated; a change at one step does not imply that every enzyme is inhibited.

question.prompt: For an enzyme following Michaelis–Menten kinetics, what does Km specify?

options.text: The maximum reaction rate at saturating substrate
options.reason: That is Vmax. Km has units of concentration rather than amount converted per unit time.

options.text: The amount of product present at equilibrium
options.reason: Equilibrium composition depends on thermodynamics and starting conditions, not on the definition of Km.

options.text: The substrate concentration at half the limiting initial rate
options.reason: When [S] equals Km, the Michaelis–Menten equation gives v = Vmax/2 under its stated assumptions.

recall.prompt: Connect the main concepts in a one-minute explanation, including the assumptions behind your prediction.
recall.answer: Enzymes lower activation barriers without moving equilibrium. For the simple initial-rate model, Km is a concentration and Vmax is a rate. Competitive inhibition raises apparent Km without lowering Vmax; decreasing active enzyme lowers Vmax. Feedback and allosteric regulation connect reaction activity to cellular demand.

objectives: Distinguish catalytic rate from equilibrium composition.
Use Km and Vmax with their correct units and model assumptions.
Predict the effect of reversible competitive inhibition on apparent Km and Vmax.
Explain feedback inhibition without equating allostery with one inhibition pattern.

workedExample.title: Worked Example
workedExample.prompt: A hypothetical enzyme follows Michaelis–Menten kinetics with Vmax = 80 µmol/min and Km = 2 mmol/L. What initial rate is predicted at [S] = 2 mmol/L?
solution: The substrate concentration equals Km, so the predicted rate is half Vmax.
Substitute consistent units: v = 80 × 2 / (2 + 2) = 40 µmol/min. The concentration units cancel.
This is an initial-rate prediction for the stated model and active enzyme amount. It is not a patient measurement or a prediction of total product at equilibrium.

oralExamination.prompt: Why can two assays give different Vmax values for the same enzyme?
oralExamination.answer: Vmax depends on the amount of active enzyme as well as catalytic turnover under the assay conditions. Compare enzyme amount, temperature, pH and other conditions before interpreting the difference.

oralExamination.prompt: How can a pathway product regulate its own production?
oralExamination.answer: A product can inhibit an earlier enzyme through feedback regulation. Reduced activity limits pathway flux under the relevant conditions; substrate supply and other regulated steps also matter.

summaryChecklist: Distinguish catalytic rate from equilibrium composition.
Use Km and Vmax with their correct units and model assumptions.
Predict the effect of reversible competitive inhibition on apparent Km and Vmax.
Explain feedback inhibition without equating allostery with one inhibition pattern.

lessons.subject: genetics
lessons.title: Genetics Foundations: Genome, Inheritance and Gene Expression
lessons.summary: Separate DNA organisation from gene expression, use a defined inheritance model, and build the vocabulary needed for medical genetics and immunology.
lessons.section: Genome and gene definitions; transcription and translation; autosomal inheritance and independent pregnancy probabilities

steps.title: Organise the genome
steps.body:
The human genome includes nuclear DNA and mitochondrial DNA. A typical diploid nucleated somatic cell has 23 pairs of nuclear chromosomes; a gamete normally has one set of 23. A chromosome contains many genes and non-coding regions, not just one gene.

A gene is a DNA sequence whose expression contributes a functional product: an RNA or, for a protein-coding gene, a polypeptide through an RNA intermediate. Non-coding DNA is not synonymous with non-functional DNA; some regions regulate gene expression.

steps.title: Distinguish a gene from an allele
steps.body:
An allele is a version of a DNA sequence at a particular locus. At a typical autosomal locus, a diploid person has one copy inherited from each parent. Homozygous means the two alleles are the same; heterozygous means they differ.

Dominant and recessive describe relationships between genotype and a specified phenotype. They do not mean common and rare, or strong and weak. A dominant condition can arise from a new variant, so absence of an affected parent does not exclude it.

steps.title: Trace expression rather than replication
steps.body:
Replication copies DNA. Transcription produces RNA from a DNA template. For a nuclear protein-coding gene, RNA processing produces a mature messenger RNA (mRNA), which is translated by ribosomes into a polypeptide.

Some RNAs function without being translated. Different cell types can express different sets and amounts of genes despite sharing most of their DNA sequence. Thus detecting a gene does not establish how much functional protein is present.

steps.title: Apply a stated inheritance model
steps.body:
For an illustrative autosomal recessive condition, let a denote the disease-associated allele and A a normal-function allele. Assume aa is affected and Aa carriers are unaffected. Two heterozygous parents each transmit A or a with probability one half.

Each pregnancy has probabilities 1/4 AA, 1/2 Aa and 1/4 aa, independently of previous outcomes. These assumptions do not describe all genetic disease: penetrance, different inheritance patterns and multiple genes can change interpretation. Use the defined model before applying a percentage.

question.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes a chromosome, a gene and an allele?

options.text: A chromosome contains many genes; an allele is a version at a locus.
options.reason: Chromosomes organise long DNA molecules containing many loci; alleles describe sequence versions at a particular locus.

options.text: Each chromosome contains exactly one gene with many proteins inside it.
options.reason: A chromosome contains many genes and non-coding regions. Proteins are gene products or associated molecules, not sequences inside a gene.

options.text: An allele is an RNA copy made whenever a chromosome is transcribed.
options.reason: An allele is a sequence version. Transcription makes RNA; it does not create an inherited allele each time it occurs.

recall.prompt: Connect the main concepts in a one-minute explanation, including the assumptions behind your prediction.
recall.answer: The genome includes nuclear and mitochondrial DNA. Genes specify functional RNA or protein products; alleles are sequence versions at loci. Replication copies DNA, transcription makes RNA and translation makes a polypeptide. Inheritance probabilities require a stated model, and gene presence alone does not establish expression or function.

objectives: Distinguish genome, chromosome, gene and allele.
Separate replication, transcription and translation.
Calculate offspring probabilities for a defined autosomal recessive cross.
Explain why DNA sequence and gene expression are different kinds of information.

workedExample.title: Worked Example
workedExample.prompt: Two unaffected Aa carriers plan a pregnancy in the autosomal recessive model above. Their first child is affected. What is the probability that their next child is affected?
solution: Each parent independently supplies A or a with probability 1/2 at this locus.
The four equally likely combinations are AA, Aa, aA and aa; only aa is affected in this model.
The next pregnancy therefore has a 1/4 (25%) affected probability. The first child’s outcome does not change either parent’s genotype or the segregation probabilities.

oralExamination.prompt: Why is “one gene makes one protein” an incomplete definition?
oralExamination.answer: Some genes produce functional RNAs rather than proteins, and processing can allow a protein-coding gene to yield different RNA and protein products. Distinguish the DNA locus from its expressed products.

oralExamination.prompt: How does this foundation prepare you for immunology?
oralExamination.answer: Immune-cell functions depend on expressed receptors, signalling molecules and other proteins. Separate the inherited DNA sequence from which genes a cell expresses before studying immune-cell activation and special mechanisms of receptor diversity.

summaryChecklist: Distinguish genome, chromosome, gene and allele.
Separate replication, transcription and translation.
Calculate offspring probabilities for a defined autosomal recessive cross.
Explain why DNA sequence and gene expression are different kinds of information.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Biophysics Foundations: Diffusion, Osmosis and Membranes
lessons.summary: Predict passive exchange by stating the gradient, the membrane’s permeability and the geometry, then distinguish water movement from solute movement.
lessons.section: Diffusion and osmosis; Fick diffusion model; membrane permeability and cell-volume responses

steps.title: Define the moving substance and its gradient
steps.body:
Diffusion arises from random molecular motion. For an uncharged solute under simple conditions, a concentration difference produces net movement from higher to lower concentration, even though molecules move in both directions. At equilibrium, random motion continues but there is no net flux.

A membrane is selectively permeable: a gradient cannot drive appreciable transfer through an effectively impermeable barrier. Ion movement also depends on voltage, so an uncharged-solute model must not be applied to ions without considering electrical forces.

steps.title: Relate transfer to area and thickness
steps.body:
For steady diffusion of a neutral solute through a uniform planar layer, transfer rate = D × A × Δc / L. D is the diffusion coefficient (m²/s), A area (m²), Δc the concentration difference (mol/m³), and L thickness (m). The result is mol/s.

With other quantities fixed, doubling area doubles transfer; doubling thickness halves it. This ideal model assumes a constant diffusion coefficient and maintained boundary concentrations. Partitioning, channels and active transport can require a more detailed membrane model.

steps.title: Predict osmosis using permeability
steps.body:
Osmosis is net water movement across a selectively permeable membrane. In an ideal dilute model with equal initial hydrostatic pressures, water moves towards the side with a greater concentration of solute particles that cannot cross the membrane. Aquaporins provide water pathways in many cell membranes.

As water redistributes, concentration and pressure differences may change. An opposing hydrostatic pressure can balance the osmotic drive; equilibrium does not necessarily require equal solute concentrations.

steps.title: Separate osmolarity from tonicity
steps.body:
Osmolarity counts dissolved particles per litre of solution. Tonicity describes a solution’s effect on cell volume and depends on solute permeability and the time considered, especially solutes that remain effectively non-penetrating. Equal total osmolarity alone does not guarantee equal tonicity.

In a simple cell model with water permeability and impermeant solute, a hypertonic exterior draws water out and the cell shrinks; a hypotonic exterior drives water in and the cell swells. This is a physical model, not a prescription for choosing a clinical fluid.

question.prompt: At diffusion equilibrium for a freely permeating neutral solute, which statement is correct?

options.text: Molecular motion has stopped on both sides.
options.reason: Thermal motion continues at equilibrium; equality concerns net transfer, not the movement of individual molecules.

options.text: Movement continues in both directions, with zero net flux.
options.reason: Opposing molecular transfers balance at equilibrium, so the average net flux is zero.

options.text: The membrane must actively pump equal amounts in each direction.
options.reason: Passive diffusion equilibrium does not require an active pump; it follows from balanced driving forces.

recall.prompt: Connect the main concepts in a one-minute explanation, including the assumptions behind your prediction.
recall.answer: Diffusion needs a permeable pathway and a driving force. In a simple planar model, transfer increases with area and concentration difference and decreases with thickness. Osmosis concerns water, while tonicity concerns cell-volume effects of effective solute gradients. State permeability, pressure and time assumptions before predicting movement.

objectives: Distinguish random molecular movement from net diffusion.
Use area, concentration difference and thickness to predict relative transfer rate.
Predict osmosis with stated permeability and pressure assumptions.
Distinguish osmolarity from tonicity when interpreting cell-volume change.

workedExample.title: Worked Example
workedExample.prompt: Two hypothetical neutral-solute barriers have the same diffusion coefficient and concentration difference. Barrier B has twice the area and three times the thickness of barrier A. What is the ratio of their steady transfer rates?
solution: Use rate ∝ area / thickness only because the diffusion coefficient and maintained concentration difference are the same.
The ratio B/A is (2 × area)/(3 × thickness), relative to area/thickness: 2/3.
Barrier B transfers two thirds as much solute per unit time. Increased area partly compensates for thickness; these data do not establish transport in a real patient.

oralExamination.prompt: Why does a large concentration difference not guarantee rapid diffusion?
oralExamination.answer: Transfer also depends on permeability, area, path length and molecular properties. An effectively impermeable barrier can prevent transfer despite a large concentration difference.

oralExamination.prompt: Why can an isosmotic solution still change a cell’s volume?
oralExamination.answer: Osmolarity counts all dissolved particles. A solute that penetrates the cell can redistribute, altering the effective osmotic gradient; tonicity therefore depends on permeability and time, not just total particle concentration.

summaryChecklist: Distinguish random molecular movement from net diffusion.
Use area, concentration difference and thickness to predict relative transfer rate.
Predict osmosis with stated permeability and pressure assumptions.
Distinguish osmolarity from tonicity when interpreting cell-volume change.

lessons.subject: biostatistics
lessons.title: Histograms: count observations within defined bins
lessons.summary: Turn a small invented dataset into bin counts, explain boundary conventions, and distinguish a change in grouping from a change in the observations.
lessons.section: NIST Dataplot: Histogram; original fictional examples and calculations.
objectives: Count observations using explicit interval boundaries.
Explain how regrouping changes the displayed pattern.
Distinguish count heights from density heights.

steps.title: Start with observations and a rule
steps.body: A histogram groups numerical observations into intervals, or bins. The horizontal axis identifies the measured quantity; the vertical axis must say whether it shows counts, relative frequencies or density. A bin is an interval of values rather than a separate named category. Before counting, specify which endpoints belong to each interval. In this lesson, [a, b) includes a and excludes b. This is a chosen convention, not a claim that every software package uses it. Each included observation must belong to exactly one bin.

steps.title: Count before interpreting the shape
steps.body: Use the invented values 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 6. The intervals [0, 2), [2, 4), [4, 6) and [6, 8) contain 1, 3, 2 and 2 observations. Both occurrences of 2 belong to the second interval; 4 belongs to the third. The counts sum to eight, matching the dataset size. With equal bin widths, taller count bars mean more observations in that interval. No patient data or measured biological result is represented.

steps.title: Regroup the same data
steps.body: Replace the four intervals with [0, 4) and [4, 8). Their counts are four and four. The observations did not change, but the wider grouping hides the previous differences between narrower intervals. A visual impression depends partly on bin placement and width. Inspect the raw values when available, compare sensible groupings, and avoid treating a peak in eight invented observations as proof of a population pattern.

steps.title: Check height, width and area
steps.body: For a count histogram with equal widths, comparing heights compares counts. If widths differ, a density display instead divides a bin count by its width, so bar area represents count; dividing again by the total count makes total area one. For example, two observations across width one and four across width four give count densities two and one. The second bin contains more observations despite its lower density. Always read the axis definition before comparing bars.

workedExample.title: Worked calculation
workedExample.prompt: For 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 6, calculate the four narrow-bin counts and the two wide-bin counts using lower-inclusive, upper-exclusive intervals.
solution: Assign 1 to [0, 2); assign 2, 2 and 3 to [2, 4).
Assign 4 and 5 to [4, 6); assign 6 and 6 to [6, 8). The counts are 1, 3, 2, 2 and sum to eight.
Combine the first two bins and the last two bins: [0, 4) has four observations and [4, 8) has four. Only the grouping changed.

question.prompt: With [0, 4) and [4, 8), where does the value 4 belong?

options.reason: The lower endpoint is included. The upper endpoint of [0, 4) is excluded, so 4 is counted once in the second bin.
Counting 4 twice would violate the stated upper-exclusive rule and inflate the total count.
The second interval includes its lower endpoint, so 4 must be included there.

oralExamination.prompt: Explain why a histogram can look different when the observations are unchanged.
oralExamination.answer: Bin boundaries and widths determine how observations are grouped. Replacing four narrow bins by two wide bins can conceal local differences without changing any value. Check endpoint conventions and whether the vertical axis reports count or density before interpreting the shape.

recall.prompt: Explain why a histogram can look different when the observations are unchanged.
recall.answer: Bin boundaries and widths determine how observations are grouped. Replacing four narrow bins by two wide bins can conceal local differences without changing any value. Check endpoint conventions and whether the vertical axis reports count or density before interpreting the shape.

summaryChecklist: I can count observations using explicit interval boundaries.
I can explain how regrouping changes the displayed pattern.
I can distinguish count heights from density heights.

lessons.subject: biostatistics
lessons.title: Mean and median: effect of one extreme value
lessons.summary: Calculate two measures of centre, trace the effect of changing one value, and explain why a summary must be chosen in context.
lessons.section: NIST: Measures of Location; original fictional examples and calculations.
objectives: Calculate a mean and a median from ordered values.
Explain the effect of one changed extreme value.
Separate a numerical summary from a judgement about data quality.

steps.title: Two definitions of centre
steps.body: The arithmetic mean is the sum of the observations divided by their number. Every value contributes its magnitude. To find the median, first sort the values. For an odd number of observations, use the middle value; for an even number, average the two central values. These definitions answer related but different questions about location. Neither definition identifies the most common value, which is the mode.

steps.title: Sort and check the central positions
steps.body: For four invented ordered values 1, 2, 6, 9, the two central values are two and six, so the median is (2 + 6) / 2 = 4. The median need not be an observed value. Sorting is essential: selecting the middle item in an unsorted list can produce the wrong answer. When a central value or the number of observations changes, recalculate the median rather than assuming resistance means complete immunity to change.

steps.title: Follow one deliberate change
steps.body: The invented values 2, 3, 3, 4, 8 sum to 20. Their mean is 20 / 5 = 4 and their median is the third value, 3. Replace 8 with 18. The sum rises by ten while the count remains five, so the mean rises by 10 / 5 = 2, from four to six. The ordered middle value remains three. Here the median is unchanged because the central ordering is unchanged, not because medians can never change.

steps.title: Do not turn a summary into a verdict
steps.body: An extreme value can be a recording error or a valid observation; the arithmetic alone cannot decide. Check units, measurement procedures and provenance before excluding it. The median resists some extreme changes, but it does not describe the tails or prove that the data are accurate. The mean can be useful when totals matter. Report which measure was used and, where useful, show the distribution and a measure of spread rather than declaring one measure universally best.

workedExample.title: Worked calculation
workedExample.prompt: Compare the mean and median before and after replacing 8 by 18 in 2, 3, 3, 4, 8.
solution: The original sum is 20, giving mean 20 / 5 = 4. The third ordered value gives median 3.
The replacement sum is 30, giving mean 30 / 5 = 6. The third ordered value is still 3.
The ten-unit increase affects the mean by two units. No central rank changed, so this particular median is unchanged.

question.prompt: For 2, 3, 3, 4, 18, which pair is correct?

options.reason: The sum is 30 and there are five observations. The middle ordered observation is 3.
This reverses the roles: 3 is the middle ordered value, whereas 6 is the sum divided by five.
The largest value is not the median. With five sorted observations, use the third value.

oralExamination.prompt: Why did the mean change while the median stayed at three in this example?
oralExamination.answer: The mean uses every magnitude, so adding ten to one value increases the mean by ten divided by five. The median uses the ordered central position; the replacement leaves that position unchanged. This is an example of resistance, not permission to discard an extreme observation.

recall.prompt: Why did the mean change while the median stayed at three in this example?
recall.answer: The mean uses every magnitude, so adding ten to one value increases the mean by ten divided by five. The median uses the ordered central position; the replacement leaves that position unchanged. This is an example of resistance, not permission to discard an extreme observation.

summaryChecklist: I can calculate a mean and a median from ordered values.
I can explain the effect of one changed extreme value.
I can separate a numerical summary from a judgement about data quality.

lessons.subject: biostatistics
lessons.title: Same centre, different spread
lessons.summary: Compare datasets with identical centres but different ranges, then explain what the range omits and what a small sample cannot establish.
lessons.section: NIST: Measures of Scale; original fictional examples and calculations.
objectives: Calculate centre and range for two datasets.
Explain why a shared centre does not imply shared variation.
Identify what a range comparison cannot establish.

steps.title: Separate location from variation
steps.body: A measure of centre says where values are located; a measure of spread says how separated they are. Knowing one does not determine the other. Consider invented dataset A: 4, 5, 6, and dataset B: 0, 5, 10. Both have sum 15, mean five and median five. B places its outer observations farther from that centre. A single central number would conceal this difference.

steps.title: Calculate the range and its limits
steps.body: The range is the maximum minus the minimum. A has range 6 - 4 = 2; B has range 10 - 0 = 10. This establishes that B has the larger range in these observed datasets. The range uses only the two extremes: changing an interior observation can leave it unchanged. Range alone does not describe clustering, gaps or multiple peaks, and it does not tell you which observation is erroneous.

steps.title: Connect spread measures without overgeneralising
steps.body: Sample variance uses the squared deviations from the sample mean, divided by n - 1; sample standard deviation is its square root and has the original measurement units. For A, squared deviations are 1, 0, 1, giving sample variance one and sample SD one. For B they are 25, 0, 25, giving sample variance 25 and sample SD five. Here range and SD agree about the ordering, but that agreement is not a universal rule for arbitrary datasets.

steps.title: Keep the inference within the evidence
steps.body: These are three invented values per group, not a biological experiment. A larger observed range does not prove a larger population variance or a meaningful clinical difference. A confidence interval would require an estimator, a sampling design and appropriate assumptions. Before comparing real groups, establish compatible units and measurements and inspect their distributions; sample size also affects how likely a sample is to include extreme observations.

workedExample.title: Worked calculation
workedExample.prompt: Compare the mean, median, range and sample SD of A = 4, 5, 6 and B = 0, 5, 10.
solution: Both sums are 15, so both means are five. Both middle values are five.
A has range two; B has range ten. Their ranges differ despite identical centres.
Divide squared-deviation sums two and fifty by n - 1 = 2. Sample variances are one and 25, so sample SDs are one and five. These calculations describe the invented samples.

question.prompt: Which statement follows from A = 4, 5, 6 and B = 0, 5, 10?

options.text: B has a larger observed range, although both means are five.
options.reason: The ranges are ten and two; both sums are fifteen across three observations.

options.text: The two datasets have identical spread because their means match.
options.reason: Matching centres do not fix the distances around those centres. The ranges explicitly differ.

options.text: B proves that its source population has greater variance.
options.reason: Three supplied values do not establish a population comparison; a sampling design and inferential assumptions are missing.

oralExamination.prompt: Why should centre and spread be described separately?
oralExamination.answer: Different datasets can share the same mean and median while differing greatly in their distances from the centre. The range compares extremes; SD uses all squared deviations. Neither a matching centre nor one sample spread comparison establishes the corresponding population relationship.

recall.prompt: Why should centre and spread be described separately?
recall.answer: Different datasets can share the same mean and median while differing greatly in their distances from the centre. The range compares extremes; SD uses all squared deviations. Neither a matching centre nor one sample spread comparison establishes the corresponding population relationship.

summaryChecklist: I can calculate centre and range for two datasets.
I can explain why a shared centre does not imply shared variation.
I can identify what a range comparison cannot establish.

lessons.subject: biostatistics
lessons.title: Standard deviation and standard error: what varies?
lessons.summary: Distinguish the spread of observations from the sampling uncertainty of a mean, calculate an estimated standard error, and state the assumptions that make the calculation meaningful.
lessons.section: NIST: Confidence Limits for the Mean; original fictional examples and calculations.
objectives: Distinguish observation spread from mean-estimation uncertainty.
Calculate an estimated standard error under an independent-sampling model.
Explain why a smaller standard error does not remove bias.

steps.title: Name the quantity that varies
steps.body: A sample standard deviation describes how observations in one sample vary around their sample mean. A standard error describes the sampling distribution of an estimator: how that estimator would vary across repeated samples under a specified model. Here the estimator is the arithmetic mean. These quantities have the same units as the observations, but they describe different levels of variation. A smaller SE is not the same statement as more uniform individual observations.

steps.title: Derive the square-root relationship
steps.body: Assume n independent observations with a common finite variance sigma squared. Variances of independent sums add. The variance of the sample mean is therefore n times sigma squared divided by n squared, which equals sigma squared / n. Taking the square root gives SE(mean) = sigma / square root of n. If the population SD sigma is unknown, estimate this SE by s / square root of n, where s is the sample SD. This variance calculation does not itself require normally distributed individual observations.

steps.title: Compare two explicitly assigned examples
steps.body: Assign sample SD s = 10 units to both invented samples. At n = 25, estimated SE = 10 / 5 = 2 units; at n = 100, estimated SE = 10 / 10 = 1 unit. The second estimated SE is half the first because sample size is four times as large while the assigned SD is held constant. Real samples need not have identical sample SDs, so state this assumption when using the comparison.

steps.title: State what the formula leaves out
steps.body: Correlated or clustered observations require a variance calculation that accounts for their dependence; weighted or complex samples may need a different SE estimate. The formula alone supplies neither a confidence level nor a confidence interval. A one-sample t interval introduces additional assumptions. Increasing sample size cannot automatically correct a biased measurement procedure or an unrepresentative recruitment process: precision under a model and validity of the model are separate questions.

workedExample.title: Worked calculation
workedExample.prompt: Both invented samples have sample SD 10 units. Estimate the mean SE for sample sizes 25 and 100 using the stated independent common-variance model.
solution: For n = 25, square root of n is five, so estimated SE is 10 / 5 = 2 units.
For n = 100, square root of n is ten, so estimated SE is 10 / 10 = 1 unit.
The SD was assigned to be equal. The difference concerns uncertainty of the mean under the sampling model, not a reduction of individual spread or proof that bias is absent.

question.prompt: Both samples have SD 10; their sizes are 25 and 100. Does the smaller estimated SE prove that the second sample has smaller individual spread?

options.text: No; the assigned SD is ten in both samples.
options.reason: Estimated SE changes from two to one because n changes. Individual sample spread was explicitly held equal.

options.text: Yes; its individual SD must be one.
options.reason: One is the estimated SE, not the sample SD. The sample SD was supplied as ten.

options.text: Yes; a larger sample also guarantees unbiased measurement.
options.reason: Sample size does not automatically repair systematic measurement error or a biased sampling procedure.

oralExamination.prompt: Explain SD and SE without interchanging what varies.
oralExamination.answer: SD summarises the spread of observations. The SE of a mean summarises the repeated-sampling spread of that estimator under a model. Under independent common finite variance, estimate SE by s divided by the square root of n. A smaller estimated SE need not imply smaller individual SD, unbiased data or a justified confidence interval.

recall.prompt: Explain SD and SE without interchanging what varies.
recall.answer: SD summarises the spread of observations. The SE of a mean summarises the repeated-sampling spread of that estimator under a model. Under independent common finite variance, estimate SE by s divided by the square root of n. A smaller estimated SE need not imply smaller individual SD, unbiased data or a justified confidence interval.

summaryChecklist: I can distinguish observation spread from mean-estimation uncertainty.
I can calculate an estimated standard error under an independent-sampling model.
I can explain why a smaller standard error does not remove bias.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: ATP amount and energy charge: track the whole pool
lessons.summary: Work through adenylate-kinase conservation, compare equal-charge pools and combine unequal pools without confusing a ratio with an amount.
lessons.section: Energy charge: definition, conservation and weighted-pool examples
objectives: Calculate adenylate energy charge for a defined nonempty pool.
Explain why isolated adenylate-kinase redistribution preserves this index.
Show why equal charge need not imply equal ATP amount or ATP/ADP.
Combine pools using adenylate amounts as weights.

steps.title: Define the pool and the index
steps.body:
Let A, D and M denote ATP, ADP and AMP amounts in the same defined pool and consistent units. Total adenylates N = A + D + M. For nonnegative amounts and N > 0, adenylate energy charge is e = (A + D/2)/N. ATP has weight 1, ADP weight 1/2 and AMP weight 0 in this defined index. An empty pool gives 0/0: it is undefined, not zero.

The examples here are invented amounts, not physiological concentrations, normal ranges or measurements from a person. No equilibrium or reaction rate is imposed. Energy charge is a composition index; it does not supply every quantity and condition needed for an ATP-hydrolysis free-energy calculation.

steps.title: Track adenylate kinase without losing AMP
steps.body:
Write a bookkeeping direction of adenylate kinase as 2 ADP → ATP + AMP. A stipulated extent x changes the pool to (A + x, D − 2x, M + x). Negative x represents the reverse direction. Nonnegative amounts require max(−A, −M) ≤ x ≤ D/2.

The total stays unchanged because x − 2x + x = 0. The weighted numerator also stays unchanged: A + x + (D − 2x)/2 = A + D/2. Thus the isolated redistribution preserves the defined energy charge. Starting at 8 ATP, 2 ADP and 0 AMP, one forward unit gives 9 ATP, 0 ADP and 1 AMP. Both charges are 0.90. ATP increases in the bookkeeping step, but this is not a source of unlimited energy or a prediction of a cellular endpoint.

steps.title: Compare equal charge without assuming equal composition
steps.body:
Pool A has 10 ATP, 10 ADP and 0 AMP units. Pool B has 14 ATP, 2 ADP and 4 AMP units. Each totals 20. The weighted numerators are 10 + 10/2 = 15 and 14 + 2/2 = 15, so both charges are 0.75. Yet ATP/ADP is 1 in A and 7 in B. Equal charge and equal total do not identify all three amounts.

Scaling every amount by the same positive factor also preserves charge. The pool (100, 100, 0) still has charge 0.75 although its total is ten times that of (10, 10, 0). A ratio leaves information out. If ADP is zero, ordinary ATP/ADP division is undefined; do not assign a finite ratio.

steps.title: See the possible fractions at a fixed charge
steps.body:
Write a = A/N, d = D/N and m = M/N. The fractions sum to 1 and e = a + d/2. Rearranging gives d = 2(e − a) and m = 1 − 2e + a. Requiring nonnegative fractions gives max(0, 2e − 1) ≤ a ≤ e.

At e = 0.75, the permitted ATP fraction in this purely algebraic family runs from 0.50 to 0.75. The first endpoint has d = 0.50 and m = 0; the second has d = 0 and m = 0.25. These are stipulated compositions without an equilibrium constraint, not measured limits in living cells.

steps.title: Combine unequal pools using amounts
steps.body:
Suppose a first invented pool totals N1 = 2 units with e1 = 0.90, and a second totals N2 = 8 units with e2 = 0.50. Their weighted numerators are 1.8 and 4.0. Combining their amounts without an intervening reaction gives e = (1.8 + 4.0)/(2 + 8) = 0.58. The unweighted mean of the two charge values is 0.70 and overweights the smaller pool.

In general, combined e = (N1e1 + N2e2)/(N1 + N2). If concentrations come from different volumes, first convert them to amounts using those volumes. This arithmetic summary does not imply that living compartments physically mix or acquire identical compositions.

steps.title: Stop at the conclusion the model supports
steps.body:
The examples separate an amount, a proportion, a concentration and a ratio. Report the molecules, pool boundary, units and assumptions before interpreting a result. A total pool can hide a compositional difference; a combined index can hide differences between compartments.

The isolated reaction is only one process. Real metabolism includes other reactions, transport and regulatory conditions. Neither a conserved index in this model nor one illustrative number establishes reaction direction, speed, cellular health or a clinical decision.

workedExample.title: Combine two invented pools
workedExample.prompt: Pool 1 has total adenylates 2 and charge 0.90. Pool 2 has total adenylates 8 and charge 0.50. Combine the amounts with no intervening reaction. What is the combined charge?
solution: Recover each weighted numerator: 2 × 0.90 = 1.8 and 8 × 0.50 = 4.0.
Add the numerators: 1.8 + 4.0 = 5.8. Add total amounts: 2 + 8 = 10.
Divide: 5.8/10 = 0.58. The simple mean 0.70 uses equal weights, which these pools do not have.

One compatible composition is (ATP, ADP, AMP) = (1.8, 0, 0.2) in the first pool and (0, 8, 0) in the second. The combined (1.8, 8, 0.2) gives (1.8 + 4)/10 = 0.58. These are invented amounts, not equilibrium predictions.

question.prompt: The two invented pools have totals 2 and 8, and charges 0.90 and 0.50 respectively. What is their combined charge when their amounts are added without a reaction?

options.reason: Weight each charge by its total adenylate amount: (2 × 0.90 + 8 × 0.50)/10 = 0.58.
This averages the two charge values with equal weights; the total adenylate amounts differ.
Adding the two charge values does not calculate a combined ratio. For a nonempty pool with nonnegative amounts, the defined charge lies between 0 and 1.

oralExamination.prompt: Why can ATP increase while the defined charge stays unchanged in the isolated adenylate-kinase model?
oralExamination.answer: The reaction also decreases ADP and increases AMP. Its total change is x − 2x + x = 0, and the weighted numerator changes by x − 2x/2 = 0.

oralExamination.prompt: Give two reasons equal energy charge does not uniquely describe a pool.
