oralExamination.answer: Scaling all amounts preserves charge while changing total amount. Even with a fixed total, the examples (10,10,0) and (14,2,4) have equal charge but different ATP/ADP ratios.

recall.prompt: What should you identify before interpreting an energy-charge value?
recall.answer: Define ATP, ADP and AMP in one pool with consistent units, confirm a nonzero total, and state the model assumptions. Charge is a weighted composition index, not an ATP amount, a complete free-energy calculation or a clinical conclusion.

summaryChecklist: Name the pool, units and nonzero denominator.
Track ATP, ADP and AMP together through the isolated reaction.
Keep total amount, ATP/ADP and energy charge distinct.
Use amount-weighted aggregation when pools differ in size.
Keep invented model results separate from cellular and clinical claims.

lessons.subject: physiology
lessons.title: Cochlear fluids: which side and which voltage reference?
lessons.summary: Calculate cochlear compartment potential differences, then distinguish a new voltage reference from a changed compartment.
lessons.section: Original reference/timing exercises; biological context from named primary studies

steps.title: Draw the boundary before the arrow
steps.body: In this simplified mature mammalian cochlear model, name three locations: endolymph outside the hair bundle, the hair-cell interior, and perilymph-like fluid at the basolateral surface. The sensory epithelium separates the extracellular environments. Potassium-rich endolymph remains extracellular: the cell membrane, rather than a potassium label, determines what is inside. This model concerns cochlear hair cells; it does not describe every developmental stage or every sensory organ.

steps.title: Use one reference for three locations
steps.body: For an invented bookkeeping exercise, assign perilymph 0 mV, endolymph +80 mV and the cell interior −45 mV. These are potentials relative to the same reference. The cell relative to perilymph is −45 − 0 = −45 mV. The cell relative to endolymph is −45 − 80 = −125 mV. The endocochlear potential concerns two extracellular compartments; it is not the same quantity as the voltage across the apical or basolateral membrane surface.

steps.title: Change the zero without changing the differences
steps.body: Add 20 mV to every assigned potential. Perilymph becomes +20, endolymph +100 and the cell interior −25 mV. The apical difference remains −25 − 100 = −125 mV; the basolateral difference remains −25 − 20 = −45 mV. A common reference shift cannot change the physical potential differences. Changing only one compartment instead describes a different model.

steps.title: Separate a new reference from a changed compartment
steps.body: Use the assigned baseline values: perilymph 0, endolymph +80 and interior −45 mV. First subtract 80 from all three: the numbers change but neither membrane difference changes. Next consider a different invented model in the original reference: keep perilymph at 0 and interior at −45, but assign endolymph 0 mV. Interior minus endolymph is now −45 mV rather than −125 mV. Only one compartment changed, so this is a changed electrical arrangement, not a new zero. Holding the interior fixed is an explicit mathematical assumption; a real cell may respond differently.

steps.title: Do not turn a voltage difference into an ion current
steps.body: The calculation finds electrical potential differences. It does not specify the ion concentrations, channel opening, selectivity, conductance or coupling needed to calculate an ionic current. Even a correctly signed voltage difference is insufficient for a complete electrochemical prediction. In particular, the difference between the invented scenarios is not a percentage loss of hearing, a current ratio or a universal hair-cell voltage.

steps.title: Connect the calculation to the biological experiment
steps.body: The endocochlear potential is an extracellular difference between endolymph and a perilymph reference. It is distinct from the voltage across the hair-cell membrane. Russell’s 1983 primary study relates cochlear compartment arrangement to receptor potentials; Nin and colleagues’ 2008 experiments investigate how the stria supports the endocochlear potential. These studies supply biological context. The reference-shift arithmetic here follows from subtraction and does not reproduce their recordings or establish a clinical model.

question.prompt: In the invented original reference, keep the interior at −45 mV and perilymph at 0 mV, but change endolymph from +80 to 0 mV. What is interior minus endolymph now?

options.reason: That was the original apical difference. Only endolymph changed here; this is not a common reference shift.
The new difference is −45−0. The change is real within the assigned model, with the interior explicitly held fixed; it does not predict a current or a hearing outcome.
That reverses the requested subtraction. Interior minus outside is negative for these assigned numbers.

recall.prompt: Why can a potassium-rich extracellular fluid still be extracellular?
recall.answer: Extracellular describes location relative to the cell membrane. Composition does not define whether a compartment is inside the cell. Identify the membrane, both compartments and the reference before calculating.

objectives: Place the apical bundle and basolateral surface in their respective extracellular environments.
Calculate a potential difference after naming the reference.
Separate the electrical part of a driving force from a complete current prediction.
Distinguish changing every reference value from changing only one compartment.

oralExamination.prompt: A tutor subtracts 80 mV from all three locations. Has the apical membrane difference changed? Explain without recalculating every number.
oralExamination.answer: No. In (inside−80)−(outside−80), the common subtraction cancels. The change is a coordinate choice.

oralExamination.prompt: Why does assigning endolymph 0 mV while retaining the other original numbers describe a different model?
oralExamination.answer: It changes one location relative to the other two. The apical difference becomes −45 mV; the basolateral difference remains −45 mV. No current or hearing outcome follows from these values alone.

summaryChecklist: Name the apical, intracellular and basolateral locations before using a number.
State one voltage reference for all assigned values.
Subtract outside from inside in the requested direction.
Distinguish a common offset from changing one compartment.
Do not infer ionic current or hearing outcome from voltage subtraction alone.

workedExample.title: Recalculate after changing the reference
workedExample.prompt: Move the reference from perilymph to endolymph without changing the model. What are the three potentials now?
solution: Use the original assigned values relative to perilymph: perilymph 0 mV, endolymph+80 mV and interior−45 mV.
Subtract 80 mV from every location: endolymph 0 mV, perilymph−80 mV and interior−125 mV.
Basolateral difference: −125−(−80)=−45 mV. Apical difference: −125−0=−125 mV.
Both physical differences are unchanged. Assigned illustrative values are not universal measurements; no current or hearing outcome is inferred.

lessons.subject: physiology
lessons.title: Hearing: separate sound cycles, spike count and spike timing
lessons.summary: Compare sound cycles with invented neural event counts and timing; equal mean rates need not give equal phase fractions.
lessons.section: Original reference/timing exercises; biological context from named primary studies

steps.title: Name the variable and unit
steps.body: An acoustic frequency counts sound cycles per second in hertz. A spike rate counts neural events per second. Matching dimensions do not make them the same measurement: specify what event is being counted and where. Sound-pressure level is another physical quantity. Perceived loudness is a perceptual outcome, so equal sound-pressure levels at different frequencies do not by themselves establish equal loudness.

steps.title: Connect with existing place-based teaching
steps.body: Cochlear responses have frequency-dependent spatial tuning. Existing ear and sensory lessons introduce this place relationship; use them for the overview. This exercise adds a different question: can two spike sequences contain the same number of events while placing those events differently within sound cycles? A temporal comparison requires the sound period, a stated phase origin and the event times, not just a mean count.

steps.title: Follow the change in signal type
steps.body: A sound wave, a hair-cell receptor potential and a neural spike train are different signals. Russell and Sellick recorded intracellular cochlear receptor potentials in guinea pigs; Johnson compared auditory-nerve discharge rate and synchronization in cats. Neither experiment licenses treating acoustic hertz as the spike rate of every human auditory fibre. The invented event lists below are arithmetic counterexamples, not animal recordings or predicted biological performance.

steps.title: Make only the inference supported by the comparison
steps.body: Let tone T1 be 500 Hz, T2 be 2,000 Hz at the same sound-pressure level as T1, and T3 be 500 Hz at a higher level than T1. Comparing T1 with T2 changes frequency by construction; comparing T1 with T3 changes level by construction. Those statements do not require predicting a person’s loudness judgment. Tone labels T1–T3 refer to stimuli; sequence labels A and B below refer to invented neural event lists.

steps.title: Keep the observation interval with the rate
steps.body: For a 500 Hz waveform, one cycle lasts 2 ms. Define a half-open observation window from 0 up to, but not including, 10 ms. Five complete cycles fit inside it. Invent sequence A with events at 0.5, 2.5 and 6.5 ms. Its interval mean is 3/0.010 = 300 spikes per second, and its count per cycle is 3/5 = 0.6. These are two descriptions of the same finite count. Neither implies 500 spikes per second or one spike on every cycle.

steps.title: Compare timing without changing the count
steps.body: Sequence B has events at 0.5, 3.0 and 7.0 ms in the same window. A and B both contain three events, giving the same 300-per-second interval mean. Relative to a cycle starting at time zero, define phase fraction as (event time modulo 2 ms)/2 ms. A has fractions 0.25, 0.25 and 0.25; B has 0.25, 0.50 and 0.50. Equal count therefore does not determine phase distribution. Three invented events are not enough to establish an empirical phase-locking limit or a statistical property of a real neuron.

question.prompt: The two invented sequences have three events each within the same 10 ms window, but their listed phase fractions differ. Which conclusion follows?

options.text: Their specified 500 Hz sound waveform must change to 300 Hz
options.reason: 300 per second describes the interval mean spike count divided by time; it does not redefine the sound-cycle frequency.

options.text: Their interval mean rates are equal, but their event timing within the sound cycle differs
options.reason: Both give 3/0.010=300 per second. A has phase fractions 0.25,0.25,0.25 while B has 0.25,0.50,0.50, so count does not fix timing.

options.text: Every sound cycle must contain exactly one spike in both sequences
options.reason: There are five cycles but only three events in each invented list; a one-event-per-cycle claim is contradicted by the data.

recall.prompt: Why are acoustic frequency and neural firing frequency easy to confuse?
recall.answer: Both count events per second, but the events differ. Identify sound cycles versus spikes, the physical or neural recording location, and what is controlled before interpreting a number.

objectives: Keep an acoustic frequency separate from a neural spike rate.
Use controlled tone comparisons without inferring loudness from level alone.
Distinguish spatial frequency tuning from the timing information in a stated event list.
Calculate a finite-window mean event rate and compare phase fractions without treating a toy sequence as biological evidence.

oralExamination.prompt: Sequence A has no event in the cycle from 4 to 6 ms. Does that alter the acoustic frequency?
oralExamination.answer: No. The specified waveform still has a 2 ms period. A neural event is absent from that cycle; the two event types are separate.

oralExamination.prompt: Can you conclude that a real auditory fibre is phase-locked from these three invented events?
oralExamination.answer: No. The constructed list illustrates the distinction between count and timing. A biological inference requires measured responses, an appropriate analysis and enough observations.

summaryChecklist: Name whether an event is a sound cycle or a neural spike.
Retain the observation duration when calculating a mean rate.
State the sound period and phase origin before comparing event timing.
Compare both count and phase; check for missing cycles.
Treat the event lists as invented counterexamples, not measurements or physiological cutoffs.

workedExample.title: Same count, different timing
workedExample.prompt: A 500 Hz waveform has a 2 ms period. Over [0,10) ms, sequence A contains events at 0.5,2.5,6.5 ms; B contains 0.5,3.0,7.0 ms. Compare count, interval mean rate and phase fraction relative to a cycle starting at time zero.
solution: Count within the stated window[0,10) ms: A and B each have three events. The duration is 0.010 seconds.
Both interval mean rates are 3/0.010=300 spikes per second. The specified 500 Hz sound waveform still has a 2 ms period.
Calculate each phase fraction as(time modulo 2 ms)/2 ms: A gives 0.25,0.25,0.25; B gives 0.25,0.50,0.50.
Equal count and mean rate do not fix phase distribution. A has no event from 4 to 6 ms. The six invented events do not establish biological phase-locking limits or a real neuron’s statistics.

lessons.subject: cell-biology
lessons.section: Selected compartmental-targeting mechanisms: original source-checked explanation
lessons.title: Peroxisomal import: cargo signal and receptor
lessons.summary: Separate the PTS1 signal, its PEX5 receptor and their different destinations; explain why a molecular label alone is not a complete mechanism.

steps.title: Identify two different molecular roles
steps.body: A targeting signal belongs to eligible cargo; a receptor is a separate molecule that recognizes it. For the selected PTS1 pathway, the signal lies at the cargo’s C terminus and PEX5 is the receptor. Draw two labelled objects before drawing an arrow. Otherwise, it is easy to turn the signal into a transporter or to send the receptor to the cargo’s final destination.

steps.title: Use the classic targeting result within its tested scope
steps.body: In a classic reporter experiment, adding terminal Ser–Lys–Leu redirected a reporter toward peroxisomes. This supports a targeting role for the tested terminal sequence. It does not mean that finding those three letters anywhere in a sequence establishes import. Position, the eligible cargo and cellular context still matter.

steps.title: Place recognition on the cytosolic side
steps.body: PEX5 can bind newly synthesized eligible cargo in the cytosol and engage peroxisomal import machinery. The cargo’s destination is the peroxisomal matrix. Do not route this selected cytosolic recognition event through the ER and Golgi simply because the neighbouring lysosomal lesson uses those compartments.

steps.title: Follow receptor return separately from cargo delivery
steps.body: PEX5 can return to the cytosol for reuse after its participation at the import machinery. An arrow labelled “receptor return” is therefore not an arrow showing cargo leaving the matrix. The shared word “transport” does not make all moving molecules identical.

steps.title: Interpret ubiquitination with its context
steps.body: A 2024 rat-liver-based cell-free study examined reversible cysteine ubiquitination of PEX5 and its extraction from the peroxisomal membrane. This is a specific example in which a ubiquitin modification participates in receptor recycling. A ubiquitin label alone is insufficient to conclude that its carrier is being destroyed by the proteasome.

steps.title: State the limits of this route map
steps.body: This lesson follows selected PTS1 cargo and PEX5. It does not describe every matrix protein, membrane protein or import route. A proposed address is not the same observation as delivery, and location at one time is not a measurement of transport rate. Ask which molecule was tracked, in which compartment, and over which interval.

objectives: Distinguish a cargo signal from a separate receptor.
Place selected PTS1 recognition in the cytosol.
Trace cargo delivery and receptor return as different paths.
Limit conclusions from a targeting motif or one localization snapshot.

workedExample.title: Two arrows after a recognition event
workedExample.prompt: In a fictional route sketch, cargo C bears a terminal targeting feature S and binds receptor R. After delivery, R is found again in the cytosol. Must C have returned with R?
solution: Keep C, S and R as distinct labels: S is a feature on C, whereas R is a separate molecule.
The return observation concerns R. It does not by itself locate C.
In the selected PTS1 map, cargo delivery and PEX5 return are different parts of a cycle. Establish the cargo location with its own evidence.

question.prompt: Which statement correctly separates the roles in the selected PTS1 route?

options.text: PTS1 is a cargo signal and PEX5 is a separate receptor.
options.reason: Correct: the targeting feature belongs to eligible cargo; the receptor recognizes it.

options.text: PEX5 is the terminal three-amino-acid signal on cargo.
options.reason: This confuses the recognizing protein with the feature it recognizes.

options.text: Receptor return proves that delivered cargo returned too.
options.reason: The observation concerns the receptor, so cargo location requires separate evidence.

recall.prompt: Explain the selected PTS1 route using the words signal, receptor, cytosol, matrix and return.
recall.answer: Eligible cargo carries a terminal signal recognized by the separate PEX5 receptor in the cytosol. The route delivers cargo toward the peroxisomal matrix and permits receptor return for reuse; the cargo and receptor arrows must be tracked separately.

oralExamination.prompt: Why must a targeting feature have a specified molecular location?
oralExamination.answer: The terminal location is part of the proposed address. A similar sequence elsewhere does not reproduce the tested reporter arrangement, and even a terminal motif needs an eligible cargo and cellular context.

oralExamination.prompt: Why does receptor recycling not establish cargo recycling?
oralExamination.answer: A return observation tracks the receptor. Cargo and receptor are separate molecules, so the cargo requires its own localization evidence.

oralExamination.prompt: Why is ubiquitination not a complete explanation of a protein’s fate?
oralExamination.answer: The carrier, modification and experimental context matter. The selected PEX5 example concerns receptor extraction and reuse; a ubiquitin label alone does not establish proteasomal destruction.

summaryChecklist: Name the eligible cargo and its signal separately.
Place recognition in the cytosol.
Keep cargo and receptor destinations distinct.
Name the experimental context before generalizing a modification.

lessons.subject: cell-biology
lessons.section: Selected compartmental-targeting mechanisms: original source-checked explanation
lessons.title: Lysosomal enzyme sorting: tag, receptor and destination
lessons.summary: Trace a selected hydrolase from ER/Golgi processing to receptor-dependent sorting, then separate cargo delivery from receptor reuse.

steps.title: Name the cargo before tracing the route
steps.body: The selected cargo is a soluble lysosomal hydrolase travelling through the secretory pathway. Its ER/Golgi processing places it on the lumen-facing side of the route. This is a different starting arrangement from a cytosolic PTS1 cargo meeting PEX5. A common final word such as “organelle” does not establish a common itinerary.

steps.title: Distinguish a glycan tag from a peptide signal
steps.body: Mannose-6-phosphate, or M6P, is a modification on suitable carbohydrate chains of eligible hydrolase cargo. It is not the amino-acid sequence Ser–Lys–Leu. The M6P receptor is another protein, not the phosphate group and not the hydrolase itself.

steps.title: Separate tag formation from tag recognition
steps.body: The M6P marker is formed through distinct enzymatic steps. GlcNAc-1-phosphotransferase initiates a modification on the cargo glycan, and an uncovering enzyme removes the outer sugar to expose the marker. These processing steps are different from a receptor subsequently recognizing suitable tagged cargo in the trans-Golgi network.

steps.title: Follow the cargo toward endosomes
steps.body: M6P receptors help sort eligible cargo from the trans-Golgi network toward endosomes. A receptor-binding event is one stage of delivery, not proof that every downstream step has succeeded. This selected route does not account for every lysosomal protein.

steps.title: Keep separation and recycling as different events
steps.body: Endosomal conditions can favour separation of suitable hydrolase cargo from its receptor. The receptor can recycle toward the Golgi while cargo continues along its delivery route. A classic cultured-hepatocyte study used compartment markers and receptor redistribution to investigate this cycle; its experimental timing is not a timetable for all cells.

steps.title: Treat a static distribution as a limited readout
steps.body: More receptor in one compartment could reflect more arrival, less departure, changed production or changed loss. A snapshot does not uniquely identify those contributions. Track cargo and receptor separately and specify the interval before interpreting a change as faster delivery.

objectives: Distinguish the hydrolase cargo, its glycan marker and its receptor.
Separate marker formation from recognition.
Trace cargo and receptor after their separation.
Explain why a compartment amount does not uniquely measure traffic.

workedExample.title: The same compartment amount can hide different traffic
workedExample.prompt: In a fictional one-minute model, a compartment begins with 10 receptor units. Case A has 3 units arrive and 3 leave; case B has 1 arrive and 1 leave. Assume no other production or loss. Can the final amount distinguish these cases?
solution: Use final amount = starting amount + arrivals − departures.
Case A ends at 10 + 3 − 3 = 10; case B ends at 10 + 1 − 1 = 10.
The equal amount hides different stipulated traffic. These are invented units, not measured cellular kinetics; a single amount cannot select the case.

question.prompt: After a selected hydrolase separates from its M6P receptor in an endosome, which statement follows the simplified route correctly?

options.text: The receptor can return toward the Golgi separately from cargo.
options.reason: Correct: recycling concerns the recognizing protein; cargo can continue along its delivery route.

options.text: The receptor has become the carbohydrate tag on the hydrolase.
options.reason: The tag is a modification of cargo glycans, whereas the receptor is a separate protein.

options.text: An unchanged compartment amount proves that no receptors moved.
options.reason: Equal arrival and departure can preserve an amount while traffic continues.

recall.prompt: Explain the difference between tag formation, receptor recognition and receptor reuse.
recall.answer: Enzymatic processing generates the M6P marker on eligible cargo glycans. A separate receptor recognizes suitable tagged cargo for sorting. After cargo separation, receptor return is a distinct event and does not require the cargo to retrace that path.

oralExamination.prompt: Why is M6P not interchangeable with a peptide targeting sequence?
oralExamination.answer: M6P is a carbohydrate modification on eligible cargo glycans. The selected PTS1 example is a terminal peptide feature; they are different molecular features recognized in different compartmental routes.

oralExamination.prompt: Which event is performed by the tagging enzymes, and which by the receptor?
oralExamination.answer: Tagging enzymes process the cargo glycan to generate the marker. A separate receptor recognizes suitable marked cargo for sorting; making the feature and recognizing it are different events.

oralExamination.prompt: Why do equal compartment amounts not prove equal traffic?
oralExamination.answer: An amount records the net balance under the stated assumptions. The invented cases have equal final amounts despite different arrivals and departures, so an amount alone does not identify those contributions.

summaryChecklist: Name cargo, tag and receptor separately.
Distinguish processing from recognition.
Place recognition in the trans-Golgi network.
Separate cargo delivery from receptor return.
State assumptions when interpreting a traffic model.

lessons.subject: genetics
lessons.title: Synonymous variants: separate coding consequence from measured function
lessons.summary: Trace one fictional substitution through explicit strand and reading-frame contexts, then separate a coding prediction from RNA and protein measurements.
lessons.section: Sequence context, coding consequence and the scope of functional readouts

steps.title: Start with the transcript and the claim
steps.body: For a specified coding transcript and genetic code, a synonymous coding substitution leaves the encoded amino acid unchanged at that position. This describes a coding consequence. It does not establish that RNA processing, RNA abundance, translation or every biological outcome is unchanged. Keep the reference transcript and annotation context explicit; the label alone is not a pathogenicity classification.

steps.title: Fix the reference and the local coordinates
steps.body: Use this fictional internal DNA window, written in the plus-strand 5′→3′ direction: reference ATGAAACCC; altered ATGAAGCCC. Number the displayed bases 1 through 9. Exactly position 6 changes A→G. These are local exercise coordinates, not a real locus or a complete variant report. A real description needs an identifiable reference and appropriate annotation; RefSeq and Ensembl identifiers require their sequence version. This nine-base fragment supplies neither a complete transcript nor its start site. It does not establish that any stipulated product is expressed.

steps.title: Hold the substitution fixed while changing the stated frame
steps.body: Assume the standard genetic code (table 1) and use the DNA alphabet: the code table writes T where the corresponding RNA codon uses U. In fictional coding context P1, the affected triplet uses plus positions 4, 5, 6: AAA→AAG, lysine→lysine. It is synonymous for P1. Context P2 instead uses plus positions 6, 7, 8: ACC→GCC, threonine→alanine. The same changed base now lies at a different place in a triplet. These are stipulated internal coding fragments in different hypothetical annotations, not alternative observations of a real transcript or proof of overlapping expression. The consequence belongs to the stated context.

steps.title: Reverse and complement before reading the other strand
steps.body: The opposite strand is complementary and antiparallel. Written 5′→3′, the reverse complements of the full windows are reference GGGTTTCAT and altered GGGCTTCAT. Plus position 6 appears at opposite-display position 9 − 6 + 1 = 4. Its A→G change becomes T→C. In fictional opposite-strand coding context M, read the complements of plus positions 6, 5, 4 in that order: TTT→CTT, phenylalanine→leucine under the standard code. Complementing without reversing can put the selected triplet in the wrong orientation. This annotation exercise does not determine a biological effect or a clinical classification.

steps.title: Separate amount from the process that produces it
steps.body: In a fictional construct comparison, A and B have the same predicted amino-acid sequence. Suppose normalized RNA amounts are 100 and 50 arbitrary units, while normalized protein amounts are 100 and 40. These invented steady-state amounts do not directly measure an RNA decay rate or translation rate. A difference in a pool can have several causes. A suitable time-course or other process-specific experiment is needed to distinguish them. Protein abundance also does not measure activity per molecule. No replicates, uncertainty or mechanism are established by these illustrative values.

steps.title: Use primary experiments as bounded counterexamples
steps.body: Presnyak and colleagues report synonymous recoding experiments associated with altered mRNA stability in a budding-yeast system. [1] That provides a counterexample to the universal claim that an unchanged amino-acid sequence guarantees unchanged RNA behavior; it does not predict the effect of every single human variant. Duan and colleagues report effects of selected synonymous changes on DRD2 expression-related readouts and dependence on the tested combination of changes. [2] A result for specific constructs and conditions is not an individual clinical interpretation or proof that all synonymous variants are harmful.

steps.title: Build a readout ladder
steps.body: First ask whether the intended DNA change is verified. Next separate the predicted coding sequence from observed RNA processing or isoform structure. Then ask what was measured: steady-state RNA amount, an RNA turnover time-course, protein amount or protein function under a specified normalization. A computational folding prediction is a prediction rather than a direct structure measurement. Different readouts can support different parts of a mechanism; none should silently stand in for all the others.

steps.title: Practice stopping at the supported conclusion
steps.body: An original worksheet reports identical predicted amino-acid sequences and different normalized RNA amounts. The supported statement is that the specified coding prediction agrees while the fictional RNA amounts differ. Do not conclude from those facts alone that translation is slower, protein folding is altered, an individual has a disease or an intervention will help. Clinical interpretation needs evidence beyond this teaching exercise. Reuse the existing RNA-processing and turnover explanations for those mechanisms instead of importing a full textbook chapter.

question.prompt: Fictional constructs A and B have the same predicted amino-acid sequence but RNA amounts of 100 and 50 arbitrary units. What follows from those statements alone?

options.text: The specified coding prediction is unchanged, but a steady-state RNA amount differs; the cause needs separate evidence.
options.reason: A sequence annotation and an amount measurement answer different questions. No RNA decay or translation rate was directly measured.

options.text: The unchanged coding prediction proves all molecular and clinical outcomes are unchanged.
options.reason: Synonymous coding consequence does not guarantee absence of effects at other levels.

options.text: The lower RNA amount proves translation slowed by exactly one half.
options.reason: RNA abundance is not a translation-rate measurement, and these values contain no process-specific or uncertainty evidence.

recall.prompt: Why does an unchanged predicted amino acid leave other questions unanswered?
recall.answer: The coding annotation answers one question for a named reference, coding context and genetic code. RNA processing, RNA abundance, turnover, protein amount and protein activity are different readouts. A synonymous label does not measure those processes or classify a real variant clinically.

objectives: State what a synonymous coding annotation does and does not establish.
Match sequence, RNA and protein claims to the readout needed.
Keep experimental counterexamples separate from individual clinical interpretation.
Trace a single fictional substitution through stated frames and an opposite-strand display.

workedExample.title: One base, three explicit annotation contexts
workedExample.prompt: For plus-strand 5′→3′ reference ATGAAACCC and altered ATGAAGCCC, identify the changed local position. Compare context P1 (plus 4,5,6), context P2 (plus 6,7,8) and context M (complements of plus 6,5,4, read in that order). Assume standard code table 1 and internal coding fragments, not initiation sites. Does any row establish RNA abundance or clinical significance?
solution: The only difference is local plus position 6: A→G. The exercise specifies fragments and annotations; it does not identify a real gene or transcript.
P1 is AAA→AAG, lysine→lysine: synonymous for P1. P2 is ACC→GCC, threonine→alanine. Different stipulated triplet boundaries explain the different codon-level results.
Reverse complements of the full windows are GGGTTTCAT and GGGCTTCAT. Plus position 6 maps to displayed opposite position 4, where T→C. Context M is TTT→CTT, phenylalanine→leucine.
None of these code lookups measures RNA processing, RNA amount, translation, protein amount or activity. A real classification requires its own reference and evidence; no patient conclusion follows.

oralExamination.prompt: Why can P1 and P2 have different consequences for the same changed base?
oralExamination.answer: The coding-triplet boundaries differ. Plus position 6 is third in P1 (AAA→AAG) but first in P2 (ACC→GCC). Hold the underlying substitution fixed and state the annotation before naming its consequence.

oralExamination.prompt: What changes when the plus window is displayed on the opposite strand?
oralExamination.answer: Reverse the order and complement the bases to write the other strand 5′→3′. In this nine-base window, plus position 6 becomes displayed position 4 and A→G becomes T→C. This is a new description of the same stipulated change, not a second mutation.

oralExamination.prompt: Does RNA amount 50 rather than 100 prove that decay doubled or translation halved?
oralExamination.answer: No. These invented steady-state amounts do not identify the underlying production, processing or loss rates. A process-specific experiment and uncertainty evidence would be needed. Protein abundance and protein function are also separate readouts.

oralExamination.prompt: What do the named primary experiments contribute?
oralExamination.answer: They provide bounded counterexamples: selected synonymous recoding can affect RNA-related readouts in the tested systems. They do not predict every human variant, show every proposed mechanism or determine an individual clinical outcome.

summaryChecklist: Name the reference, coding context and genetic code.
Locate the single changed base before interpreting it.
Reverse and complement the opposite strand.
Separate coding annotation from RNA and protein readouts.
Stop before an unsupported mechanism or clinical conclusion.

lessons.subject: genetics
lessons.title: Antibody diversification: mutation, selection and class switching
lessons.summary: Track which antibody feature changed, distinguish mutation from selection, and explain why endpoint labels do not reconstruct a biological history.
lessons.section: Variable-region sequence, heavy-chain class and the scope of lineage evidence

steps.title: Name the two features before following an event
steps.body: An antibody has variable regions that contribute to antigen binding and heavy-chain constant regions associated with its class and effector interactions. In the fictional model below, V0 and V1 label different rearranged heavy-chain variable sequences, while Cmu and Cgamma label mu and gamma constant-region categories. The light chain is held fixed. These labels are bookkeeping symbols, not actual sequences, measured affinities or a complete antibody description.

steps.title: A variable-region mutation creates a different candidate
steps.body: Somatic hypermutation introduces changes in immunoglobulin variable-region genes. Selection among variants can favor improved binding; mutation alone is not equivalent to affinity maturation. In the symbolic model, changing V0 to V1 records a stipulated variable-region mutation. It supplies no binding measurement, no population-frequency comparison and no evidence that the altered cell was retained. A sequence difference and an advantage under a specified response are separate claims. Do not convert a new V label into a numerical affinity or guaranteed improvement.

steps.title: A class switch changes a different part of the comparison
steps.body: Class-switch recombination changes the heavy-chain constant region and associated effector properties while preserving the rearranged variable region during that event. Later variable-region mutations can change binding. The stipulated transition (V0, Cmu) to (V0, Cgamma) changes the constant-region category while retaining the V label. That is the feature comparison used here for a switch event. It does not prove identical results in every antibody format or assay, and it does not measure protection. Keep the molecular event separate from a later functional comparison.

steps.title: Selection asks which variants contribute afterward
steps.body: Mutation concerns which sequence differences arise; selection concerns which variants are retained or expanded in a defined response. In their experimental germinal-center study, Gitlin and colleagues connected antigen capture and presentation to T-cell help with regulated expansion and diversification. That bounded result helps explain why the responding population need not be a random sample of all variants. It is not proof that every mutation improves affinity, that sequence frequency alone measures binding, or that the same quantitative rule holds in every response.

steps.title: Endpoints leave intermediate events unobserved
steps.body: Stipulate a known fictional lineage beginning at (V0, Cmu) and ending at (V1, Cgamma), with no intermediate record. Both labels differ. The symbolic operations can be written as V-change then C-change, or C-change then V-change, and both arrive at the displayed endpoint. This establishes missing information in the worksheet, not equal biological frequencies, independent molecular operations or permission to invent an actual clone history. Time-resolved lineage and molecular evidence would be needed to reconstruct that history.

steps.title: A shared factor does not make two outcomes identical
steps.body: Muramatsu and colleagues studied AID perturbation in experimental cell and animal systems and found effects on both class switching and variable-region mutation accumulation. A shared requirement links outcomes without making the measured outcomes the same process. The historical title describes a potential RNA-editing role; it is not a current mechanism established by that title. Petersen-Mahrt and colleagues later used AID expression in E. coli and a DNA-mutation readout to support a DNA-deamination explanation. That distinct model is evidence to interpret in context, not a complete account of mammalian repair, regulation or every antibody-diversification outcome.

steps.title: Keep a typical pattern separate from an individual history
steps.body: Roco and colleagues examined class-switch timing using multiple approaches. In the analyzed lineages, most inferred switch events preceded the onset of somatic hypermutation, with switching greatly diminished in germinal centers. This qualifies a simple teaching picture that places switching inside a germinal-center cycle. It does not mean switching never occurs there, supply a missing intermediate for this fictional clone, or make the two symbolic paths equally frequent. A population pattern cannot substitute for an individual lineage record.

steps.title: Match the proposed conclusion to the missing readout
steps.body: To establish an actual variable-sequence difference, inspect sequence observations and their lineage context. To establish a switch, examine the relevant molecular rearrangement and context. To compare binding, use a suitable functional measurement with stated format, normalization and uncertainty. To infer selection, examine contribution to the response rather than a label alone. The worksheet supplies none of those measurements and no evidence of clinical protection. Use its explicit assumptions to practice the distinctions, then stop at the model boundary.

objectives: Distinguish variable-region mutation from heavy-chain constant-region switching.
Separate a new sequence variant from selection or measured binding improvement.
Explain why a shared experimental requirement does not identify two outcomes as one process.
Keep a symbolic endpoint comparison separate from the timing of a real lineage.

question.prompt: In a fictional comparison explicitly stipulated to be a class-switch event, (V0, Cmu) becomes (V0, Cgamma), with the light chain held fixed. Which feature comparison is supported?

options.text: The constant-region category changed while the rearranged variable-region label stayed fixed.
options.reason: The stipulated switch changes Cmu to Cgamma and retains V0. Binding improvement, selection and clinical protection were not measured.

options.text: The unchanged V0 label proves that every assay will give an identical binding result.
options.reason: A retained sequence label is not a measurement across every antibody format or assay. The model supplies no such results.

options.text: The new constant-region label proves a new variable-region sequence was selected.
options.reason: The V label remains V0. A class change does not establish a new variable sequence or selection of such a sequence.

workedExample.title: Two feature changes without an intermediate record
workedExample.prompt: A known fictional lineage starts at (V0, Cmu) and is later observed at (V1, Cgamma). Only variable-label changes and constant-category changes are allowed in this symbolic worksheet, and the light chain is fixed. What changed, and can the observed endpoints identify the order?
solution: Compare each coordinate separately: V0 differs from V1, and Cmu differs from Cgamma. Both stipulated features differ.
Path A is (V0, Cmu) → (V1, Cmu) → (V1, Cgamma). Path B is (V0, Cmu) → (V0, Cgamma) → (V1, Cgamma). Each is a symbolic completion of the missing record.
The displayed endpoints therefore do not identify the intermediate or order. The worksheet does not prove that these paths are equally likely or both occur in the biological system under study.
A population timing result does not fill in this individual record. Neither path measures affinity, selection, protection or a patient outcome.

recall.prompt: Explain why mutation, selection and class switching are three different questions.
recall.answer: Mutation describes a sequence alteration, selection concerns which variants contribute afterward, and class switching changes the heavy-chain constant-region arrangement while retaining the rearranged variable region during that event. The worksheet labels do not measure binding or reconstruct unobserved biological intermediates.

oralExamination.prompt: Does V0 becoming V1 already establish improved binding?
oralExamination.answer: No. It records a stipulated sequence difference. Binding improvement needs an appropriate comparison, and selection requires evidence about which variants contributed to the response.

oralExamination.prompt: Why does one AID perturbation affecting two outcomes not make them identical?
oralExamination.answer: A common requirement can participate in different processes. Keep the class-switch readout and the variable-region mutation readout distinct; the perturbation does not identify every downstream step.

oralExamination.prompt: Can the two symbolic paths be described as equally common biological histories?
oralExamination.answer: No. They show that endpoint labels alone omit information. The exercise supplies no frequencies or biochemical independence, and a typical population pattern cannot reconstruct the individual missing record.

oralExamination.prompt: What stays fixed during the stipulated class-switch comparison?
oralExamination.answer: The rearranged heavy-chain variable label stays V0 and the light chain is fixed by assumption, while Cmu becomes Cgamma. This identifies the modeled feature change, not a universal functional-assay result.

summaryChecklist: Name variable and constant features separately.
Distinguish mutation from selection.
State what the class-switch comparison preserves.
Avoid inferring event order from endpoints alone.
Match binding, lineage and protection claims to their own evidence.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Serine and glycine: donor, carrier and cofactor
lessons.summary: Trace a specified carbon transfer, distinguish the folate carrier from catalytic PLP, and separate gross reaction events from net change.
lessons.section: Amino-acid carbon skeletons and one-carbon metabolism; original reaction-role and event-ledger introduction
objectives: Assign the donor, folate carrier and catalytic-cofactor roles in the specified SHMT reaction.
Balance substrate-derived carbon without counting the carrier backbone as a one-carbon molecule.
Distinguish a reaction equation and fictional event count from physiological net flux.
Distinguish gross forward/reverse events from their net stoichiometric change.
Compare a specified carbon transfer with an amino-group transfer without assuming urea production.
Keep the studied organism, ligand and measurement distinct from a human physiological claim.

steps.title: Read one specified reversible reaction
steps.body: Serine hydroxymethyltransferase, commonly abbreviated SHMT, catalyses the reversible relationship L-serine + tetrahydrofolate ⇌ glycine + 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate + water. The enzyme nomenclature entry writes the same reaction in the reverse direction. Read the arrow as reversibility, not proof of a preferred net direction in every tissue. [1] THF is used below as shorthand for tetrahydrofolate; the named methylene product is a specific folate form.

steps.title: Assign roles without treating the labels as synonyms
steps.body: In the written serine-to-glycine direction, the serine carbon skeleton supplies a one-carbon unit to the folate product. Tetrahydrofolate is the accepting carrier in this reaction. SHMT uses pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) as a catalytic cofactor; PLP participates in catalysis rather than serving as the net carbon feedstock in the equation. [1, 2] Folate derivatives and PLP can both be discussed as coenzyme-related molecules, but their roles here are different. A cofactor label alone does not tell you that the reaction is an amino-group transfer.

steps.title: Use a narrow carbon-count map
steps.body: Serine has three carbon atoms and glycine two. For bookkeeping of the substrate-derived carbon, write 3 = 2 + 1: two remain with glycine and one is transferred into the folate-bound unit. This does not mean the folate molecule has only one carbon, nor does it propose an unbound one-carbon intermediate. The carrier’s pre-existing carbon backbone is outside this small count map. The map is a stoichiometric explanation, not a complete catalytic mechanism.

steps.title: Work an explicitly fictional event count
steps.body: Suppose an isolated accounting model contains 100 net forward reaction events, with sufficient reactants and no reverse or side reactions. It consumes 100 serine molecules, produces 100 glycine molecules and adds 100 transferred one-carbon units to folate products. Substrate-derived carbon balances as 300 = 200 + 100 atoms. This does not imply net consumption of 100 PLP molecules, nor predict metabolite concentrations or whole-cell flux. All counts are invented to illustrate the equation.

steps.title: Separate gross events from net change
steps.body: Extend the fictional accounting model: define 100 forward and 70 reverse events of the same equation, with sufficient reactants for the stated events and no side reactions. There are 170 counted reaction events but 30 net forward events. Net serine use and glycine production are 30 molecules each; 30 units are transferred into the net folate product. For substrate-derived carbon, 90 = 60 + 30. This is an invented event ledger, not a measured rate, concentration, cell pathway or energy calculation. Event order, enzyme abundance and compartment volumes have not been supplied.

steps.title: Read the stated products before calling a process nitrogen disposal
steps.body: The specified serine/folate equation produces glycine and a named folate product, with water in its written forward form. Free ammonia and urea are not products in that net equation. Its carbon-transfer role therefore must not be relabelled as urea production just because serine is an amino acid. Conversely, the existing alanine example transfers an amino group without directly producing urea. Compare the equations and the stated transferred group before deciding which downstream problem remains. This net-equation comparison does not reconstruct transient catalytic intermediates.

steps.title: Keep a research ligand distinct from the reaction product
steps.body: The cited mouse cSHMT study describes a ligand-bound analogue of an inactive complex containing 5-formyltetrahydrofolate. That is not the 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate named in the reaction equation. Keep the molecule and experimental state attached to the claim; a bound structure is not a human tissue-flux measurement.

steps.title: Connect carbon transfer with the enzyme and nitrogen lessons
steps.body: Use the enzyme-foundations lesson to review catalysis and cofactors, then contrast this carbon transfer with the alanine amino-group transfer in the amino-acid nitrogen lesson. A shared PLP context does not make the two net reactions interchangeable. The named folate product also does not stand for every folate form or every one-carbon reaction. Keep the reaction and molecular form explicit. This exercise does not establish nutritional status or a supplement requirement.

steps.title: Match the conclusion to the kind of evidence
steps.body: An enzyme-nomenclature entry defines a reaction and cofactor context. A chosen toy event ledger supplies arithmetic under its own assumptions. A ligand-bound mouse-enzyme structure concerns a particular experimental complex. These are useful but different kinds of evidence. None alone gives net flux, metabolite concentration, nutritional status or an individual supplement requirement. Use the reaction to answer a reaction question, and require measurements of the relevant system for a physiological or clinical claim.

question.prompt: For the written SHMT direction, L-serine + tetrahydrofolate → glycine + 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate + water, which role assignment fits?

options.text: Serine supplies the transferred carbon unit; folate accepts it; PLP supports enzyme catalysis.
options.reason: The names describe different roles in this reaction. PLP is not the net substrate carbon donor in the balanced equation.

options.text: PLP supplies all carbon atoms in the folate-bound unit and must be consumed once per product molecule.
options.reason: That is not the net carbon accounting shown by this reaction; a catalytic cofactor is not automatically a stoichiometric feedstock.

options.text: The folate product contains only one carbon atom in total.
options.reason: “One-carbon unit” refers to the transferred group, not the entire carrier molecule.

recall.prompt: How can a carbon donor, a carrier and a catalytic cofactor participate in the same reaction while having different roles?
recall.answer: In the specified serine-to-glycine direction, substrate-derived carbon is transferred onto the folate carrier. PLP supports enzyme catalysis. These role labels are not interchangeable, and the equation alone does not measure tissue net flux.

workedExample.title: Two counts, two meanings
workedExample.prompt: An invented isolated ledger specifies 80 forward and 30 reverse SHMT reaction events, sufficient reactants and no side reactions. Find the gross event count, net forward change and net substrate-derived carbon balance. No time or volume is given.
solution: The total number of defined reaction events is 80 + 30 = 110.
The opposing changes leave 80 − 30 = 50 net forward events.
In this model, net serine use and glycine production are 50 molecules each, with 50 units transferred into the net folate product.
The substrate-derived carbon balances as 150 = 100 + 50 atoms; the pre-existing carrier backbone is outside this small map.
The ledger supplies neither a reaction rate nor concentrations, a tissue measurement or a nutritional requirement.

oralExamination.prompt: What does 3 = 2 + 1 count here?
oralExamination.answer: Only the serine-derived carbon: two carbons remain with glycine and one is transferred into the folate-bound unit. It excludes the carrier backbone and is not a complete catalytic mechanism.

oralExamination.prompt: Why is PLP not counted as 100 net carbon-feedstock molecules in the 100-event model?
oralExamination.answer: It is identified as a catalytic cofactor, not a carbon substrate with a net coefficient in the specified reaction. The equation supplies no such net carbon-consumption count.

oralExamination.prompt: How do 100 forward and 70 reverse events differ from 100 net forward events?
oralExamination.answer: The first ledger has 170 total events and 30 net forward changes; the second defines 100 net forward changes. Their net product counts differ.

oralExamination.prompt: Why name the folate form in both a reaction and a structural study?
oralExamination.answer: The equation product and the study ligand are different named forms in different contexts. A common folate backbone does not make their roles interchangeable.

oralExamination.prompt: Has urea been produced merely because an amino acid appears in the equation?
oralExamination.answer: No. Read the stated net products and the separate nitrogen-disposal process. Amino-acid conversion does not itself establish urea synthesis or excretion.

oralExamination.prompt: Can the toy ledger identify a nutritional deficiency or tissue net flux?
oralExamination.answer: No. It supplies invented reaction-event counts, not measurements of the relevant organism, tissue, pools or clinical state.

summaryChecklist: Write the specified reversible reaction and identify the chosen teaching direction.
Assign carbon-donor, folate-carrier and PLP catalytic roles without merging the labels.
Balance only the stated substrate-derived carbon and keep the carrier backbone outside that small map.
Separate gross forward/reverse events from their net difference.
Keep the reaction product and the cited mouse-study ligand distinct.
Explain why a reaction equation or toy ledger is not a measurement of flux, excretion or nutritional need.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Pentose phosphate pathway: separate NADPH from ribose needs
lessons.summary: Separate oxidative products, pentose isomerization, carbon rearrangements and NADPH use through explicit invented ledgers.
lessons.section: Carbohydrate branch points and reducing-equivalent bookkeeping
objectives: Distinguish reducing-equivalent production from sugar-phosphate interconversion.
Explain an erythrocyte redox example without assuming a fixed pathway flux.
Name the immediate pentose product and distinguish its later isomerization.
Compute a stipulated single-pass carbon and NADPH balance without assigning ATP yield.
Cancel shared intermediates in a selected two-reaction rearrangement pair.
Distinguish balanced reaction bookkeeping from physiological net flux.
Keep the selected erythrocyte observation within its stated variant and experimental conditions.

steps.title: Start at the branch point
steps.body: Glucose-6-phosphate can enter the pentose phosphate pathway as well as other metabolic routes. The oxidative branch produces NADPH and a five-carbon sugar phosphate. NADPH provides reducing power for several reactions; it is a different bookkeeping pool from ATP.

steps.title: Name the immediate pentose product
steps.body: In the oxidative sequence, glucose-6-phosphate first undergoes an NADP+-linked oxidation to a lactone. Hydrolysis opens the lactone to 6-phosphogluconate. The next NADP+-linked oxidation releases CO2 and yields ribulose-5-phosphate. Ribulose-5-phosphate and ribose-5-phosphate are different molecules; an isomerase interconverts them. A diagram labelled only pentose hides this distinction. [1, 2, 3, 4]

steps.title: Keep a separate redox ledger
steps.body: One complete pass through these three oxidative reactions reduces two NADP+ molecules to two NADPH molecules: one at each dehydrogenase. The hydrolysis step adds no NADPH. NADPH counts reducing equivalents in this ledger, not ATP molecules. This is reaction stoichiometry, not a prediction of a cell’s pathway rate. [1, 2, 3]

steps.title: Work a bounded carbon example
steps.body: Invent a batch of three glucose-6-phosphate molecules entering the oxidative sequence once each, with no diversion or recycling. Eighteen substrate carbon atoms become fifteen in three ribulose-5-phosphate molecules and three in three CO2 molecules. The redox ledger gives six NADPH. Isomerizing all three pentoses to ribose-5-phosphate would add no further NADPH. The stipulated batch does not describe a measured tissue flux. [1, 2, 3, 4]

steps.title: Follow the carbon separately
steps.body: The non-oxidative branch interconverts sugar phosphates, linking pentose phosphates with intermediates associated with glycolysis. These reversible reactions let the pathway connect changing needs for ribose-containing molecules and reducing power; a pathway diagram does not by itself measure the direction or magnitude of flux in a particular cell.

steps.title: Read rearrangements in both directions
steps.body: Consider the transketolase reaction written as xylulose-5-phosphate plus ribose-5-phosphate forming glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate plus sedoheptulose-7-phosphate. Carbon counts are 5 + 5 = 3 + 7. Transaldolase can then pair that seven-carbon sugar with the three-carbon intermediate to form erythrose-4-phosphate and fructose-6-phosphate: 7 + 3 = 4 + 6. Adding these two written steps cancels the shared intermediates and leaves a ten-carbon balance. This is a selected reaction pair, not the complete net equation for every non-oxidative pathway mode. [5, 6]

steps.title: Do not infer flux from a balanced arrow
steps.body: Neither selected rearrangement has NADPH or ATP in its written reaction. Reversing a sugar rearrangement therefore does not reverse an NADPH-producing oxidation. A carbon-balanced equation establishes allowable bookkeeping; substrate availability, enzyme activity and competing demands are separate questions. It cannot establish a universal glucose percentage or reaction direction in every cell. [5, 6]

steps.title: Apply the idea to red blood cells
steps.body: In erythrocytes, NADPH supports regeneration of reduced glutathione, which participates in defense against oxidative damage. This is a mechanistic relationship, not a diagnostic interpretation. The contribution of any route depends on conditions; do not assume a fixed percentage of glucose enters the pathway in all states.

steps.title: Connect reducing power to a specific reaction
steps.body: Read glutathione reductase in the reduction direction: glutathione disulfide plus NADPH and a proton gives two reduced glutathione molecules and NADP+. This is an enzymatic coupling between the NADPH pool and glutathione recycling, not conversion of NADPH into ATP. The nomenclature record prints the reverse bookkeeping direction; follow the named substrates and products rather than assuming every displayed arrow represents the cellular net direction. Erythrocyte physiology needs its own stage- and condition-specific evidence. [7]

steps.title: Keep the erythrocyte experiment inside its conditions
steps.body: A selected 1976 study examined human Mediterranean-variant G6PD-deficient erythrocytes under mild oxidative stimulation. Its abstract reports lower NADPH with insufficient glutathione disulfide reduction. [8] This is a bounded redox example, not a universal normal-cell pathway fraction or a diagnosis from a diagram. Full experimental methods were not reviewed.

steps.title: Avoid a common shortcut
steps.body: Ribose production and NADPH production are connected but are not interchangeable outcomes. Before predicting a pathway response, specify the cell type, conditions, available substrates and what was actually measured. This lesson is not a guide to interpreting a patient result.

steps.title: Separate a result from a clinical conclusion
steps.body: If a teaching account reports NADPH production, first ask which reactions and how many passes were counted. If it reports sugar output, identify the named pentose and any later rearrangement. Neither ledger alone determines a diagnosis, a patient’s oxidative injury, or the share of glucose using this route. Clinical interpretation, fixed flux fractions and treatment instructions are outside this proposed lesson. [1, 3, 4, 7]

question.prompt: What is the best distinction between the oxidative and non-oxidative branches in this introductory model?

options.text: The oxidative branch produces NADPH; the non-oxidative branch interconverts sugar phosphates.
options.reason: The branches perform different linked roles; actual net flux depends on the cell and conditions.

options.text: Both branches exist only to make ATP directly.
options.reason: The pathway is discussed here in terms of reducing power and sugar-phosphate rearrangement, not direct ATP production.

options.text: A fixed fraction of glucose always enters the pathway.
options.reason: The fraction changes with cell type and conditions and cannot be inferred from a generic diagram.

recall.prompt: How do the carbon ledger and the reducing-equivalent ledger answer different questions?
recall.answer: The carbon ledger tracks named carbon-containing molecules and CO2. The redox ledger counts NADP+ reduction to NADPH in specified reactions. Neither alone supplies a cell’s flux or a patient interpretation.

workedExample.title: Follow three stipulated oxidative passes
workedExample.prompt: An invented batch contains three glucose-6-phosphate molecules. Each completes one oxidative pass; no diversion or recycling occurs. All pentose products are then isomerized to ribose-5-phosphate. Count carbon and NADPH before and after isomerization.
solution: Start with 3 × 6 = 18 carbon atoms in the stipulated glucose-6-phosphate inputs.
The oxidative passes produce 3 × 5 = 15 carbon atoms in ribulose-5-phosphate and 3 × 1 = 3 in CO2: 18 = 15 + 3.
The two oxidative dehydrogenase steps per pass produce 3 × 2 = 6 NADPH. This is not six ATP.
Isomerization changes the named pentose product to ribose-5-phosphate without adding NADPH or losing carbon in that written reaction.
No time, tissue flux fraction or clinical measurement was stipulated. These counts cannot supply them.

oralExamination.prompt: Why distinguish ribulose-5-phosphate from ribose-5-phosphate?
oralExamination.answer: The oxidative decarboxylation gives ribulose-5-phosphate. An isomerase interconverts it with ribose-5-phosphate; the molecules are not interchangeable names.

oralExamination.prompt: Where do the two NADPH per oxidative pass arise?
oralExamination.answer: One arises at glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase and one at 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase. Lactone hydrolysis adds none.

oralExamination.prompt: What does the three-pass carbon equation 18 = 15 + 3 mean?
oralExamination.answer: Fifteen input-derived carbon atoms remain in three pentose products and three leave as three CO2 molecules under the stipulated no-diversion, no-recycling model.

oralExamination.prompt: Why can C3 and C7 cancel in the selected two-reaction example?
oralExamination.answer: They are generated by the first written reaction and used by the second. Cancellation leaves C5 + C5 → C4 + C6, a ten-carbon balance for this pair only.

oralExamination.prompt: Does the glutathione reductase equation mean more NADPH always guarantees better cell function?
oralExamination.answer: No. It states a specified reaction relationship. Enzyme behavior, conditions and cellular measurements require separate evidence.

oralExamination.prompt: Can these invented ledgers identify a fixed fraction of glucose using PPP in a red cell?
oralExamination.answer: No. Reaction stoichiometry does not specify pathway rate, tissue allocation, erythroid stage or the conditions of a measured cell.

summaryChecklist: Name the immediate oxidative pentose and its isomerization product.
Keep carbon, NADPH and ATP counts separate.
State pass count, diversion and recycling assumptions before calculating.
Cancel only shared intermediates in the stated reaction pair.
Explain the selected NADPH–glutathione coupling without a clinical conclusion.
Identify what conditions and measurements are missing before discussing net flux.

lessons.subject: biostatistics
lessons.title: Cohort and case-control studies: identify the denominator
lessons.summary: Calculate risk and odds in a complete cohort, then construct two fictional populations compatible with the same case-control sample. Explore which denominators are missing and why sampling design matters.
lessons.section: Study design and denominators
objectives: Calculate risk and odds ratios in a completely observed fictional cohort.
Explain why case-control sample proportions do not establish population risk.
Construct two populations with the same odds ratio but different risks and risk ratios.
Distinguish a possible selected sample from a guaranteed random result.
State the cumulative-control assumptions and limits of this model.

steps.title: Follow the cohort
steps.body: In a fictional cohort observed over the same period with complete follow-up, 20 of 100 exposed and 10 of 100 unexposed participants experience the outcome. The observed risks are 0.20 and 0.10, so the risk ratio is 2. The outcome odds ratio is (20/80)/(10/90) = 2.25. Neither measure alone establishes causation.

steps.title: Follow the case-control selection
steps.body: In a separate fictional study, investigators select 20 cases and 20 controls. Fifteen cases and five controls were exposed; five cases and 15 controls were unexposed. The exposure odds ratio is (15/5)/(5/15) = 9. The equal selected group sizes do not establish that population risk is 50%. How the odds ratio estimates a population measure depends on control sampling and other assumptions. The two examples are unrelated.

steps.title: Read the selected sample in its sampling direction
steps.body: The fictional selected sample contains 20 cases and 20 end-of-period noncase controls. Of the cases 15 are exposed and 5 unexposed; of the controls 5 are exposed and 15 unexposed. Its exposure odds ratio is (15/5)/(5/15)=9. The case fraction 20/40 is a property of this selected sample; its population denominator was not supplied.

steps.title: Construct one complete source population
steps.body: Population A contains 1000 fictional units followed over one common period: 75 exposed outcomes, 225 exposed non-outcomes, 25 unexposed outcomes and 675 unexposed non-outcomes. Overall outcome fraction is 100/1000. The exposed risk is 75/300=1/4; unexposed risk 25/700=1/28; risk ratio 7. Its outcome odds ratio is(75 × 675)/(225 × 25)=9.

steps.title: Construct a different compatible population
steps.body: Population B also contains 1000 units, but has 375 exposed outcomes,125 exposed non-outcomes,125 unexposed outcomes and 375 unexposed non-outcomes. Its overall outcome fraction is 500/1000. Risks are 375/500=3/4 and 125/500=1/4; risk ratio 3. The outcome odds ratio remains 9. Both populations have exposed fractions 3/4 among cases and 1/4 among noncases.

steps.title: Separate compatibility from a guaranteed sample
steps.body: Both populations contain enough of each category for the same 15/5 case split and 5/15 control split to be a possible selected result. This does not say that random sampling always yields those exact counts or that cases should be selected by exposure to force a result. The two constructed tables prove that the selected table alone does not uniquely identify the source population’s absolute risks.

steps.title: Use the explorer without changing the question
steps.body: The explorer changes only the fictional number of outcomes in Population B, keeping its total 1000 and the two conditional exposure fractions fixed. Every slider state is an integer table. Risks change while the cross-product odds ratio remains 9. The selected sample display stays fixed as a compatible result. This is an algebraic sensitivity illustration, not repeated sampling, a risk calculator or a causal model.

steps.title: State which design supports which interpretation
steps.body: Our controls are end-of-period noncases in a cumulative model. Other control-sampling strategies, including risk-set sampling, can target different population quantities and require their own assumptions. Do not turn this worksheet into an assertion that every case-control odds ratio has one interpretation, that a rare-outcome condition is always required, or that an odds ratio is a causal risk ratio.

question.prompt: Why do 20 cases and 20 controls in this selected sample not establish 50% population risk?

options.text: The numbers were selected by design and do not supply the source population denominator.
options.reason: The case fraction is fixed by sampling and cannot alone establish the outcome risk in the source population.

options.text: A case-control study must have more controls than cases.
options.reason: The ratio of controls to cases can vary; that is not why the sample fraction fails to establish population risk.

options.text: The risk ratio must always equal the odds ratio.
options.reason: The measures differ, and the selected numbers do not provide the population risk denominator.

workedExample.title: Calculate with the population denominator
workedExample.prompt: For Population A use 75 exposed outcomes, 225 exposed non-outcomes, 25 unexposed outcomes and 675 unexposed non-outcomes. All 1000 fictional units start outcome-free, keep their exposure group and have complete follow-up over one common period. Controls are selected from end-of-period noncases.
solution: Exposed denominator: 75 + 225 = 300; risk = 75/300 = 1/4.
Unexposed denominator: 25 + 675 = 700; risk = 25/700 = 1/28.
Risk ratio = (1/4)/(1/28) = 7. Outcome odds ratio = (75/225)/(25/675) = 9.
Population B has risks 3/4 and 1/4, so risk ratio 3 and odds ratio 9. Its overall outcome fraction is 500/1000, compared with 100/1000 in A.
Both permit the displayed 20-case/20-control sample. No probability distribution over possible source populations has been supplied; compatibility does not mean equal likelihood.

oralExamination.prompt: Why is 75/1000 not the exposed risk in A?
oralExamination.answer: 1000 includes unexposed units. Exposed risk uses all and only the 300 exposed units at risk at the start of the common period.

oralExamination.prompt: What remains fixed when the explorer changes its outcome count?
oralExamination.answer: The total 1000 and exposure fractions 3/4 among outcomes and 1/4 among non-outcomes. These stipulated fractions keep the cross-product odds ratio at 9.

oralExamination.prompt: Does this establish that a real exposure causes an outcome?
oralExamination.answer: No. These are invented descriptive tables without randomization or causal identification. Control selection and the target measure must be examined in each real study.

recall.prompt: Explain why a selected case fraction cannot alone identify population risk.
recall.answer: Selection fixed the case and control counts. The source population denominator and design are additional information; populations A and B demonstrate different risks compatible with the same displayed selected table.

summaryChecklist: Use the exposed denominator for exposed risk.
Keep the unrelated introductory cohort separate from populations A and B.
Distinguish risk, odds and their ratios.
Describe compatibility without claiming a guaranteed sample.
Attach the cumulative-control definition and complete-follow-up assumptions.

lessons.subject: genetics
lessons.title: Allele copies and genotypes: count the denominators
lessons.summary: Count allele copies separately from people, compare three fictional genotype tables with the same allele frequencies, and derive an independent-pairing expectation without replacing observed data.
lessons.section: Population counting and model assumptions
objectives: Calculate allele frequencies from diploid genotype counts.
Distinguish a sample count from Hardy–Weinberg model assumptions.
Show why the same allele-copy fractions can coexist with different observed heterozygote fractions.
Derive p², 2pq and q² from two explicitly independent allele draws.
Disclose no-call records and keep the complete diploid-autosomal denominator within its scope.

steps.title: Count fictional observations
steps.body: Among 100 diploid individuals, suppose 36 are AA, 48 are Aa and 16 are aa at one autosomal locus. There are 200 allele copies: 120 A and 80 a. The allele frequencies are p = 0.60 and q = 0.40; the observed heterozygote frequency is 48/100 = 0.48.

steps.title: Compare with a model
steps.body: In the simple two-allele Hardy–Weinberg model, expected genotype frequencies p², 2pq and q² equal 0.36, 0.48 and 0.16 for these values. The invented counts were chosen to match. That match does not prove that a real population meets the model assumptions or remains in equilibrium.

steps.title: Name the counting unit before calculating
steps.body: Use one autosomal locus, two alleles, complete calls and two copies per fictional person. If nAA, nAa and naa are observed counts, N = nAA + nAa + naa. Count A copies as 2nAA + nAa and a copies as 2naa + nAa; divide each by 2N. A genotype proportion instead divides one genotype count by N. Write the unit beside the denominator so that a correct numerator cannot be paired with the wrong total.

steps.title: Keep the same allele frequency and change the genotype distribution
steps.body: Compare three invented 100-person groups with genotype counts AA/Aa/aa of 36/48/16, 50/20/30 and 60/0/40. Each contains 120 A copies and 80 a copies, giving p = 0.60 and q = 0.40. Their observed heterozygote proportions are 0.48, 0.20 and 0.00. Allele frequency alone therefore does not determine the observed genotype distribution. No group is labelled a real disease population.

steps.title: Derive an expectation only after stating the pairing model
steps.body: In a separate ideal model, draw two allele copies independently from an unchanged pool with A probability p and a probability q. The ordered pairs AA, Aa, aA and aa have probabilities p², pq, qp and q². Merging the two heterozygote orders gives 2pq. At p = 3/5, the expected proportions are 9/25, 12/25 and 4/25. These are model probabilities, not replacement observations for an already counted sample.

steps.title: Explain what a match does and does not show
steps.body: The first invented group was deliberately chosen to equal those expectations. This arithmetic match does not verify random mating, absence of population structure, stable allele frequencies through time or any other biological premise. Conversely, a mismatch is not a label for a particular mechanism by itself. Explain the model, the observation and the additional evidence needed rather than declaring a biological cause from one table.

steps.title: Keep missing calls and changed biological scope outside this example
steps.body: The denominator 2N belongs to the complete diploid-autosomal setup. If five records have no genotype call, do not count them as aa or quietly treat them as two observed a copies. Redefine the called-sample denominator and describe the missingness. This exercise does not supply rules for sex-linked loci, copy-number changes or mixed ploidy. Those situations need an explicitly different counting model.

question.prompt: What does q = 0.40 count in this example?

options.text: The fraction of allele copies that are a.
options.reason: Allele frequency uses gene copies; the heterozygote frequency uses people and is 0.48 here.

options.text: The fraction of people who are heterozygotes.
options.reason: The observed Aa fraction is 48/100 = 0.48, whereas q = 80/200 = 0.40 counts a allele copies.

options.text: The fraction of people with genotype aa.
options.reason: The observed aa fraction is 16/100 = 0.16 in this invented group; it is not the a-copy fraction q = 0.40.

workedExample.title: Same copy counts, different genotype table
workedExample.prompt: A second fictional group has 50 AA, 20 Aa and 30 aa complete calls at the same two-allele autosomal locus. Compare its observed proportions with the independent-pairing model.
solution: N = 50 + 20 + 30 = 100 people; the observed allele-copy denominator is 2N = 200.
A copies = 2×50 + 20 = 120; a copies = 2×30 + 20 = 80. Therefore p = 3/5 and q = 2/5.
Observed Aa fraction = 20/100 = 1/5. This differs from the independent-pairing expectation 2pq = 12/25.
The expected proportions under that separate model are 9/25, 12/25 and 4/25. They are not replacement observations for the supplied 50/20/30 table.
The mismatch alone identifies no particular biological cause. No disease, phenotype, equilibrium test or real-population mechanism is specified.

oralExamination.prompt: Why does the allele-copy denominator differ from the genotype denominator?
oralExamination.answer: The complete diploid-autosomal setup supplies two allele copies per called person. Allele-copy fractions divide by 2N; genotype fractions divide by N.

oralExamination.prompt: Why can the same p coexist with different observed Aa fractions?
oralExamination.answer: One A-copy total can be allocated across different numbers of AA and Aa individuals. The three constructed tables show the non-unique genotype allocations directly.

oralExamination.prompt: Does a numeric match to p², 2pq and q² establish equilibrium through time?
oralExamination.answer: No. A constructed match to one-step model probabilities supplies neither the biological assumptions nor observations through generations.

recall.prompt: Explain the difference between observed allele-copy fractions, observed genotype fractions and expected genotype probabilities.
recall.answer: Count copies over 2N and people over N in the stated complete diploid setup. Expected probabilities p², 2pq and q² additionally use the independent-pairing model; they do not overwrite the observed genotype table.

summaryChecklist: Name the locus, ploidy and complete-call scope.
Count A and a copies separately from people.
Compare observed heterozygote fractions even when p is fixed.
State the independent-pairing assumptions before multiplying probabilities.
Keep no-call records visible and avoid assigning unobserved genotypes.

lessons.subject: physiology
lessons.title: Venous return: trace a muscle pump through compression and refill
lessons.summary: Use a deliberately ideal two-valve segment to calculate refill, compression and stored volume, then distinguish model output from local venous measurements.
lessons.section: Valve direction, prescribed pressure and cycle accounting
objectives: Orient two one-way paths before calculating pressure-driven flow.
