lessons.subject: anatomy
lessons.title: Gallbladder and extrahepatic biliary pathways
lessons.summary: The right and left hepatic ducts form the common hepatic duct.
lessons.section: 18. Gallbladder and Biliary Tract

steps.title: Gallbladder and Biliary Tract
steps.body: The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile and lies on the visceral surface of the liver. Right and left hepatic ducts form the common hepatic duct; its junction with the cystic duct forms the common bile duct. The cystic duct permits filling and emptying of the gallbladder.

steps.title: Relationships and functional organization
steps.body: Parts of gallbladder are fundus, body, neck, and cystic duct. Common bile duct is formed by union of common hepatic duct and cystic duct. Common bile duct descends in the hepatoduodenal ligament, passes posterior to the first part of duodenum, then approaches the pancreatic head and second part of duodenum. The fundus projects near the right costal margin at the tip of the 9th or 10th costal cartilage region, depending on surface-anatomy convention.

steps.title: How can one obstruction affect both biliary and pancreatic drainage?
steps.body: The common bile duct and main pancreatic duct usually converge near their entry into the descending duodenum, often through a shared ampullary region. An obstruction near that shared outlet can therefore affect both systems, whereas an isolated cystic-duct obstruction mainly alters gallbladder drainage. The ducts may join in different configurations, so the usual map is not universal. Distinguish the duct carrying bile from the artery supplying the gallbladder: they travel nearby but obstruction has a different meaning in each.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: The right and left hepatic ducts form the common hepatic duct. Joining the cystic duct creates the common bile duct; bile does not have to traverse the gallbladder on its way from liver to duodenum. Flow in the cystic duct can be toward storage or away during emptying. The common bile duct passes behind the proximal duodenum and through or behind the pancreatic head before usually joining the pancreatic duct. Variants are common, so this is the typical pattern.

lessons.title: Pancreas and its duct relationships

lessons.section: 19. Pancreas

steps.title: Pancreas
steps.body: The pancreas is a mostly secondarily retroperitoneal foregut organ behind the stomach and related to the C-loop of duodenum and splenic vessels. It has head, uncinate process, neck, body, and tail.

steps.title: Relationships and functional organization
steps.body: Head lies in the duodenal curve. Uncinate process extends posterior to superior mesenteric vessels. Neck lies anterior to formation of portal vein. Body crosses toward the spleen; splenic artery runs along superior border and splenic vein posterior to the pancreas. Tail reaches the splenic hilum in the splenorenal ligament region.

steps.title: How do the pancreatic duct and arterial patterns fit its position?
steps.body: The main duct generally runs from tail toward head and joins the bile-duct outlet region; an accessory duct may open separately at the minor papilla. Pancreaticoduodenal arcades supply the head around the duodenal curve, while branches of the splenic artery supply much of body and tail. Thus the organ spans linked arterial territories and a longitudinal drainage route. Endocrine secretions enter blood directly, whereas exocrine secretions use ducts; those two outputs should not be drawn as one pathway.

These distinctions explain why pancreatic, splenic and portal anatomy must be learned together rather than as isolated organ lists.

lessons.subject: anatomy
lessons.title: Spleen, hilum and splenic ligaments
lessons.summary: The spleen develops in dorsal mesogastric mesenchyme, not as an endodermal gut-tube outgrowth.
lessons.section: 20. Spleen

steps.title: Spleen
steps.body: The spleen is an intraperitoneal lymphoid organ in the left hypochondrium, commonly related to ribs 9-11. It has diaphragmatic and visceral surfaces, a hilum, and peritoneal ligaments to stomach and posterior abdominal wall.

steps.title: Relationships and functional organization
steps.body: Visceral surface relates to stomach, left kidney, colon, and pancreatic tail. Gastrosplenic ligament carries short gastric and left gastro-omental vessels. Splenorenal ligament carries splenic vessels and pancreatic tail. Splenic artery is a tortuous branch of the celiac trunk. Branches of the splenic artery: pancreatic branches, short gastric arteries, left gastro-omental artery, and terminal splenic branches entering the splenic hilum.

steps.title: Why is the spleen's relation to the lower ribs important without making it an intrathoracic organ?
steps.body: The spleen lies below the diaphragm but projects deep to the left lower ribs, classically around ribs 9-11 with its long axis near the tenth rib. The diaphragm separates it from pleura and lung above. A surface view can therefore place ribs over an abdominal organ without relocating that organ into the thorax. Its thin capsule, vascular parenchyma and nearby pancreatic tail explain the importance of regional relationships. Spleen size and position vary with body form and disease.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: The spleen develops in dorsal mesogastric mesenchyme, not as an endodermal gut-tube outgrowth. Its adult celiac supply does not make it a foregut epithelial derivative. The gastrosplenic ligament connects it with the stomach and carries short gastric and left gastro-omental vessels. The splenorenal ligament contains splenic vessels and the pancreatic tail. Naming the ligament predicts the adjacent structures that must be considered in regional anatomy.

lessons.subject: anatomy
lessons.title: Jejunum, ileum and the mesenteric root
lessons.summary: Jejunum and ileum blend gradually; there is no sharp external boundary.
tags: Jejunum, ileum and the mesenteric root
lessons.section: 22. Jejunum and Ileum

steps.title: Jejunum and Ileum
steps.body: Jejunum and ileum are intraperitoneal midgut structures suspended by the mesentery proper. Jejunum is usually more proximal, thicker-walled, more vascular, and has more prominent circular folds than ileum.

steps.title: Relationships and functional organization
steps.body: Root of mesentery runs obliquely from duodenojejunal flexure to ileocecal region. Jejunal arterial arcades are fewer with longer vasa recta. Ileal arterial arcades are more numerous with shorter vasa recta. Lymphatics drain through mesenteric nodes toward superior mesenteric nodes.

steps.title: What does the mesenteric root carry, and why does its short attachment matter?
steps.body: The mesentery carries arterial branches, veins, lymphatics, nodes, nerves and fat between the posterior wall and bowel. Its root is much shorter than the intestinal border, permitting many mobile loops to fan out from an oblique attachment. Mobility allows changing loop positions, while the root constrains the whole arrangement. Mesenteric vessels approach the bowel through arcades and vasa recta, giving a second identification clue beyond wall thickness. A drawing should show both the short attached edge and the long folded bowel edge.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: Jejunum and ileum blend gradually; there is no sharp external boundary. Compare several features together: jejunum tends to have thicker walls, larger folds, less mesenteric fat near the bowel and longer straight vessels. Ileum tends to have more arcades, shorter straight vessels and more aggregated lymphoid nodules. The long mobile bowel attaches to a much shorter oblique mesenteric root, so a loop's current position alone is unreliable for identification.

lessons.subject: anatomy
lessons.title: Cecum, appendix and colon
lessons.summary: The appendiceal tip can be retrocecal, pelvic or elsewhere, while the teniae guide you toward its base.
lessons.section: 23. Cecum and Appendix; 24. Colon: Parts and External Features

steps.title: Cecum and Appendix
steps.body:
The cecum is the first part of the large intestine in the right iliac fossa. The appendix is a narrow lymphoid diverticulum from the posteromedial cecum, with variable position, commonly retrocecal or pelvic.

Appendix base is located where the three teniae coli converge. Surface projection is commonly near McBurney point, between umbilicus and right ASIS. Appendicular artery usually comes from ileocolic artery. Pain may begin as visceral periumbilical pain and later localize to right iliac fossa when parietal peritoneum is irritated.

steps.title: Colon: Parts and External Features
steps.body:
The colon extends from cecum to rectum and has characteristic external features: teniae coli, haustra, and epiploic appendages. Ascending and descending colon are usually secondarily retroperitoneal; transverse and sigmoid colon are intraperitoneal.

Large intestine has teniae coli, haustra, and omental/epiploic appendages. Ascending colon runs to right colic flexure; transverse colon runs to left colic flexure; descending colon runs down the left side; sigmoid colon enters pelvis. Transverse mesocolon suspends transverse colon; sigmoid mesocolon suspends sigmoid colon. Arterial supply transitions from SMA to IMA near the distal transverse colon.

steps.title: Why is colon mobility different in different regions?
steps.body: Transverse and sigmoid colon usually retain mesocolons, allowing substantial mobility. Ascending and descending colon are commonly fixed secondarily to the posterior abdominal wall, although variation occurs. These attachments explain why a loop's position on one image may be misleading and why the mesenteric border is an important orientation clue. Teniae coli condense longitudinal muscle in the colon and converge at the appendix base; at the rectum the longitudinal layer becomes continuous rather than remaining as three distinct bands.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: The appendiceal tip can be retrocecal, pelvic or elsewhere, while the teniae guide you toward its base. Midgut visceral afferents help explain early poorly localized periumbilical pain; later irritation of somatically innervated parietal peritoneum can localize pain. This is an anatomical explanation of a classic pattern, not a rule that every presentation follows. The colon's taeniae and haustra distinguish it from small intestine, but these features change at the rectum.

lessons.subject: anatomy
lessons.title: Rectum and the anal transition
lessons.summary: The pectinate line marks a developmental and neurovascular transition within the anal canal.
lessons.section: 25. Rectum and Anal Canal; 41. Hindgut, Cloaca, and Anal Canal Development

steps.title: Rectum and Anal Canal
steps.body:
The rectum continues from sigmoid colon and follows the sacral curve. The anal canal passes through the pelvic floor and has important arterial, venous, lymphatic, epithelial, and nerve distinctions above and below the pectinate line.

Upper rectum is related to peritoneum anteriorly and laterally; lower rectum becomes infraperitoneal. Superior rectal artery is from IMA; middle rectal from internal iliac; inferior rectal from internal pudendal. Above pectinate line: visceral innervation, portal venous drainage through superior rectal vein, lymph toward internal iliac/inferior mesenteric routes. Below pectinate line: somatic innervation via inferior rectal nerves, systemic venous drainage, superficial inguinal lymph drainage.

steps.title: Hindgut, Cloaca, and Anal Canal Development
steps.body:
The hindgut forms distal transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum, and upper anal canal. The cloaca is partitioned by the urorectal septum into anorectal canal posteriorly and urogenital sinus anteriorly.

Upper anal canal derives from endodermal hindgut. Lower anal canal derives from ectodermal proctodeum. Pectinate line marks the transition between these developmental territories. Developmental origin explains differences in innervation, blood supply, venous drainage, lymphatics, and epithelium.

steps.title: How do the two anal sphincters differ in tissue and control?
steps.body: The internal anal sphincter is a thickening of smooth muscle and contributes involuntary resting tone. The external anal sphincter is skeletal muscle with somatic innervation and contributes voluntary control. Puborectalis is a separate sling affecting the anorectal angle. Continence depends on coordinated sphincters, pelvic support, rectal sensation and stool properties, so no single ring explains it fully. The pectinate line is a mucosal developmental landmark within the canal and is not identical to either sphincter's full extent.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: The pectinate line marks a developmental and neurovascular transition within the anal canal. Above it, visceral afferents predominate; below it, somatic afferents convey well-localized pain. Venous and lymphatic territories overlap rather than forming impermeable borders. The rectum has no discrete teniae coli or haustra. Distinguish a mucosal landmark from the anorectal junction at the pelvic floor: they are at different levels and answer different anatomical questions.

lessons.subject: anatomy
lessons.title: Celiac, superior mesenteric and inferior mesenteric territories
lessons.summary: The three unpaired arteries organize gut territories, but anastomoses bridge their borders.
tags: Celiac, superior mesenteric and inferior mesenteric territories
lessons.section: 28. Celiac Trunk; 29. Superior Mesenteric Artery; 30. Inferior Mesenteric Artery

steps.title: Celiac Trunk
steps.body:
The celiac trunk is the unpaired foregut artery from the abdominal aorta near T12/L1. Its classic branches are left gastric, splenic, and common hepatic arteries.

Left gastric supplies abdominal esophagus and lesser curvature region. Splenic artery supplies spleen, pancreas, fundus, and greater curvature through branches. Name its branches clearly: pancreatic branches, short gastric arteries to the fundus, left gastro-omental artery along the greater curvature, and terminal splenic branches to the spleen. Common hepatic gives gastroduodenal artery and continues toward proper hepatic artery. The celiac territory includes abdominal foregut organs and the spleen; the spleen is mesodermal rather than a gut endoderm derivative.

steps.title: Superior Mesenteric Artery
steps.body:
The superior mesenteric artery supplies the midgut from distal duodenum to approximately proximal two-thirds of transverse colon. It arises from the abdominal aorta and passes anterior to the third part of the duodenum.

Branches include inferior pancreaticoduodenal, jejunal and ileal arteries, ileocolic, right colic, and middle colic arteries. It supplies distal duodenum, jejunum, ileum, cecum, appendix, ascending colon, and proximal transverse colon. Superior mesenteric vein joins splenic vein behind the neck of pancreas to form portal vein.

steps.title: Inferior Mesenteric Artery
steps.body:
The inferior mesenteric artery supplies the hindgut from distal one-third of transverse colon to upper anal canal. Its branches include left colic, sigmoid, and superior rectal arteries.

Left colic supplies descending colon and participates in marginal artery. Sigmoid arteries supply sigmoid colon. The superior rectal artery supplies the rectum. The superior rectal vein, a separate vessel, participates in portal-systemic venous connections. The marginal artery connects colic branches along the colon.

steps.title: Why are watershed regions vulnerable despite arterial anastomoses?
steps.body: An anastomosis provides a possible alternative route, but its capacity depends on caliber, pressure and individual anatomy. Border territories between major arterial supplies may receive less effective flow during generalized low perfusion or proximal obstruction. The splenic flexure is a classic meeting region of superior and inferior mesenteric territories; the rectosigmoid region is another commonly discussed boundary. The existence of a marginal artery therefore does not guarantee protection. Describe the dominant sources, connecting channel and physiological limitation separately.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: The three unpaired arteries organize gut territories, but anastomoses bridge their borders. Pancreaticoduodenal arcades connect celiac and superior mesenteric supply; the marginal artery links colic branches. At the splenic flexure, superior and inferior mesenteric territories meet, creating a potential watershed when perfusion is poor. Do not confuse an arterial connection with a portal-systemic venous connection. Both involve vessels, but the pressures, directions and clinical implications differ.

lessons.subject: anatomy
lessons.title: Portal venous routes and systemic connections
lessons.summary: Portal means blood reaches a second capillary bed before returning to the heart.
tags: Portal venous routes and systemic connections
lessons.section: 26. Portal-Systemic Anastomoses; 31. Portal Vein and Caval Drainage

steps.title: Portal-Systemic Anastomoses
steps.body:
Portal-systemic anastomoses are venous communications between portal tributaries and systemic veins. They are clinically important when portal pressure rises.

Lower esophagus: left gastric vein with azygos system. Around umbilicus: paraumbilical veins with superficial epigastric veins. Anal canal: superior rectal vein with middle and inferior rectal veins. Retroperitoneal colon region: colic veins with retroperitoneal body wall veins.

steps.title: Portal Vein and Caval Drainage
steps.body:
The portal vein carries nutrient-rich venous blood from the gastrointestinal tract, spleen, pancreas, and gallbladder to the liver. It is formed behind the neck of the pancreas by the union of superior mesenteric and splenic veins.

Inferior mesenteric vein usually drains into splenic vein. Portal vein enters the hepatoduodenal ligament and lies posterior to hepatic artery proper and bile duct. Hepatic veins drain blood from liver into the inferior vena cava. Caval structures such as kidneys, suprarenal glands, gonads, posterior abdominal wall, and lower limbs drain directly or indirectly to IVC, not portal vein.

steps.title: Why is the portal vein different from the hepatic veins on a liver diagram?
steps.body: Portal vein enters the liver and branches toward sinusoids, bringing blood from abdominal digestive territories and associated organs. Hepatic veins collect blood after sinusoidal passage and leave for the inferior vena cava. Hepatic artery also enters but provides a different inflow source. Drawing both portal and hepatic veins as equivalent exits reverses the circuit. To check a diagram, follow one red cell from intestinal capillary to heart and ensure that it passes through liver microcirculation before entering systemic venous return.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: Portal means blood reaches a second capillary bed before returning to the heart. Gut capillaries drain into portal tributaries, the portal vein feeds hepatic sinusoids, and hepatic veins drain into the inferior vena cava. Portal-systemic connections provide alternate venous routes when portal pressure rises. They are not arterial shunts. Rectal venous anastomoses exist, but common hemorrhoidal disease should not be equated automatically with portal hypertension or rectal varices.

lessons.subject: anatomy
lessons.title: Abdominal lymphatics and autonomic pathways
lessons.summary: A plexus mixes fibers with different directions and functions.
lessons.section: 32. Abdominal Lymphatics; 33. Autonomic Innervation of Abdominal Viscera

steps.title: Abdominal Lymphatics
steps.body:
Abdominal lymph drainage follows arteries toward pre-aortic nodes for gut organs and para-aortic nodes for posterior abdominal wall and paired retroperitoneal organs. Lymph eventually reaches intestinal and lumbar trunks and cisterna chyli.

Foregut lymph drains toward celiac nodes. Midgut lymph drains toward superior mesenteric nodes. Hindgut lymph drains toward inferior mesenteric nodes. Kidneys, gonads, suprarenal glands, and posterior abdominal wall drain toward lumbar/para-aortic nodes. Cisterna chyli receives intestinal and lumbar trunks and continues as thoracic duct.

steps.title: Autonomic Innervation of Abdominal Viscera
steps.body:
Abdominal viscera receive sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers through prevertebral plexuses. Sympathetic fibers travel mainly through thoracic and lumbar splanchnic nerves; parasympathetic fibers come from vagus nerve and pelvic splanchnic nerves.

Vagus supplies parasympathetic innervation to foregut and midgut derivatives up to proximal transverse colon. Pelvic splanchnic nerves S2-S4 supply parasympathetic innervation to hindgut derivatives from distal transverse colon onward. Sympathetic efferents generally reduce gut motility and constrict vessels. Visceral pain afferents often accompany sympathetic routes but are distinct sensory fibers. Visceral afferent pain localization follows embryologic origin: foregut epigastric, midgut periumbilical, hindgut hypogastric.

steps.title: Where do autonomic fibers synapse, and why is the distinction useful?
steps.body: Many sympathetic preganglionic fibers reach prevertebral ganglia, after which postganglionic fibers follow arterial routes to viscera. Parasympathetic fibers generally synapse near or within the organ in enteric or terminal ganglia. Enteric circuits coordinate local motility and secretion while receiving autonomic modulation. Thus a plexus near an artery contains a mixture of passing fibers and ganglionic structures rather than one uniform neuron type. Sensory afferents returning from viscera must be kept distinct from either autonomic motor pathway.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: A plexus mixes fibers with different directions and functions. Sympathetic efferents reach prevertebral ganglia through splanchnic routes, while visceral afferents often travel alongside them in the opposite direction. Vagal parasympathetic supply extends through the midgut; pelvic splanchnics serve the hindgut. Lymphatic vessels are a separate transport system, often following arterial routes toward regional nodes. Sharing an anatomical corridor does not make nerve, blood and lymph pathways interchangeable.

lessons.subject: anatomy
lessons.title: Foregut rotation and organ development
lessons.summary: Rotation changes adult relationships without changing tissue lineage.
lessons.section: 36. Gut Tube Overview; 37. Stomach Rotation and Peritoneal Consequences; 38. Duodenum, Pancreas, and Biliary Development; 39. Liver, Gallbladder, and Spleen Development

steps.title: Gut Tube Overview
steps.body:
The primitive gut tube is formed during folding of the embryo and is divided into foregut, midgut, and hindgut. Endoderm forms most epithelial lining and glands, while surrounding splanchnic mesoderm forms connective tissue, smooth muscle, vessels, and visceral peritoneum.

Foregut is supplied by celiac trunk in adult anatomy. Midgut is supplied by superior mesenteric artery. Hindgut is supplied by inferior mesenteric artery. Dorsal mesentery is broadly present; ventral mesentery persists mainly in the foregut region and contributes to lesser omentum and falciform ligament.

steps.title: Stomach Rotation and Peritoneal Consequences
steps.body:
The stomach dilates from the foregut and rotates around longitudinal and anteroposterior axes. Rotation helps create the lesser sac and changes the positions of vagal trunks, curvatures, and peritoneal attachments.

The left side of stomach becomes anterior and receives anterior vagal trunk; right side becomes posterior and receives posterior vagal trunk. Greater curvature grows faster and becomes the large convex border. Dorsal mesogastrium expands and contributes to greater omentum and spaces related to the lesser sac. Ventral mesogastrium contributes to lesser omentum and falciform ligament.

steps.title: Duodenum, Pancreas, and Biliary Development
steps.body:
The duodenum rotates with the stomach and becomes mostly secondarily retroperitoneal. The pancreas develops from dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds; the ventral bud rotates posteriorly to fuse with the dorsal bud.

Ventral pancreatic bud forms uncinate process and inferior part of pancreatic head. Dorsal pancreatic bud forms most of the head, body, and tail. Main pancreatic duct is formed from ventral duct and distal dorsal duct; accessory duct may persist from proximal dorsal duct. Hepatic diverticulum gives rise to liver parenchyma, bile ducts, and gallbladder/biliary apparatus components.

steps.title: Liver, Gallbladder, and Spleen Development
steps.body:
The liver and biliary system develop from foregut endodermal hepatic diverticulum growing into septum transversum mesenchyme. The spleen is not an endodermal gut derivative; it develops from mesenchyme in the dorsal mesogastrium.

Hepatocytes and biliary epithelium are endodermal in origin. Connective tissue and vascular elements are mesenchymal. Falciform ligament and lesser omentum relate to ventral mesentery. Spleen develops in dorsal mesogastrium and is associated with gastrosplenic and splenorenal ligaments.

steps.title: Why are dorsal and ventral mesenteries not interchangeable?
steps.body: The dorsal mesentery extends broadly along the gut, whereas ventral mesentery persists mainly in the foregut region. Stomach rotation and differential growth expand dorsal mesogastric derivatives, including greater-omental and splenic relationships. Ventral mesenteric derivatives include lesser omentum and falciform ligament, associated with the developing liver. Naming an adult ligament without its attachments can hide this pattern. First identify which organs it connects, then relate those attachments to the embryonic mesentery from which the fold developed.

steps.body: Rotation changes adult relationships without changing tissue lineage. The ventral pancreatic bud moves around the duodenum to join the dorsal bud. Their ducts usually combine, while duct variants can persist. Stomach rotation carries the left vagus mainly anteriorly and the right vagus mainly posteriorly. The spleen develops within dorsal mesogastric mesenchyme, unlike the endodermal epithelium of the gut and pancreatic buds. lessons.subject: anatomy
lessons.title: Midgut herniation, rotation and fixation
lessons.summary: The standard model describes an initial 90-degree rotation during physiological herniation and a further 180 degrees during return.
lessons.section: 40. Midgut Herniation and Rotation

steps.title: Midgut Herniation and Rotation
steps.body: The midgut elongates rapidly, forms a primary intestinal loop, temporarily herniates into the umbilical cord, rotates around the superior mesenteric artery, and later returns to the abdomen.

steps.title: Relationships and functional organization
steps.body: Physiologic umbilical herniation occurs because the midgut grows faster than the early abdominal cavity. Total rotation is classically described as 270 degrees counterclockwise around SMA when viewed from the front. Cecal bud initially lies high and later descends toward the right iliac fossa. Errors can cause malrotation, volvulus risk, nonrotation, reversed rotation, or abnormal fixation.

steps.title: Why does abnormal fixation matter even after bowel has returned to the abdomen?
steps.body: Return and rotation place bowel in a general arrangement, but mesenteric fixation determines how broad and stable its attachment becomes. A narrow mesenteric base can allow bowel and vessels to twist together, threatening perfusion. The cecum normally migrates from a relatively high position toward the right iliac region, while different mesenteries remain mobile or fuse. These later spatial events mean that being inside the abdominal cavity is not enough to establish normal rotational and fixation anatomy.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: The standard model describes an initial 90-degree rotation during physiological herniation and a further 180 degrees during return. State the viewing direction because reversing the view reverses apparent clockwise movement. After return, the cecum descends and mesenteries fix selectively. A narrow mesenteric attachment in malrotation permits twisting of bowel and its vessels. Normal temporary herniation is not the same as persistence of bowel outside the abdominal cavity after the expected return.

lessons.title: Reconstruct an upper abdominal section
lessons.summary: Begin with orientation, then identify solid reference structures rather than guessing from an isolated shape.
lessons.section: 11. Lesser Sac and Epiploic Foramen; 16. Duodenum; 19. Pancreas; 31. Portal Vein and Caval Drainage

steps.title: Lesser Sac and Epiploic Foramen
steps.body:
The lesser sac is the omental bursa behind the stomach and lesser omentum. It communicates with the greater sac through the epiploic foramen, also called the omental foramen.

Anterior wall of the lesser sac includes stomach, lesser omentum, and gastrocolic ligament. Posterior wall relates to pancreas, left kidney, left suprarenal gland, aorta, and related retroperitoneal structures. Epiploic foramen boundaries: anterior hepatoduodenal ligament, posterior IVC, superior caudate lobe, inferior first part of duodenum.

steps.title: Duodenum
steps.body:
The duodenum is the first part of the small intestine and forms a C-shaped curve around the head of the pancreas. It has superior, descending, horizontal, and ascending parts. Most of it is secondarily retroperitoneal except the proximal first part.

First part is partly intraperitoneal and is related posteriorly to bile duct, portal vein, and IVC. Second part receives bile duct and main pancreatic duct at the major duodenal papilla; accessory pancreatic duct may open at the minor papilla. Third part crosses anterior to IVC and aorta and posterior to superior mesenteric vessels. Fourth part ascends to the duodenojejunal flexure, supported by the suspensory muscle/ligament of duodenum.

steps.title: Pancreas
steps.body:
The pancreas is a mostly secondarily retroperitoneal foregut organ behind the stomach and related to the C-loop of duodenum and splenic vessels. It has head, uncinate process, neck, body, and tail.

Head lies in the duodenal curve. Uncinate process extends posterior to superior mesenteric vessels. Neck lies anterior to formation of portal vein. Body crosses toward the spleen; splenic artery runs along superior border and splenic vein posterior to the pancreas. Tail reaches the splenic hilum in the splenorenal ligament region.

steps.title: Portal Vein and Caval Drainage
steps.body:
The portal vein carries nutrient-rich venous blood from the gastrointestinal tract, spleen, pancreas, and gallbladder to the liver. It is formed behind the neck of the pancreas by the union of superior mesenteric and splenic veins.

Inferior mesenteric vein usually drains into splenic vein. Portal vein enters the hepatoduodenal ligament and lies posterior to hepatic artery proper and bile duct. Hepatic veins drain blood from liver into the inferior vena cava. Caval structures such as kidneys, suprarenal glands, gonads, posterior abdominal wall, and lower limbs drain directly or indirectly to IVC, not portal vein.

steps.title: How would you check a proposed pancreatic label on a section?
steps.body: Use multiple independent relations: the pancreas is behind the stomach and lesser sac, the head lies within the duodenal curve, and the neck is anterior to portal venous formation. The body extends toward the splenic hilum, with splenic vein posteriorly. Not every relation appears at one axial level, so follow neighboring slices or a multiplanar reconstruction. If a proposed structure violates several relationships, reconsider orientation before memorizing its appearance. Anatomy is a connected spatial model, not a collection of isolated silhouettes.

The stomach is anterior to the lesser sac and pancreas; the pancreatic neck is anterior to portal vein formation. The third duodenal part lies behind the superior mesenteric vessels. Combining these independent relationships lets you check a proposed label against its neighbours. lessons.subject: anatomy
lessons.title: Pelvic inlet, outlet and walls
lessons.summary: The inlet is a ring, the outlet another boundary, and the pelvic cavity lies between them.
lessons.section: 1. Pelvic Overview and True Pelvis; 2. Pelvic Inlet, Outlet, and Diameters; 3. Pelvic Walls: Bones, Ligaments, Membranes, and Muscles

steps.title: Pelvic Overview and True Pelvis
steps.body:
The true pelvis is the part of the pelvis below the pelvic brim. It contains the pelvic viscera, including urinary bladder, internal genital organs, rectum, vessels, nerves, lymphatics, and pelvic fascia. The pelvic brim separates the false pelvis above from the lesser or true pelvis below.

The pelvic brim follows the sacral promontory and alae, arcuate lines, pectineal lines, pubic crests and superior symphyseal border. The false pelvis supports abdominal viscera; the true pelvis encloses pelvic organs. The pelvis opens inferiorly into the perineum through the pelvic outlet. The pelvic cavity communicates with the abdomen superiorly and perineum inferiorly.

steps.title: Pelvic Inlet, Outlet, and Diameters
steps.body:
The pelvic inlet is the superior aperture of the true pelvis. The pelvic outlet is the inferior opening bounded by pubic arch anteriorly, ischial tuberosities laterally, and coccyx/sacrotuberous ligaments posteriorly. Obstetric diameters describe the anteroposterior capacity of the pelvic inlet.

True conjugate runs from sacral promontory to superior margin of pubic symphysis. Obstetric conjugate runs from sacral promontory to the closest point on the posterior pubic symphysis. Diagonal conjugate runs from sacral promontory to inferior margin of pubic symphysis. The outlet is bounded by the pubic arch anteriorly, ischial tuberosities laterally, sacrotuberous ligaments posterolaterally and coccyx posteriorly.

steps.title: Pelvic Walls: Bones, Ligaments, Membranes, and Muscles
steps.body:
The true pelvis is formed by hip bones, sacrum, coccyx, pelvic ligaments, obturator membrane, and muscles lining the pelvic wall and floor. Its walls are not just bone; the piriformis, obturator internus, levator ani, and coccygeus form essential muscular boundaries.

Bones: hip bones, sacrum, coccyx. Ligaments: sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments convert sciatic notches into foramina. Membrane: obturator membrane closes most of the obturator foramen, leaving the obturator canal. Muscles: piriformis posteriorly, obturator internus laterally, levator ani and coccygeus inferiorly.

steps.title: How do the sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments change the sciatic notches?
steps.body: The ligaments bridge bony landmarks and convert the greater and lesser sciatic notches into foramina. Sacrospinous attaches near the ischial spine, while sacrotuberous extends toward the ischial tuberosity. Piriformis traverses the greater opening, creating superior and inferior routes for nerves and vessels. The lesser opening provides access toward the perineum. A bone alone therefore does not show the final soft-tissue-defined passage. Add the ligaments before trying to trace the pudendal or obturator-internus routes.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion

lessons.subject: anatomy
lessons.title: Pelvic diaphragm and visceral support
lessons.summary: Puborectalis is part of levator ani and helps maintain the anorectal angle.
lessons.section: 5. Pelvic Diaphragm and Levator Ani

steps.title: Pelvic Diaphragm and Levator Ani
steps.body: The pelvic diaphragm is formed by levator ani and coccygeus muscles with their fasciae. It supports pelvic organs, maintains continence, resists increases in intra-abdominal pressure, and separates pelvic cavity from perineum.

steps.title: Relationships and functional organization
steps.body: Levator ani includes puborectalis, pubococcygeus, and iliococcygeus. Coccygeus lies posteriorly on the sacrospinous ligament region. Anal hiatus transmits anal canal. Urogenital hiatus transmits urethra in male and urethra plus vagina in female. Innervation is mainly from nerve to levator ani and branches from sacral plexus/pudendal region.

steps.title: Why does supporting pelvic organs require more than a flat sheet of muscle?
steps.body: The floor has openings for outlets and is shaped around them, so support depends on muscle tone, connective-tissue attachments and the perineal body. Pressure rises during coughing or lifting must be resisted without permanently closing those outlets. Puborectalis changes anorectal geometry, while other levator fibers support adjacent viscera. Injury or weakness can alter several relationships simultaneously. The perineal membrane lies below the levator complex in the urogenital region and should not be drawn as the entire pelvic diaphragm.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: Puborectalis is part of levator ani and helps maintain the anorectal angle. Relaxation during defecation allows that angle to change; it is not the same structure as the circular external anal sphincter. Levator ani also supports pelvic organs during pressure changes. Its direct sacral innervation, chiefly through the nerve to levator ani, should not be reduced to a statement that every pelvic-floor muscle is supplied only by the pudendal nerve.

lessons.subject: anatomy
lessons.title: Sciatic foramina and pelvic nerve routes
lessons.summary: Ligaments convert notches into foramina; piriformis then divides the greater foramen into useful compartments.
tags: Sciatic foramina and pelvic nerve routes
lessons.section: 4. Greater and Lesser Sciatic Foramina; 7. Lumbar Plexus, Sacral Plexus, and Pudendal Nerve

steps.title: Greater and Lesser Sciatic Foramina
steps.body:
The greater and lesser sciatic foramina are openings created by the sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments. They transmit major nerves and vessels between pelvis, gluteal region, and perineum.

Greater sciatic foramen transmits piriformis and structures passing above or below piriformis. Structures above piriformis: superior gluteal nerve and vessels. Structures below piriformis: inferior gluteal nerve/vessels, sciatic nerve, posterior femoral cutaneous nerve, pudendal nerve, internal pudendal vessels, nerve to obturator internus, nerve to quadratus femoris. Lesser sciatic foramen transmits tendon of obturator internus plus pudendal nerve/internal pudendal vessels returning into the perineum.

steps.title: Lumbar Plexus, Sacral Plexus, and Pudendal Nerve
steps.body:
The lumbar plexus arises mainly from L1-L4 and the sacral plexus from L4-S4. The pudendal nerve, from S2-S4, is the major somatic nerve of the perineum and supplies external urethral and anal sphincter regions.

Lumbar plexus branches include iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, genitofemoral, lateral femoral cutaneous, femoral, and obturator nerves. Sacral plexus branches include superior gluteal, inferior gluteal, sciatic, posterior femoral cutaneous, pudendal, and muscular branches. Pudendal nerve exits the pelvis below piriformis, crosses the ischial spine, enters lesser sciatic foramen, runs in pudendal canal, then gives inferior rectal, perineal, and dorsal nerve of penis/clitoris. Pudendal S2-S4 supply serves external sphincters and perineal structures; direct sacral branches also supply pelvic-floor muscles.

steps.title: How do somatic pudendal fibers differ from pelvic splanchnic fibers despite shared root levels?
steps.body: Both involve S2-S4, but root level does not specify function. Pudendal nerve carries somatic sensory and motor fibers to perineal skin and skeletal muscles, including external sphincter pathways. Pelvic splanchnic nerves carry parasympathetic preganglionic fibers to pelvic plexuses and viscera, with visceral afferents also using related routes. They follow different courses and targets. A learner who labels every S2-S4 branch pudendal would lose the distinction between voluntary skeletal control and visceral autonomic regulation.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: Ligaments convert notches into foramina; piriformis then divides the greater foramen into useful compartments. Most major exiting structures are inferior to it. The pudendal bundle leaves below piriformis and turns around the ischial spine to enter the perineum through the lesser foramen. This is a route with an exit and return, not a nerve ending in the buttock. Variation exists, especially in sciatic nerve division around piriformis.

lessons.subject: anatomy
lessons.title: Pelvic vessels and lymphatic drainage
lessons.summary: Internal iliac branching is variable, so start with territories and then learn the usual named branches.
lessons.section: 6. Internal Iliac Artery; 8. Pelvic Lymphatics

steps.title: Internal Iliac Artery
steps.body:
The internal iliac artery is the main arterial supply of the pelvis, gluteal region, perineum, and many pelvic organs. For oral exams, organize branches into parietal and visceral branches.

Parietal branches supply pelvic wall, gluteal region, and perineum. Visceral branches supply pelvic organs. Important parietal branches: iliolumbar, lateral sacral, obturator, superior gluteal, inferior gluteal, internal pudendal. Important visceral branches: umbilical/superior vesical, inferior vesical in male, uterine and vaginal in female, middle rectal. Internal pudendal artery exits and re-enters via sciatic foramina to supply perineum and external genitalia.

steps.title: Pelvic Lymphatics
steps.body:
Pelvic lymph drainage follows pelvic vessels. External iliac nodes drain anterior pelvic and lower abdominal structures; internal iliac nodes drain most pelvic viscera and deep perineum; sacral nodes drain posterior pelvic structures; common iliac nodes receive from external, internal, and sacral nodes.

External iliac nodes receive lymph from lower limb pathways, anterior abdominal wall, bladder, uterus/vagina regions, and anterior pelvic organs. Internal iliac nodes receive from pelvic viscera, deep perineum, gluteal region, and thigh region. Sacral nodes receive from posterior pelvic wall, rectum, bladder, prostate, and cervix. Common iliac nodes are the collecting station before lumbar nodes.

steps.title: Why is gonadal drainage an exception to a simple pelvic-node rule?
steps.body: Ovaries and testes develop on the posterior abdominal wall and retain lymphatic connections toward lumbar nodes. Other pelvic organs drain through internal, external or sacral iliac routes according to region and connections. The uterine fundus can also use ovarian-associated and round-ligament pathways, illustrating overlapping routes. Therefore present-day organ location alone cannot predict the first node group. Tissue origin and vascular companions provide additional clues, but a complete map should acknowledge communications rather than assigning one exclusive node to every organ.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: Internal iliac branching is variable, so start with territories and then learn the usual named branches. Internal pudendal branches accompany the pudendal nerve into the perineum; superior gluteal branches pass above piriformis. Lymphatic drainage is not a simple copy of arterial supply: organs may have multiple routes, and gonads retain lumbar drainage related to development. Follow a node chain toward common iliac and lumbar nodes rather than treating each node group as an isolated endpoint.

lessons.subject: anatomy
lessons.title: Kidney coverings, hilum and collecting system
lessons.summary: Urine and blood travel through different branching systems.
tags: Kidney coverings, hilum and collecting system
lessons.section: 9. Kidney Position, Capsules, Hilum, and Sinus; 10. Kidney Internal Morphology and Collecting System; 11. Kidney Relations, Vessels, Lymphatics, and Nerves

steps.title: Kidney Position, Capsules, Hilum, and Sinus
steps.body:
The kidneys are paired retroperitoneal organs on the posterior abdominal wall, roughly from T12 to L3, with the right kidney slightly lower because of the liver. Each kidney has fibrous capsule, perirenal fat, renal fascia, and pararenal fat. The medial hilum opens into the renal sinus.

Right kidney lies slightly lower than left. Capsules from inside outward: fibrous capsule, perirenal fat/adipose capsule, renal fascia, pararenal fat. Hilum is the medial entry-exit cleft. Renal sinus contains renal pelvis, major and minor calyces, renal vessels, lymphatics, nerves, and fat. Typical anterior-posterior order at hilum: vein, artery, pelvis/ureter.

steps.title: Kidney Internal Morphology and Collecting System
steps.body:
In coronal section, the kidney has cortex externally and medulla internally. Medullary pyramids project as renal papillae into minor calyces; minor calyces join into major calyces, which form the renal pelvis and then ureter.

Cortex includes cortical labyrinth and medullary rays. Medulla is organized into renal pyramids. Renal columns are cortical tissue between pyramids. Papilla drains into minor calyx; minor calyces drain into major calyces; major calyces drain into renal pelvis. A renal lobe is a pyramid plus overlying cortex; a cortical lobule centers around a medullary ray.

steps.title: Kidney Relations, Vessels, Lymphatics, and Nerves
steps.body:
Kidney relations differ on right and left. The right kidney relates anteriorly to liver, duodenum, right colic flexure, small intestine, and right suprarenal gland. The left kidney relates to stomach, spleen, pancreas, left colic flexure, small intestine, descending colon, and left suprarenal gland. Renal arteries arise from the abdominal aorta and renal veins drain to the inferior vena cava.

Renal arteries are paired visceral branches of the abdominal aorta. Left renal vein is longer and crosses anterior to aorta; it receives left gonadal and left suprarenal veins. Right renal vein is shorter and drains directly to IVC. Lymph drains mainly to lumbar/para-aortic nodes. Autonomic fibers reach kidney through renal plexus.

steps.title: Why should a renal lobe not be confused with a cortical lobule?
steps.body: A renal lobe includes a medullary pyramid and its associated overlying cortex. A cortical lobule is a smaller cortical organization centered around a medullary ray and associated tubules. Renal columns are cortex extending between pyramids, despite their position among medullary structures. These different scales are easy to confuse when moving between gross sections and microscopic images. Start by locating cortex, medulla, papilla and collecting space, then add the smaller histological units without replacing the gross landmarks.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: Urine and blood travel through different branching systems. Collecting ducts end at papillae, urine enters minor then major calyces and the renal pelvis, and the ureter carries it onward. Renal arteries divide into segmental branches supplying parenchyma; the renal vein returns blood. At the hilum the usual anterior-to-posterior order is vein, artery, pelvis. This positional mnemonic describes a typical arrangement, not every branch or anatomical variant.

lessons.subject: anatomy
lessons.title: Ureters and the route into the bladder
lessons.summary: Trace the ureter continuously from renal pelvis to bladder rather than memorizing three isolated narrowing points.
tags: Ureters and the route into the bladder
lessons.section: 12. Ureter

steps.title: Ureter
steps.body: The ureter is a muscular retroperitoneal tube conducting urine from renal pelvis to urinary bladder. It descends on the psoas major, crosses the pelvic brim near iliac vessels, then enters the bladder obliquely to form an anti-reflux mechanism.

steps.title: Relationships and functional organization
steps.body: Three classic constrictions: ureteropelvic junction, crossing of pelvic brim/iliac vessels, and intramural passage through bladder wall. Blood supply is segmental: renal, gonadal, common/internal iliac, superior/inferior vesical, uterine/vaginal or ductus deferens arteries. In female pelvis, ureter passes under uterine artery near cervix: water under the bridge. Autonomic pain referral follows T11-L2 region and can radiate toward groin. Separate ureteric constrictions from ureteric crossings. Constrictions are stone-lodging points; crossings are topographic relationships the examiner may ask on a specimen. Main crossings to recite: the ureter descends anterior to psoas major/genitofemoral nerve region, is crossed anteriorly by gonadal vessels, crosses the iliac vessels at the pelvic brim, and then passes under ductus deferens in male or under uterine artery in female. Sex-specific trap: in male, ductus deferens crosses over ureter; in female, uterine artery crosses over ureter near cervix/parametrium.

steps.title: Why does ureteral blood supply need to be described as segmental?
steps.body: Branches reach the ureter from nearby renal, gonadal, iliac and pelvic arterial sources along its course. These create longitudinal communications in surrounding tissue rather than one single artery running from kidney to bladder. The regional sources explain why abdominal and pelvic segments have different vascular neighbors. Peristaltic urine transport occurs in the muscular ureteral wall, while the intramural course at the bladder supports resistance to reflux. Blood supply, propulsion and anti-reflux geometry are distinct parts of its functional anatomy.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: Trace the ureter continuously from renal pelvis to bladder rather than memorizing three isolated narrowing points. It descends retroperitoneally, crosses the pelvic brim near iliac vessels and passes beneath the uterine artery in the female pelvis or beneath the ductus deferens in the male pelvis. Its oblique intramural course helps resist reflux as bladder pressure rises. A crossing landmark and a functional narrowing are related concepts but are not identical claims about every ureter.

A crossing landmark and a functional narrowing are related concepts but are not identical claims about every ureter.

lessons.subject: anatomy
lessons.title: Bladder, trigone and urethral differences
lessons.summary: The trigone is a smooth internal region, not the whole bladder base viewed from outside.
lessons.section: 13. Urinary Bladder; 14. Trigone and Bladder Wall; 15. Female Urethra; 16. Male Urethra

steps.title: Urinary Bladder
steps.body:
The urinary bladder is a distensible muscular reservoir in the anterior pelvis behind the pubic symphysis. Its main parts are apex, body, fundus/base, neck, and trigone. The detrusor muscle forms the muscular wall.

Empty bladder lies mostly in pelvis; full bladder rises into abdomen. Apex points anteriorly toward the median umbilical ligament. Base/fundus faces posteriorly; neck is inferior and continuous with urethra. Detrusor muscle contracts during micturition. Peritoneum covers superior surface and reflects to rectum in male or uterus in female.

steps.title: Trigone and Bladder Wall
steps.body:
The trigone is a smooth triangular area on the internal base of the bladder bounded by the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice. Unlike the rest of the bladder mucosa, the trigone is smooth and tightly attached.

Angles of trigone: right ureteric orifice, left ureteric orifice, internal urethral orifice. Interureteric fold lies between ureteric openings. Mucosa elsewhere forms folds/rugae when empty. Submucosa is absent or poorly developed in trigone, making it smooth. Trigone has a different developmental contribution from mesonephric duct incorporation, though adult epithelium is endodermalized.

steps.title: Female Urethra
steps.body:
The female urethra is a short tube passing from bladder neck through pelvic floor and perineal membrane to the vestibule of the vagina. It is closely related to the anterior vaginal wall and is surrounded by sphincteric muscles in the deep perineal region.

Shorter than male urethra. Opens into vestibule anterior to vaginal opening. Passes through urogenital hiatus and deep perineal pouch region. External urethral sphincter complex contributes voluntary continence. Blood and lymph follow vaginal/bladder pathways to internal and external iliac nodes.

steps.title: Male Urethra
steps.body:
The male urethra is a long tube serving urinary and reproductive functions. It has preprostatic/intramural, prostatic, membranous, and spongy parts. It passes through prostate, deep perineal pouch, and corpus spongiosum.

Prostatic urethra receives prostatic ducts and ejaculatory ducts. Membranous urethra passes through external urethral sphincter and perineal membrane region. Spongy urethra runs in corpus spongiosum and opens at external urethral orifice of glans. Bulbourethral ducts open into proximal spongy urethra. Navicular fossa is the distal dilatation in the glans. In the prostatic urethra, identify the seminal colliculus as the raised midline landmark. The ejaculatory ducts open on either side of the prostatic utricle; prostatic ducts open into the prostatic sinuses.

steps.title: Why can bladder filling change its relations to the abdomen?
steps.body: An empty bladder lies mainly within the pelvis behind the pubic symphysis. As it fills, its superior part rises and changes the position of the peritoneal reflection and adjacent viscera. The neck remains relatively fixed compared with the expanding body. Thus a single outline cannot represent every filling state. The internal trigone remains a useful outlet landmark, while the detrusor wall expands and later contracts. Always state whether an anatomical description assumes an empty or distended bladder.

The shorter female urethra opens separately into the vestibule anterior to the vaginal opening. Use the same proximal-to-distal direction when comparing them.

lessons.subject: anatomy
lessons.title: Testis, scrotum and spermatic cord
lessons.summary: The testis develops high on the posterior abdominal wall and retains abdominal vessels and lymphatic drainage after descent.
lessons.section: 17. Testis and Scrotum; 19. Spermatic Cord Coverings and Contents

steps.title: Testis and Scrotum
steps.body:
The testis is a paired male gonad located in the scrotum. It produces spermatozoa in seminiferous tubules and testosterone from interstitial Leydig cells. It is covered by tunica albuginea and partially by tunica vaginalis, a remnant of processus vaginalis.

Testis has superior and inferior poles, medial/lateral surfaces, anterior/posterior borders. Epididymis lies along posterior aspect of testis. Tunica vaginalis has parietal and visceral layers around the anterior/lateral testis region. Arterial supply is testicular artery from abdominal aorta. Venous drainage is pampiniform plexus to testicular veins: right to IVC, left to left renal vein. Lymph drains to lumbar/para-aortic nodes, not superficial inguinal nodes. Developmental orientation: the testis develops high on the posterior abdominal wall near the kidney region, then descends through the inguinal canal into the scrotum. Thermoregulation has three practical mechanisms: dartos wrinkles scrotal skin, cremaster elevates the testis, and the pampiniform plexus cools testicular arterial blood by countercurrent heat exchange.

steps.title: Spermatic Cord Coverings and Contents
steps.body:
The spermatic cord extends from deep inguinal ring to testis and contains ductus deferens, testicular vessels, pampiniform plexus, autonomic nerves, lymphatics, genital branch of genitofemoral nerve, and remnants of processus vaginalis. Its coverings derive from layers of the abdominal wall.

External spermatic fascia derives from external oblique aponeurosis. Cremaster muscle/fascia derives from internal oblique. Internal spermatic fascia derives from transversalis fascia. Contents include ductus deferens, artery to ductus deferens, testicular artery, pampiniform plexus, lymphatics, autonomic plexus, genital branch of genitofemoral nerve, and processus vaginalis remnants. Add the cremasteric artery when giving a full contents answer. The artery to the ductus deferens usually arises from the vesical artery system of the internal iliac artery. Keep the examiner trap: ilioinguinal nerve passes through the inguinal canal but is not a true spermatic cord content.

steps.title: How do the pampiniform plexus and cremaster contribute to temperature regulation?
steps.body: The pampiniform venous plexus surrounds incoming arterial channels and supports countercurrent heat exchange, reducing the temperature of arterial blood approaching the testis. Cremaster changes testicular position relative to the body, while dartos alters scrotal skin configuration. These mechanisms operate together and do not replace the need for vascular perfusion. The plexus eventually drains to testicular veins, with the right typically entering IVC and the left entering left renal vein. Venous drainage asymmetry is separate from the bilateral arterial origin from aorta.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: The testis develops high on the posterior abdominal wall and retains abdominal vessels and lymphatic drainage after descent. Scrotal skin has a different superficial inguinal drainage pattern. The cord carries ductus deferens, testicular vessels, pampiniform plexus and associated structures; the ilioinguinal nerve runs in the canal but is not enclosed as a true cord content. Preserve the distinction between testis, its coverings and the surrounding skin when answering vessel or lymph questions.

lessons.subject: anatomy
lessons.title: Sperm pathway, seminal vesicles and prostate
lessons.summary: Sperm travels from seminiferous tubules through straight tubules, rete testis, efferent ductules, epididymis and ductus deferens.
tags: Sperm pathway, seminal vesicles and prostate
lessons.section: 18. Epididymis, Ductus Deferens, and Sperm Pathway; 20. Seminal Vesicles and Ejaculatory Duct; 21. Prostate

steps.title: Epididymis, Ductus Deferens, and Sperm Pathway
steps.body:
Sperm pass from seminiferous tubules to straight tubules, rete testis, efferent ductules, epididymal duct, ductus deferens, ejaculatory duct, and prostatic urethra. The epididymis is the maturation and storage organ; the ductus deferens is the thick-walled conducting duct.

Epididymis has head, body, tail. Ductus deferens begins at tail of epididymis, ascends in spermatic cord, passes through inguinal canal, crosses pelvic brim, and joins duct of seminal vesicle to form ejaculatory duct. Ampulla is the terminal dilated part of ductus deferens. Ejaculatory duct opens into prostatic urethra at seminal colliculus region. Named parts of the ductus deferens: testicular/scrotal part, funicular part in the spermatic cord, inguinal part in the inguinal canal, and pelvic part ending as the ampulla. Specimen rule: follow it from the tail of epididymis upward in the spermatic cord, through the inguinal canal, then posterior to the bladder toward the seminal vesicle.

steps.title: Seminal Vesicles and Ejaculatory Duct
steps.body:
Seminal vesicles are paired glands posterior to the bladder and anterior to the rectum. Each duct joins the ductus deferens to form the ejaculatory duct, which passes through prostate and opens into the prostatic urethra.

Seminal vesicles lie superior to prostate and lateral to ampulla of ductus deferens. They are posterior-inferior to bladder and anterior to rectum. Upper parts may be peritoneum-related. Ejaculatory duct forms by union of duct of seminal vesicle and ductus deferens. Ejaculatory ducts open on the seminal colliculus region of prostatic urethra.

steps.title: Prostate
steps.body:
The prostate is a fibromuscular gland inferior to the bladder, surrounding the prostatic urethra. It lies posterior to pubic symphysis, anterior to rectum, and superior to the pelvic diaphragm. It receives ejaculatory ducts and drains prostatic ducts into the prostatic urethra.

The prostate base is superior at the bladder neck; its apex is inferior near the external urethral sphincter and perineal membrane region. Anterior relation: pubic symphysis/retropubic space. Posterior relation: rectum, allowing digital rectal examination. Prostatic urethra and ejaculatory ducts pass through it. Venous drainage to prostatic venous plexus, communicating with vertebral venous plexus.

steps.title: Why does a posterior bladder diagram help locate the seminal vesicles?
steps.body: Seminal vesicles lie behind the bladder and above the prostate, lateral to the terminal deferent ampullae. Their ducts join the deferent ducts and pass through prostate as ejaculatory ducts. The rectum lies posteriorly, while the distal ureters approach the bladder near these reproductive routes. A posterior view therefore reveals relationships that are obscured on an anterior bladder outline. It also makes clear that urinary and reproductive pathways remain separate until the reproductive ducts enter the urethral system.

steps.body: Sperm travels from seminiferous tubules through straight tubules, rete testis, efferent ductules, epididymis and ductus deferens. The duct of the seminal vesicle joins the deferent duct to form an ejaculatory duct through the prostate. The seminal vesicle contributes secretion; it is not a storage sac through which sperm must pass. The prostate surrounds the proximal urethral route, while its posterior surface faces the rectum, explaining a clinically useful relationship.

lessons.subject: anatomy
lessons.title: Erectile tissues and external genital anatomy
lessons.summary: The paired corpora cavernosa continue proximally as crura; the corpus spongiosum expands as the bulb proximally and glans distally.
tags: Erectile tissues and external genital anatomy
lessons.section: 22. Penis and Mechanism of Erection; 29. External Female Genital Organs

steps.title: Penis and Mechanism of Erection
steps.body:
The penis contains paired corpora cavernosa dorsally and one corpus spongiosum ventrally surrounding the spongy urethra. Erection depends on parasympathetic vasodilation through cavernous nerves, arterial inflow, and venous compression within erectile tissue.

The penile root includes a single bulb and paired crura attached in the perineum. Body contains corpora cavernosa and corpus spongiosum. Glans is expansion of corpus spongiosum. Deep arteries of penis supply corpora cavernosa; dorsal artery supplies glans/skin region. Parasympathetic pathways support erection; sympathetic pathways contribute to emission, and somatic pudendal pathways contribute to ejaculatory expulsion. The suspensory ligament of the penis attaches the root/body region to the pubic symphysis and stabilizes the penis during erection. Specimen orientation: paired crura belong to the corpora cavernosa; the bulb belongs to the corpus spongiosum and continues into the glans.

steps.title: External Female Genital Organs
steps.body:
External female genital organs include mons pubis, labia majora, labia minora, clitoris, vestibule, external urethral opening, vaginal opening, bulbs of vestibule, and greater vestibular glands. They are mainly supplied by internal pudendal vessels and pudendal nerve branches.

Clitoris contains erectile tissue homologous to corpora cavernosa. Bulbs of vestibule are erectile tissue homologous to bulb of penis/corpus spongiosum region. Greater vestibular glands open into vestibule posterolateral to vaginal opening. Perineal nerve and dorsal nerve of clitoris are branches of pudendal nerve. Lymph from external genitalia largely drains to superficial inguinal nodes.

steps.title: Why is the urethra associated with corpus spongiosum rather than enclosed between the cavernosa?
steps.body: Corpus spongiosum surrounds the spongy urethral route and expands into bulb and glans, while paired cavernosa provide the principal rigid erectile bodies. Their connective-tissue and vascular arrangements differ, allowing the urethral channel to remain a distinct structure during erectile changes. The crura are cavernous attachments, whereas the bulb belongs to spongiosum. Labeling all erectile tissue identically would obscure the urethral course and the correspondence between root, body and distal expansions.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: The paired corpora cavernosa continue proximally as crura; the corpus spongiosum expands as the bulb proximally and glans distally. Vascular filling depends strongly on parasympathetic and local signaling. Emission involves sympathetic pathways, while expulsion also needs somatic rhythmic muscle activity through pudendal pathways. Thus ejaculation cannot be explained as a purely sympathetic event. Homologous erectile structures exist in the clitoris and vestibular bulbs, but the female urethra does not run through the clitoris.

lessons.subject: anatomy
lessons.title: Ovary and uterine tube relationships
lessons.summary: The tube opens into the peritoneal cavity near the ovary; it is not directly sealed to the ovarian surface.
lessons.section: 23. Ovary; 24. Uterine Tube

steps.title: Ovary
steps.body:
The ovary is the female gonad located on the lateral pelvic wall near the bifurcation of the common iliac vessels. It is attached to the posterior layer of the broad ligament by the mesovarium, connected to the uterus by the ovarian ligament, and connected to the lateral pelvic wall by the suspensory ligament of the ovary.

The ovary is intraperitoneal in position but has surface epithelium rather than the usual visceral peritoneal covering. The historical term germinal epithelium does not mean it produces oocytes. Suspensory ligament contains ovarian vessels, lymphatics, and nerves. Ovarian ligament connects ovary to uterus. Mesovarium attaches ovary to broad ligament. Blood supply from ovarian artery from abdominal aorta; venous drainage to ovarian veins: right to IVC, left to left renal vein. Lymph drains to lumbar/para-aortic nodes. The ovary has a tubal pole related to the uterine tube and a uterine pole attached to the uterus by the ovarian ligament. It also has a mesovarian border/hilum where vessels reach the ovary through the mesovarium, and a free border. Practical orientation: ovaries are usually easier to appreciate from the posterior aspect of the uterus/broad ligament region.

steps.title: Uterine Tube
steps.body:
The uterine tube extends from the uterine horn to the ovary region within the superior border of the broad ligament. Its parts are infundibulum with fimbriae, ampulla, isthmus, and uterine/intramural part. Fertilization usually occurs in the ampulla.

Infundibulum has fimbriae that help capture the oocyte. Ampulla is the widest and common fertilization site. Isthmus is narrow and medial. Intramural/uterine part passes through uterine wall. Blood supply from tubal branches of uterine and ovarian arteries.

steps.title: How can tubal transport occur without a sealed ovary-to-tube duct?
steps.body: The ovarian surface and fimbrial end face the peritoneal cavity. Fimbrial movement, ciliary activity and smooth-muscle contractions help move the oocyte into and along the tube. The tube is therefore a transport route with an open abdominal end, unlike a duct continuously enclosed from a gland. Its arterial supply receives both ovarian and uterine contributions, reflecting its position between those organs. Distinguish the open infundibulum from the narrow intramural segment where the tube traverses the uterine wall.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: The tube opens into the peritoneal cavity near the ovary; it is not directly sealed to the ovarian surface. Fimbriae help guide the released oocyte toward the infundibulum, then ampulla, isthmus and intramural segment. The suspensory ligament carries ovarian vessels from the lateral pelvic wall, whereas the ovarian ligament links ovary to uterus. The ovarian surface epithelium is historically called germinal epithelium, but it does not generate the oocytes.

solution: Answer: Ampulla. The tube opens into the peritoneal cavity near the ovary; it is not directly sealed to the ovarian surface.

Fimbriae help guide the released oocyte toward the infundibulum, then ampulla, isthmus and intramural segment. The suspensory ligament carries ovarian vessels from the lateral pelvic wall, whereas the ovarian ligament links ovary to uterus.
The ovarian surface epithelium is historically called germinal epithelium, but it does not generate the oocytes.

lessons.subject: anatomy
lessons.title: Uterus, supports and uterine vessel relations
lessons.summary: Anteversion compares the cervix with the vagina; anteflexion compares the uterine body with the cervix.
tags: Uterus, supports and uterine vessel relations
lessons.section: 25. Uterus: Parts, Position, and Supports; 26. Broad Ligament and Parametrium; 27. Uterine Vessels, Lymphatics, and Relations

steps.title: Uterus: Parts, Position, and Supports
steps.body:
The uterus is a thick-walled muscular organ between bladder and rectum. It has fundus, body, isthmus, cervix, and uterine cavity. Normal position is anteversion relative to vagina and anteflexion between body and cervix.

Anteversion: cervix/uterus axis inclines forward relative to vagina. Anteflexion: body bends forward relative to cervix. Anterior relation: bladder and vesicouterine pouch. Posterior relation: rectouterine pouch, rectum, and small intestine. Supports include pelvic diaphragm, perineal body, transverse cervical/cardinal ligaments, uterosacral ligaments, pubocervical fascia, round ligament, broad ligament, and vagina. Layers from inside outward: endometrium, myometrium, and perimetrium/serosa. Specimen orientation: anteriorly the uterus faces the bladder and the round ligament/broad ligament is often prominent; posteriorly it faces the rectum and rectouterine pouch, and the ovaries are often more visible. Use the organ order to orient a sagittal female pelvis: pubic symphysis, bladder, uterus/vagina, rectum, sacrum.

steps.title: Broad Ligament and Parametrium
steps.body:
The broad ligament is a double layer of peritoneum extending from the sides of the uterus to the lateral pelvic walls and floor. It is divided into mesometrium, mesosalpinx, and mesovarium. The parametrium is the connective tissue between layers near the cervix and lateral uterus.

Mesometrium is the largest part related to uterus. Mesosalpinx encloses the uterine tube. Mesovarium attaches to ovary. Contents include uterine tube, round ligament of uterus, ovarian ligament, uterine vessels, nerves, lymphatics, and remnants such as epoophoron/paroophoron. Parametrium contains uterine vessels and is clinically important near ureter.

steps.title: Uterine Vessels, Lymphatics, and Relations
steps.body:
The uterine artery, a branch of the internal iliac artery, runs medially in the base of the broad ligament and crosses superior to the ureter near the cervix. Uterine venous drainage follows uterine venous plexuses to internal iliac veins. Lymph drainage varies by region.

Uterine artery crosses over ureter: water under the bridge. Fundus drains partly to para-aortic/lumbar and superficial inguinal nodes via round ligament route. Body drains mainly to external iliac nodes. Cervix drains to internal iliac and sacral nodes. Lateral fornix of vagina is related to ureter and uterine artery. The uterine artery reaches the uterus near the cervix/isthmus region and divides into ascending and descending branches. The ascending branch supplies the body/fundus and gives tubal branches that anastomose with ovarian artery branches near the uterine tube, especially around the ampulla. The descending branch supplies the cervix and vagina and continues with vaginal arterial branches.

steps.title: Why do version and flexion require different reference axes?
steps.body: Version compares the cervical or uterine orientation with the vaginal axis; flexion compares the body with the cervix. A uterus can therefore change one angle without the same change in the other. The usual anteverted, anteflexed pattern is common but not obligatory. Bladder filling, support and individual anatomy influence position. A sagittal sketch should include vagina, cervix and body as separate segments, otherwise two different spatial relationships collapse into the vague statement that the uterus points forward.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: Anteversion compares the cervix with the vagina; anteflexion compares the uterine body with the cervix. Support comes from coordinated pelvic-floor, fascial and ligamentous structures. The broad ligament is mainly a peritoneal fold, not the principal load-bearing support. Cardinal and uterosacral support and the levator complex matter more mechanically. Uterine lymph can follow more than one route, including a fundal route toward superficial inguinal nodes along the round ligament.

lessons.subject: anatomy
lessons.title: Vagina and its pelvic relations
lessons.summary: The cervix projects into the superior vagina, creating anterior, posterior and lateral recesses called fornices.
lessons.section: 28. Vagina

steps.title: Vagina
steps.body: The vagina is a fibromuscular canal from vestibule to cervix, forming anterior, posterior, and lateral fornices around the cervix. It lies posterior to bladder and urethra and anterior to rectum and anal canal. The posterior fornix is related to the rectouterine pouch.

steps.title: Relationships and functional organization
steps.body: Anterior relations: bladder and urethra. Posterior relations: rectouterine pouch superiorly, rectum, perineal body. Lateral fornix is related to ureter and uterine artery. Upper vagina drains to internal/external iliac nodes; lower vagina drains toward superficial inguinal nodes. Vaginal wall includes mucosa, muscular layer, and adventitia.

steps.title: Why is the perineal body relevant to the lower vaginal region?
steps.body: The perineal body is a fibromuscular convergence between the vaginal outlet and anal region, linking several supporting muscles and fasciae. It contributes to the integrity of the perineal support system rather than acting as a separate organ. The upper posterior vaginal region instead relates to the rectouterine pouch, so superior and inferior relations differ substantially. A complete account should trace anterior, posterior and lateral relations along the tube's length, not apply the fornix relationships to the entire vaginal wall.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: The cervix projects into the superior vagina, creating anterior, posterior and lateral recesses called fornices. The posterior fornix is adjacent to the rectouterine pouch; the anterior vaginal wall relates to bladder and urethra. Lateral fornices lie near ureteric and uterine-vessel relationships. The vaginal wall is a fibromuscular tube with mucosa, muscular tissue and adventitia, not a peritoneal tube throughout its length. Drainage patterns change along its upper and lower regions.

lessons.subject: anatomy
lessons.title: Perineal triangles, pouches and perineal body
lessons.summary: The perineum lies below the pelvic diaphragm.
tags: Perineal triangles, pouches and perineal body
lessons.section: 30. Perineal Region and Triangles; 32. Superficial Perineal Pouch; 33. Deep Perineal Pouch and Urogenital Diaphragm

steps.title: Perineal Region and Triangles
steps.body:
The perineum is a diamond-shaped region bounded by pubic symphysis anteriorly, coccyx posteriorly, and ischial tuberosities laterally. A line between ischial tuberosities divides it into anterior urogenital triangle and posterior anal triangle.

Urogenital triangle contains external genitalia and urethral structures. Anal triangle contains anal canal, external anal sphincter, and ischioanal fossae. Perineal body is a central fibromuscular node between urogenital and anal triangles. Perineal membrane closes much of the urogenital triangle deep to superficial pouch. Pelvic diaphragm forms roof of the perineum.

steps.title: Superficial Perineal Pouch
steps.body:
The superficial perineal pouch lies between perineal membrane and superficial perineal fascia. In males it contains root of penis and associated muscles; in females it contains erectile tissues, greater vestibular glands, and corresponding muscles.

Male contents: bulb and crura of penis, proximal spongy urethra region, ischiocavernosus, bulbospongiosus, superficial transverse perineal muscles, branches of internal pudendal vessels/nerves. Female contents: clitoris crura, bulbs of vestibule, greater vestibular glands, ischiocavernosus, bulbospongiosus, superficial transverse perineal muscles. Perineal membrane forms deep boundary. Superficial perineal fascia and Colles fascia are important for spread of fluid.

steps.title: Deep Perineal Pouch and Urogenital Diaphragm
steps.body:
The deep perineal pouch lies superior to the perineal membrane and contains sphincteric urethral muscle complex and deep transverse perineal structures. In males, it also contains bulbourethral glands and membranous urethra.

Male deep pouch: membranous urethra, external urethral sphincter, deep transverse perineal muscles, bulbourethral glands, pudendal branches. Female deep pouch: urethra, external urethral sphincter complex, compressor urethrae/urethrovaginal sphincter region, deep transverse perineal structures, vessels/nerves. Perineal membrane is the inferior boundary of the deep pouch. This region is essential for continence and urethral support.

steps.title: How can fascial attachments influence the spread of fluid in the superficial perineal region?
steps.body: The superficial pouch lies between the perineal membrane and membranous superficial fascia. Attachments of that fascia to the perineal margins constrain some routes while continuity with superficial abdominal fascia permits others. The resulting pattern depends on which tissue layer contains the fluid and where a breach occurs. This is why drawing only muscles without fascia gives an incomplete explanation. The deep perineal region has different boundaries and should not be assumed to communicate with every superficial compartment in the same way.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: The perineum lies below the pelvic diaphragm. A line between the ischial tuberosities divides urogenital and anal triangles; these are regional subdivisions, not layers. The perineal membrane is a key boundary in the urogenital triangle. Traditional descriptions of a closed urogenital diaphragm can obscure the actual sphincter and connective-tissue arrangement, especially in females. Name the membrane, sphincter complex and pelvic diaphragm separately rather than treating them as interchangeable structures.
