lessons.section: 40. Neck Muscles: Superficial, Suprahyoid, Infrahyoid

steps.title: Neck Muscles: Superficial, Suprahyoid, Infrahyoid
steps.body: Neck muscle questions are easiest if grouped by layer and nerve. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius are supplied by the accessory nerve. Suprahyoids elevate hyoid/floor of mouth; infrahyoids depress/stabilize hyoid and larynx.

steps.title: Relationships and functional organization
steps.body: Platysma is facial nerve. Sternocleidomastoid: accessory nerve; contralateral rotation and ipsilateral lateral flexion. Trapezius: accessory nerve; moves scapula. Digastric anterior belly and mylohyoid: mylohyoid nerve V3. Digastric posterior belly and stylohyoid: facial nerve. Geniohyoid and thyrohyoid: C1 via hypoglossal. Most infrahyoids: ansa cervicalis.

steps.title: How can suprahyoid contraction have opposite-looking effects in different tasks?
steps.body: If the mandible is stabilized, suprahyoid muscles can elevate the hyoid and help move the laryngeal complex during swallowing. If the hyoid is stabilized by other muscles, some of the same muscles help depress the mandible. The effect depends on which attachment is fixed and the coordinated activity of neighboring groups. Infrahyoids therefore provide a functional reference point rather than simply acting as antagonists in every situation. Include both attachments when explaining action, and keep their mixed nerve sources distinct.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: A nerve can carry hitchhiking fibers from another source. C1 fibers travel with XII to thyrohyoid and geniohyoid, while most infrahyoids receive ansa cervicalis. Suprahyoid muscles can elevate the hyoid or depress the mandible depending on which attachment is stabilized. Sternocleidomastoid rotates the face contralaterally during unilateral contraction and receives XI motor supply. Distinguish the visible carrier nerve from the spinal origin and the mechanical task of the muscle.

lessons.title: Regional lymph drainage and crossing territories
lessons.summary: Lymphatic maps depend on tissue identity and development, not just present-day surface location.
tags: Regional lymph drainage and crossing territories
lessons.section: 46. Breast, Thoracic Wall, Lower Limb, and Head-Neck Lymphatics

steps.title: Breast, Thoracic Wall, Lower Limb, and Head-Neck Lymphatics
steps.body: Lymphatic drainage is best memorized by pathway. Medial breast drains to parasternal nodes; lateral breast drains to pectoral axillary nodes. Medial lower limb follows great saphenous vein to superficial inguinal nodes; lateral/posterior lower limb follows small saphenous vein to popliteal nodes.

steps.title: Relationships and functional organization
steps.body: Parasternal nodes drain medial breast and anterior thoracic wall. Intercostal nodes drain posterior thoracic wall and intercostal spaces. Superficial inguinal nodes drain superficial lower limb, infraumbilical abdominal wall, gluteal region, perineum, and external genitalia except testes. Deep inguinal nodes receive deep lower limb and popliteal drainage. Head/neck superficial ring drains to deep cervical nodes. Deep cervical nodes drain to jugular lymph trunk.

steps.title: Why can breast lymph cross toward parasternal or opposite-side routes?
steps.body: Lymphatic networks communicate across tissue planes and midline regions. Although axillary drainage is predominant for much of the breast, medial regions have parasternal connections and additional pathways exist. The breast also has superficial and deeper networks, so a single arrow to one node group is incomplete. This anatomical variability matters when interpreting regional spread, but a teaching map does not predict an individual's exact drainage. Show major routes and communications without claiming that quadrants are sealed lymphatic compartments.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: Lymphatic maps depend on tissue identity and development, not just present-day surface location. Testicular lymph reaches lumbar nodes while scrotal skin chiefly reaches superficial inguinal nodes. Breast drainage is predominantly axillary but includes parasternal and other routes that can cross the midline. Deep cervical nodes receive multiple head and neck pathways. Treat named drainage patterns as major routes with communications rather than perfectly sealed territories.

lessons.subject: anatomy
lessons.title: Early patterning and limb development
lessons.summary: Limb patterning has several axes.
lessons.section: 41. Gametogenesis, Fertilization, and Early Development; 42. Gastrulation, Notochord, and Neurulation; 43. Limb Development

steps.title: Gametogenesis, Fertilization, and Early Development
steps.body:
Spermatogenesis begins at puberty in seminiferous tubules; oogenesis begins prenatally and has meiotic arrests. After fertilization, cleavage produces morula and blastocyst, which implants in endometrium.

Spermatogonia become primary spermatocytes, secondary spermatocytes, spermatids, and spermatozoa. Sertoli cells support developing sperm. Leydig cells produce testosterone. Primary oocytes arrest in prophase I. Secondary oocyte arrests in metaphase II until fertilization. Blastocyst contains trophoblast and embryoblast.

steps.title: Gastrulation, Notochord, and Neurulation
steps.body:
Gastrulation forms the trilaminar disc. Ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm give the basic tissue plan. The notochord defines the body axis, induces the neural plate, and contributes to the nucleus pulposus.

Ectoderm gives nervous system and epidermis. Mesoderm gives muscle, bone, connective tissue, vessels, and urogenital system. Endoderm gives gut tube epithelium and respiratory epithelium. Neural tube forms CNS. Neural crest forms much of PNS, melanocytes, and important craniofacial structures. Embryonic folding converts the flat disc into a cylindrical body form.

steps.title: Limb Development
steps.body:
Limb buds appear during the fourth week, upper limb before lower limb. Lateral plate mesoderm forms bones, tendons, and ligaments, while paraxial mesoderm/somites contribute limb muscles. Patterning depends on AER, ZPA, SHH, Wnt, BMP, and HOX genes.

Upper limb bud appears around day 26. Lower limb bud appears around day 28. AER drives proximodistal outgrowth through FGF. ZPA and SHH pattern anteroposterior identity. Wnt7a patterns dorsal limb; Engrailed-1 patterns ventral limb. BMP participates in apoptosis between digits. Upper limb laterally rotates; lower limb medially rotates.

steps.title: Why do limb muscle and skeletal patterning require separate lineage statements?
steps.body: Limb skeletal and connective tissues derive largely from lateral plate mesodermal mesenchyme, while skeletal muscle precursors migrate from somites. Their coordinated patterning creates compartments and attachment relationships, but they do not originate as one homogeneous tissue mass. Nerves grow into developing targets and preserve segmental contributions as the limb elongates and rotates. This helps explain the adult mixture of segmental root maps and regional peripheral nerves. Gene-signal diagrams should be connected to these migrating cell populations and spatial axes.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: Limb patterning has several axes. The apical ectodermal ridge promotes outgrowth through FGF signaling, while posterior mesenchymal ZPA signaling helps specify thumb-to-little-finger identity. Dorsoventral cues and interdigital remodeling add further structure. Upper and lower limbs rotate differently during development, helping explain adult compartment orientation. These signals interact in networks; one molecule should not be presented as independently building an entire limb. Muscle precursors and skeletal mesenchyme also have different developmental sources.

lessons.subject: anatomy
lessons.title: Vertebral and skull development
lessons.summary: Sclerotome cells surround the notochord and neural tube, then resegment so adjacent halves contribute to each vertebra.
lessons.section: 38. Skull Divisions and Cranial Fossae; 44. Vertebral and Skull Development

steps.title: Skull Divisions and Cranial Fossae
steps.body:
The skull is divided into neurocranium and viscerocranium. The cranial fossae organize the skull base and cranial nerve exits.

Neurocranium: frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital, sphenoid, ethmoid. Viscerocranium: maxilla, zygomatic, nasal, lacrimal, palatine, inferior nasal concha, vomer, mandible. Anterior cranial fossa includes cribriform foramina. Middle cranial fossa includes optic canal, superior orbital fissure, foramina rotundum, ovale, and spinosum. Posterior cranial fossa includes foramen magnum, jugular foramen, hypoglossal canal, and internal acoustic meatus.

steps.title: Vertebral and Skull Development
steps.body:
Vertebrae arise mainly from sclerotome. Resegmentation lets spinal nerves exit between vertebrae. The skull develops through membranous neurocranium, chondrocranium, and viscerocranium components.

Vertebral body forms by fusion of caudal half of one sclerotome with cranial half of the next. Vertebral arch is sclerotome-derived. Annulus fibrosus is sclerotome mesenchyme. Nucleus pulposus is notochord-derived. Membranous neurocranium ossifies intramembranously. Chondrocranium ossifies endochondrally. Viscerocranium is largely pharyngeal arch/neural crest derived. Fontanelles allow molding at birth and brain growth.

steps.title: Why does resegmentation help explain intervertebral muscle and nerve relationships?
steps.body: Combining adjacent sclerotome halves places developing vertebral bodies out of register with the original somite segments. Muscles can then span joints between vertebrae, while segmental nerves emerge through intervertebral regions. The disc occupies a distinct boundary area with annular mesenchyme around notochord-associated tissue. A drawing with one somite becoming one entire vertebra misses this relationship. Follow two neighboring segments through the rearrangement and label muscle and nerve positions alongside the skeletal elements.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: Sclerotome cells surround the notochord and neural tube, then resegment so adjacent halves contribute to each vertebra. This positions intervertebral joints relative to segmental muscles and nerves. The annulus derives from surrounding sclerotomal mesenchyme, while notochordal tissue contributes to the nucleus pulposus. Cranial vault and base use different ossification patterns, and craniofacial tissues have mixed neural-crest and mesodermal origins. Avoid applying one germ-layer rule to every skull bone.
